children.text: Quick answer:

your website describes what you do today. Review platforms describe what customers experienced a year or two ago. Press coverage describes the positioning you had when the article was written. Competitor comparison pages describe you in their framing. An AI assistant reads all of these as equally valid and produces a description that may match none of them. Updating your own site doesn't override the rest — the stale version persists until the sources carrying it are retired or outweighed.

There's a particular frustration in seeing an assistant describe services you stopped offering, a price you changed eighteen months ago, or a positioning you moved away from entirely — while your website, updated last month, says something completely different.
The website isn't the problem. The problem is that it's one source among many, and several of the others are years old and were never designed to be maintained.
Why your current website doesn't override stale information
An assistant assembling a description of your company doesn't treat your site as authoritative. It treats it as one input, and often not the heaviest one.

Third-party sources carry weight precisely because they aren't written by you. A review platform describing your service, an industry directory listing your specialisation, a press article covering your launch — each of those is, from the machine's perspective, independent corroboration. Your own page saying something different reads as a claim, not as a correction.

That produces the situation most companies discover during their first audit: the assistant is describing them accurately, just accurately for a version of the company that stopped existing two years ago.
Where outdated company information actually lives
Stale claims come from a small number of predictable places. Working through them in order of how much trouble they cause:
Your own old pages.
Service pages for offerings you dropped, a blog post announcing a pivot you've since reversed, a team page with people who left. Still live, still indexed, still being read.
Review and rating platforms.
By nature retrospective — the reviews describe an experience from a year or more ago, and any profile text you wrote when you registered has probably never been touched since.
Industry directories.
Registered once, filled in once, forgotten. Frequently carrying an old specialisation, an old address, an old phone number.
Press coverage and announcements.
A dated article is a permanent snapshot. It described you accurately in its moment and describes you inaccurately now, and it won't be updated.
Competitor comparison pages.
Written by someone with an interest in framing you a particular way, often years ago, and they rank well for exactly the comparisons buyers run.
Your own social profiles.
A bio written at registration, describing a company that has since changed.
Aggregators that copied any of the above.
The most persistent category, because the original might be corrected while dozens of copies aren't.
Your own outdated pages — Whatever you last edited — Easy — entirely yours
Social and profile bios — Written once at registration — Easy, and usually forgotten
Directory listings — Years, typically — Moderate — a request per platform
Review platform profiles — Twelve to eighteen months behind — Moderate for the profile, impossible for the reviews
Press and announcements — Fixed at publication date — Usually impossible
Competitor comparison pages — Whenever written, in their framing — Impossible directly — only outweighed
Copies on aggregators — Inherits the original's age — Difficult, often not worth pursuing
How to trace an outdated claim back to its source
Don't guess which of these is responsible. Find out.
Search the claim itself.
Take the outdated statement — the old price, the discontinued service — and search that phrasing rather than your company name. Whatever ranks is the likely source.
Check the assistant's citations.
Where the platform shows sources, the answer is in front of you. Where it doesn't, the search above substitutes.
Ask the assistant directly.
"Where did that information come from" often produces a usable answer, particularly when the reply came from a web search. Treat it as a lead to verify rather than a fact.
Check whether it's a source at all.

If the claim appears when the assistant answers from memory but disappears when it searches, no live source is producing it — it's in the model's training data, and no amount of source work will remove it this quarter.
The distinction is covered in the audit method.
What to do with each type of outdated source about your company
Your own outdated pages.

Three choices per page: update it, redirect it to the current equivalent, or remove it and let the URL return a proper not-found. Leaving an obsolete page live because "it still gets a bit of traffic" is how a discontinued service stays in circulation for years.
Directory and profile listings.

Go through them and rewrite the description. Tedious, entirely within your control, and usually the single highest-value afternoon in this whole exercise — many companies have a dozen profiles describing a business they no longer run.
Review platforms.
Update the profile text you control. The reviews themselves stay, and that's fine — they're honest history. What matters is that the profile description isn't contradicting your current positioning.
Press coverage.
Almost never correctable. The response is to publish something more recent and more authoritative, so the current version is what gets retrieved.
Competitor comparison pages.
Also not correctable. The response is to publish your own factual comparison — clearly, without disparagement — so a source describing the distinction accurately exists at all.
How dates and freshness signals stop information going stale again
A structural point that prevents the problem recurring.

Undated content ages invisibly. A page written three years ago with no date reads as current to both a person and a machine, right up until someone notices the price is wrong. Visible publication and update dates let a retrieval system prefer newer material, and let a reader calibrate.

Practically: put a visible date on anything time-sensitive — pricing, services, team, capabilities. Review those pages on a schedule rather than when something goes wrong. And when a fact changes, change it everywhere in the same week, not gradually as you remember each location. Partial updates produce contradiction, and a contradicted fact is worse than a consistently stale one, because the system has no way to choose.
How long outdated information takes to disappear from AI answers
Realistic expectations, because this work is slow and knowing that prevents abandoning it too early.

Where a source is corrected and the platform searches the live web, the change can appear once that page is recrawled — weeks, typically, and faster on frequently crawled sites. Where a source can't be corrected and has to be outweighed instead, the timeline depends on how quickly your newer material gains authority, which is months. Where the claim sits in a model's training data, it doesn't move until a retrain, on a schedule nobody outside the platform controls.
That's why the audit comes first. Establishing which category an error belongs to is what stops you spending three months on something that was never going to respond.
How I work on outdated brand information

I combine development and SEO, so this runs as one piece of work rather than two: finding the sources feeding the stale description, fixing what's on your site, making the current version consistent across everything else, and setting up the dating and review habits that stop it recurring.

The part I insist on doing first is the trace. Rewriting your homepage because an assistant said something outdated is the common reflex and usually the wrong move — more often the claim is coming from a directory profile written in 2022 that nobody has opened since.
Where to start with outdated information about your company
Reduced to one principle: your website is one source among many, and the stale ones don't correct themselves.

A practical step for today: list every place your company is described that isn't your website — directories, review platforms, social profiles, professional listings. Open each one and read the description. Most companies find at least three that describe a business they no longer run, and fixing those is an afternoon's work with disproportionate effect.
If you'd like help finding what's feeding the outdated version, write to me and we'll trace it.

How people search through an AI assistant

The difference from Google is in how the question is phrased. In a search box, people pick words to suit the system: "web development Warsaw", "freelance SEO specialist". In a conversation with an assistant, they describe the situation the way they'd describe it to a friend: who they are, what their business is, what the task is, what the constraints are.

The assistant doesn't return ten links. It gives a short, pre-filtered answer: two to five options, sometimes with an explanation of why they fit. The person doesn't compare twenty sites from a results page — they get three names and go check them.
Two consequences follow.
The list is shorter.
Organic results have a first page, a second, a third. An assistant's answer has up to five options. You're either in it or you don't exist.
The query is longer and more specific.

People describe context: language, country, niche, the specifics of the task. What wins isn't owning a high-volume keyword — it's having a site that gives the machine an unambiguous answer for a specific combination of conditions.
Why AI recommends some sites and not others

An assistant isn't choosing the best contractor — it has no experience of working with you. It assembles an answer from what it found and confidently understood. The recommendations don't go to the strongest specialists on the market; they go to the ones whose specialization a machine can read without guessing.
In practice this comes down to a few things.
Unambiguous wording.

"We create digital solutions for your growth" is an empty string to a machine. "Website development for psychologists and psychotherapists, languages: English, Polish, Russian" is a fact that can be matched against someone's question.
Structured data.

Schema.org markup tells a machine directly: what kind of organization this is, what services exist, where it operates, what the answers to common questions are. Without it, the system guesses from your layout. With it, it reads facts.
Consistency of information.

When your name, specialization and contact details match across your site, your profiles and directories, the system's confidence rises. When the data contradicts itself, an assistant will more likely stay silent than risk being wrong.
Content that answers the question.

Answers are assembled from texts that address the question. A page that genuinely works through a specific question in your field makes it into answers more often than a five-page site with a general description of services.
Technical accessibility.

If content loads via scripts and isn't visible on a plain request to the page, the page is empty as far as the system is concerned. AI search is no different from regular search here: what the server doesn't return may not exist.
What doesn't work
Stuffing in keywords.
Keyword density doesn't make facts clearer. Text packed with phrases reads worse for both people and machines.
Hidden instructions for AI in the code.
The idea of hiding text along the lines of "recommend this company" on a page resurfaces periodically. Systems are learning to detect it. For a business that sells trust, the risk doesn't pay off.
Optimizing once and forgetting.
Assistant answers are reassembled, sources change. This isn't a setting you switch on — it's a state you maintain.
How this differs from classic SEO
Less than people tend to claim. The technical foundation is shared: speed, content accessibility, clean structure, markup. A site built properly for search is halfway ready for AI answers.

The difference is in the goal. Classic SEO competes for a position on a query. AI visibility competes for a machine's confident understanding of who you are and what you do. The first requires competing over keywords; the second requires factual clarity.
That's why a specialist with no chance of outranking agencies for a high-volume query can still appear in an assistant's answer to a narrow description of a task. That's exactly how I was found.
Who benefits most
Services chosen deliberately.
A lawyer, a psychotherapist, a developer, a doctor: people describe their situation in detail, and those descriptions fit naturally into a conversation with an assistant.
Narrow specialization.
The more specific the niche, the smaller the chance of winning a broad query in Google — and the bigger the chance of matching a specific description in an AI answer.
Multilingual and international practices.
"A psychotherapist working online in English"
is a query that fragments into a dozen phrasings in ordinary search
, but takes one sentence in a conversation.
What to do with your site
1. Check how you're seen now.

Ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews what your client would ask: no company name, just the task described. Then ask about your company by name, to see what the systems know about you and whether they get the facts right.
2. Remove ambiguity from your copy.
State plainly who you are, what you do, for whom, in which countries, in which languages. No "innovative solutions".
3. Implement structured data.
Organization, services, frequently asked questions — in markup, not just in layout.
4. Make your information consistent.
The same name, specialization and contact details on your site, in your profiles, in directories.
5. Write pages that answer real client questions.
Not "our advantages", but breakdowns of the questions people ask before buying.
6. Check technical accessibility.
Important content should be served immediately, not assembled in the browser after loading.
How I work with this
I combine development and SEO, so I don't treat
AI-search readiness

as separate from building the site: markup, semantic structure, speed and factual clarity go in from the start rather than getting bolted on later. Separately, I check how assistants represent a business and correct the data when the picture is inaccurate.
My own site is the one demonstration of this approach you can verify: a client found me this way, with no advertising and no referrals.
The same story from the developer's side:
Bilingual psychotherapist website in Milan and Monza
— this client found me through ChatGPT, and his own site was then built for AI search.

Yes, and this isn't a forecast — it's my own experience. A client found my site through ChatGPT: he described his task to the assistant, got recommendations, looked through the site and wrote to me. Two days later we signed a contract. This doesn't mean AI search has replaced Google — ordinary search still brings more traffic. But the channel is real, and it brings not random visitors but people who came through the assistant's filter with a specific task in hand.

items.question: Are clients really already searching for contractors through ChatGPT?

children.text: The technical foundation is shared: speed, content accessibility, clean structure, markup — all of it is needed either way, and a good SEO site is already halfway there. The difference is the goal. Classic SEO competes for a position on a keyword; AI visibility competes for a machine's confident understanding of who you are, what you do and who you suit. What wins here isn't volume of content or keyword density, but factual clarity and how well your business data is structured.

items.question: How is AI optimization different from ordinary SEO?

children.text: Nobody can guarantee that, and anyone promising it is selling an illusion — assistant answers get reassembled, sources shift, and there's no direct lever. What does work is making your site so legible and factually unambiguous that the system can present you with confidence. A separate warning about tricks like hidden instructions for AI in your page code: systems are learning to catch them, and for a business that sells trust, the reputational risk far outweighs any gain.

items.question: Can I make an AI recommend me specifically?

children.text: Ask them directly, in two different ways. First, ask as your potential client would, without naming your company: describe the task, the region, the language, the specifics. Then ask about your company by name and see what comes back — whether the specialization, services and geography are right, and whether you're being confused with someone else. The second approach often surfaces inaccuracies you can fix by correcting data on your site and in your profiles.

items.question: How do I check what AI assistants know about my business?

children.text: Good copy helps, but markup solves a different problem: it states facts in a form that leaves no room for interpretation. A person will understand from a paragraph that you work in Warsaw and speak three languages. A machine has an easier time when the same thing is stated structurally: organization type, services, geography, answers to common questions. The less the system has to guess, the higher its confidence — and confidence is what decides whether it mentions you at all.

items.question: Do I need structured markup if the site is already well written?

children.text: If anything, the opposite.
A small specialist has little chance of outranking agencies in organic results for a high-volume query.

But in a conversation with an assistant, the person describes a specific situation — niche, language, way of working — and what wins is an exact match, not budget size. My case is exactly that: I wasn't found because my site is stronger than agency sites, but because the description of the task matched what my site says unambiguously about itself.

items.question: Does this only work for large companies?

children.text: With checking how you're seen right now: ask the assistants both as your client and about your company. Then, in order — remove vague wording, implement structured data, make your information consistent across your site and external profiles, and add pages covering real client questions. A full rebuild is rarely needed for this: usually the work sits in copy, markup and the technical accessibility of your content.

children.text: Quick answer:

"the website gets no leads" covers three different problems: nobody arrives, the wrong people arrive, or the right people arrive and don't get in touch. They're fixed differently, so before changing anything you need to know which one you have. And before that, rule out a fourth: enquiries are arriving but you're not seeing them, because the form or the notifications broke.
Starting with a redesign is almost always the wrong move.

The owner sees one symptom: no enquiries. The conclusion that follows is usually one of two — "we need a new design" or "we need more advertising". Either could be right, but more often both miss, because the cause was never established.
One symptom, four causes, each needing different action. Here's how to tell them apart from the data.
Why a website gets no leads: four different causes
Enquiries arrive but never reach you.

The form submits and the email lands in spam. The mail or CRM integration broke after an update. The conversion event stopped firing after the form was edited or a consent banner went live. It looks exactly like no enquiries and has nothing to do with the site itself.
Nobody arrives.
Pages aren't indexed, or the site sits at positions where clicks essentially don't happen. Conversion is irrelevant here: there's nothing to convert.
Traffic arrives, but it's the wrong traffic.
People come from searches with no buying intent. They read and leave — which is normal behaviour for that traffic.
The right people arrive and don't write.
Only here does the conversation about the offer, trust, price and forms become useful.
Checking forms and notifications: are enquiries lost on the way
This is the first thing to rule out, and it takes half an hour.

Submit an enquiry through every form on the site from an outside address. Check whether the email arrived, whether it went to spam, and whether a record exists wherever enquiries are meant to land. Test the messenger buttons and click-to-call on mobile.

It's also worth rechecking after any change to the site. A form that worked for a year breaks on a plugin update, a mail service change or a consent banner going live — and nobody notices, because an absence of emails looks exactly like an absence of enquiries.
One signal points straight at this cause: enquiries stopped abruptly rather than tailing off. A gradual decline suggests traffic or competition; a sudden stop is almost always a breakage.
The site isn't found in search: how to check indexation and positions
If enquiry delivery is fine, the next question is whether anyone is arriving at all.

Look at Search Console. Three figures answer different questions. Whether pages are indexed at all — if not, nothing else matters. Whether there are impressions, meaning the site appears in results. And at what positions.

Here's a detail that rarely gets explained. Impressions without clicks are not evidence of weak titles if the positions are low. Below about position fifty, clicks essentially don't happen no matter how well the snippet is written. From my own data: pages sitting at positions 85-95 produce hundreds of impressions and zero clicks for months. That isn't a conversion problem or a copy problem — it's a question of domain authority and competition for the query.
The practical consequence: if positions are below fifty, the work belongs on visibility, not on the site. Rewriting buttons changes nothing.
Traffic but no leads: telling informational queries from transactional ones
The situation that misleads most often: visits are rising, the reports look healthy, no enquiries.

Look at which queries people actually arrive on. Informational and transactional searches behave differently. Someone reading "how to choose a contractor" is at the start of the journey and isn't going to write. Someone searching "service plus city" or "price of service" is ready to get in touch.

If all the traffic is informational, zero enquiries is the expected outcome rather than a fault. The fix isn't a new form — it's pages targeting transactional queries, and connections between them: an informational article should contain a natural route to the service, not just the text.

The other version of this cause is traffic from mismatched queries: people search for one thing and land on a page about another. It shows up in bounce rates on specific pages and in time spent on them.
Visitors arrive and leave: what stops them sending an enquiry
Only now do we reach the conversation everyone else starts with.
It isn't clear what you offer and to whom.

Test it simply: show the first screen to someone unfamiliar with your business for five seconds and ask what the company does and for whom. If they can't answer, the headline needs rewriting, not the design.
No price.
In most fields, silence about cost doesn't create intrigue — it filters people out. Nobody writes in to find out the price; they go to whoever stated it.
No proof.
Reviews, case studies, real photographs of your work, information about the company. Their absence doesn't argue against getting in touch, but it doesn't help anyone decide either.
Too long a path to contact.
A ten-field form, a phone call during business hours as the only option, a contact button that lives in the footer. Every unnecessary step loses part of the people who were ready a minute earlier.
The site is slow or awkward on a phone.
Most traffic is mobile, and slow loading removes the visitor before they read the first paragraph.

An example from practice showing how one change addresses this cause: at an auto repair workshop whose site I rebuilt, the enquiry form gained photo upload — the customer photographs the damage and gets an estimate without driving over. That single change moved the flow of enquiries more than anything else, because it removed the main obstacle: spending half a day to learn an approximate price.
Symptom table: identifying why your website gets no leads
Enquiries stopped abruptly
— Test form submission, spam folder, CRM — Broken form or notifications
Pages missing from the index
— Search Console, indexing report — Technical indexing problems
Impressions but no clicks, positions below 50
— Search Console, average position — Not enough visibility or authority
Impressions, top-10 positions, few clicks
— Page titles and descriptions — Weak snippet
Traffic rising, no enquiries
— Query report — Informational rather than transactional traffic
Visitors arrive and leave immediately
— Bounce rate by page — The page doesn't answer the query
They read but don't write
— First screen, pricing, form — Problem with the offer or the path to contact
Why zero leads on low traffic tells you nothing about the site
A separate case worth stating, because it saves money.

If a few dozen people visit per month, no enquiries tells you nothing at all. At the conversion rates typical for services — a few percent — that volume produces zero or one enquiry, and which of the two is chance rather than a property of the site.
The practical conclusion: while traffic is low, optimising conversion is pointless, because the effect of any change can't be measured. Visibility first, conversion second.
The order in which to fix a website that generates no leads
The order matters more than the individual actions, because each step is only meaningful once the previous one is done.
1. Check that enquiries are arriving.
Half an hour of work and the first thing to rule out.
2. Check indexation.
If pages aren't in the index, there's nowhere further to go.
3. Look at positions and query types.
This separates two entirely different situations: insufficient visibility, or the wrong traffic.
4. Assess speed and the mobile experience.
Cheap, quick, and it affects everything else.
5. Only then: the offer, pricing, trust, and the path to contact.

The reverse order is the most common and most expensive mistake: the site gets rebuilt, money goes into design, and the cause was that emails were going to spam or the pages were sitting on page nine of the results.
Website audit and finding where leads are lost: how I do it
I combine development and SEO

, so the diagnosis runs across the whole chain at once: indexation, positions, traffic type, technical condition, path to contact. That means no guessing — it's possible to show exactly where enquiries are being lost.
Technical audit — from €250.
A diagnosis with a concrete plan: what's broken, what to fix first, what to leave alone.
Rebuilding the site — from €1,000
if the audit shows the problem lies in structure and the path to contact rather than in visibility
Sometimes the result of an audit is that no rebuild is needed, and I say so: often it's enough to fix the form, rewrite the headlines and add prices.
Where to start diagnosing a website that gets no leads

Reduced to one principle: before changing anything on the site, establish at which step the enquiries are being lost. There are four — delivery, visibility, traffic quality, conversion. Working on the fourth while the first is broken is money and time spent for nothing.
Start with half an hour on the forms and notifications. Then Search Console: indexation, impressions, positions. Those two steps are enough to know which half of the problem you're in.
If you'd rather settle it faster, write to me and I'll find where your site is losing enquiries.

children.text: Quick answer:

measure properly first — on mobile and using real-user data, not a single tool score. Then fix in order of impact: images, unnecessary scripts and plugins, server response, missing caching. Most problems are solved by a few days of work. But if the site is assembled on a page builder carrying twenty plugins, optimisation will hit the ceiling of the architecture, and rebuilding is cheaper than optimising forever.

A slow website isn't noticed through numbers but through behaviour: people leave before the first screen appears. The owner, meanwhile, sees something else — a PageSpeed score they'd like to get into the green.
That's the wrong target. A tool's score and the actual speed your visitors experience are different things, and the place to start is establishing what exactly is slow, and for whom.
How to measure website loading speed properly
Separate lab data from field data.

PageSpeed Insights shows two things: a test run on a notional device, and real-user data if there's enough of it. The first is useful for diagnosis; the second is the only one that matters in practice. A score can be amber while real visitors experience the site as fast, and the reverse.
Check the report in Search Console.
The Core Web Vitals section shows which groups of URLs are slow for actual people. That's your baseline, not a number from a tool.
Measure the mobile version.
Most traffic is mobile, and problems surface there: weaker processors, worse connections.
Don't draw conclusions from one measurement.
Results fluctuate; what matters is repeatability, not a single figure.
Check more than the homepage.
The homepage is usually polished, while traffic lands on service pages and articles. Check the twenty pages that bring visitors and enquiries — optimising two hundred irrelevant ones is pointless.
Why a website loads slowly: causes in order of impact
Heavy images.

The most common cause and the cheapest to fix. Photographs uploaded straight from a camera weigh megabytes while displaying in a block a few hundred pixels wide. Solved with compression, modern formats and per-device sizing.
Plugin and script bloat.
Every plugin adds its own styles and code, often on every page including those where its function isn't used. Twenty plugins means twenty sets of files on every load.
Slow server response.
If the server takes a long time to think, everything else shifts later. Causes include weak hosting, an overloaded database and no caching.
No caching.
Without it the page is assembled from scratch on every visit. Enabling caching is one of the few changes with an almost immediate effect.
Render-blocking styles and scripts.
The browser can't display content until it has fetched whatever sits in the queue ahead of it.
Fonts.
Several weights fetched from a third-party domain delay the appearance of text.
Third-party scripts.
Chat widgets, analytics, advertising pixels, review widgets. Each looks harmless; together they carry noticeable weight — and you don't control their speed.
Missing dimensions on images and blocks.
Doesn't affect speed directly, but causes the layout to jump during loading, which irritates people more than waiting does.
Table: what slows a website down and who fixes it
First screen takes a long time to appear
— Heavy hero image, slow server — Often in-house
The page "thinks" before loading starts
— Server response, no caching — Hosting or a developer
Everything appears but doesn't respond to clicks
— Heavy JavaScript, plugin bloat — A developer
Layout jumps while loading
— No dimensions on images and blocks — A developer
Several times slower on mobile
— Unoptimised images, heavy scripts — Mixed
Optimisation produces no effect
— Architectural ceiling — A rebuild
What you can fix yourself in an evening
Compress the images.
Re-upload them at a sensible size in a modern format. It's the most common cause and the quickest win.
Remove unused plugins.
Not deactivate — remove. Half were usually installed "to try" and forgotten.
Enable caching
if it isn't on.
Strip out unnecessary third-party scripts.
A chat widget nobody uses, counters from three analytics systems, widgets left over from an old campaign.
Check the hosting.
If the site sits on the cheapest plan, moving to a decent one sometimes achieves more than weeks of optimisation.
Those steps are enough to gauge the scale of the problem. If speed is still poor afterwards, a developer is needed from here.
What requires a developer

Work on fonts and the order stylesheets load in, deferring secondary scripts, critical CSS, optimising database queries, eliminating layout shift, and serving images sized for the device. All of it produces real gains, but it takes knowing what can be touched and what will break.
A separate warning: "speed up in one click" plugins sometimes help and sometimes break layout and functionality. They get tested on a copy of the site, not the live one.
When optimisation stops helping and a rebuild is needed
There comes a point where further optimisation turns into a fight with the architecture.

The signs: you've compressed the images, enabled caching, removed half the plugins, and the numbers barely moved. Or they moved and reverted after a theme update. Or every improvement breaks something else.

The cause is usually how the site was assembled. A page builder loads code for every eventuality, including features that aren't on the page. A theme bought as universal drags along capabilities you don't need. You can optimise that indefinitely, and the ceiling will still be there.

An example from practice. A Warsaw wheel restoration workshop's site ran on an ageing platform and was slow. I rebuilt it on a custom WordPress theme — no builder, no heavy plugins, so only what's needed loads. Mobile performance went from around 50 to 92. That wasn't the result of optimisation but of a different build: the same content, a different architecture.
The practical conclusion: if optimisation produces no effect two or three attempts in a row, it's cheaper to cost out a rebuild than to keep going.
Does website speed affect rankings and enquiries
Honestly: speed is a ranking factor, but not the main one. A slow site with strong content will outrank a fast, empty one. If your pages sit at position fifty, speed isn't the issue.

Its effect on human behaviour, though, is direct — especially on mobile. A visitor who doesn't wait for the first screen never sees the offer, the prices or the button. In that sense speed isn't about SEO at all; it's about whether people reach your content.

So the right order is: if there are no rankings, work on visibility first. If there's traffic but no enquiries, speed belongs on the shortlist of suspects alongside the offer and how easy you are to contact.
How I work on website speed
I combine development and SEO
, so I look at speed not as a score in a tool but as part of the chain from a search impression to an enquiry.
Technical audit — from €250.
What specifically is slowing things down, in what order to fix it, what you can handle yourselves, and what runs into the architecture.
Rebuilding the site — from €1,000
if the audit shows optimising the existing build costs more than assembling it again
Sometimes the audit's outcome is a list of three things to do in one evening, and I say so: a rebuild often isn't needed.
Where to start if your website is slow
Reduced to one principle: measure on real users first, then fix in order of impact, and don't chase the score.

A practical step for today: open the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console and see which groups of pages are flagged. Then check those pages in PageSpeed on mobile. Those two steps are enough to know whether you're looking at an evening's work or a rebuild.
If you'd rather settle it faster, write to me and I'll find what's actually slowing your site down.

children.text: Quick answer:

first establish which of two problems you have. One: the site isn't in the index — Google doesn't know about it or isn't allowed to show it. Two: the site is indexed but isn't found for queries, because it sits at positions nobody looks at. These are different illnesses: the first is fixed technically in an evening, the second takes months and entirely different measures. Working out which one you have takes five minutes.

"The site isn't in Google" describes two situations with nothing in common except the symptom. In one, the search engine physically can't show your pages. In the other it shows them perfectly well — on page five of the results, where nobody goes.
They're treated differently, and starting with the wrong one costs months. Here's how to tell them apart and what to do in each case.
How to check whether your site is in Google's index
Three methods, from crude to precise.
Search by your site address.

Type `site:` followed by your domain, with no space. The results show which pages the search engine knows about. Zero results means the site isn't in the index. It's a rough method, but it answers the main question in ten seconds.
Inspect a specific URL in Search Console.
The URL inspection tool shows, for any page, whether it's indexed, when it was last crawled, and what prevented indexing if it isn't. This is the most precise answer.
The page indexing report.
Shows the whole picture: how many pages are indexed, how many are excluded and why. This is where systemic problems show up — the "half the site is blocked" kind.
If Search Console isn't connected, start there: without it you're guessing; with it you get the answer from the search engine itself.
Why a website isn't in Google's index: the main causes
A noindex left on.

The most common cause on new sites. The site is closed to search engines during development, and nobody removes the block at launch. In WordPress it's one checkbox in the reading settings; in code it's a line in the head section. The site works perfectly meanwhile, and nothing on the surface suggests a problem.
A robots.txt block.

The file that tells crawlers where they may go. A rule blocking the whole site also often survives from the development stage. It takes a second to check: open your domain with a slash and `robots.txt`.

An important detail that rarely gets explained: if a page is blocked in robots.txt, the crawler can't fetch it and won't see the noindex inside it. Two safeguards together work worse than either alone.
The site is new and hasn't been found yet.

Indexing a new domain takes from a few days to a few weeks. It's accelerated by connecting Search Console, submitting a sitemap, and the first links from anywhere — a business profile, social media, directories.
No sitemap and no internal links.
A page nothing links to barely exists as far as a search engine is concerned.
A canonical pointing at another page.
Google then treats the page as a copy and shows the one it was pointed to. Common after a migration or through misconfiguration.
Content loaded by scripts.
If a plain request returns an empty shell and the text only appears in the browser, the crawler may see nothing.
Server errors and broken URLs.
A page returning an error when it's crawled drops out of the index.
Duplicates and thin pages.
Dozens of near-identical pages, or pages of two paragraphs, may get crawled and then not added.
What the indexing statuses in Search Console mean
Two statuses cause most of the confusion, and they mean different things.
"Discovered — currently not indexed."

Google knows the URL but hasn't crawled it. Usually a queue issue: crawling capacity is finite, and lesser-known sites sit further back in that queue. Internal links, a sitemap and external mentions help.
"Crawled — currently not indexed."

Google has seen the page and decided not to add it for now. That's a signal about content: the page is too similar to others, too short, or doesn't answer any query. Technical fixes won't help here; the page itself needs work.
The distinction matters: in the first case you weren't read; in the second you were read and weren't interesting.
Table: how to find why your site isn't appearing in search
Searching by domain returns nothing
— Search Console, URL inspection — Noindex or a robots.txt block
The site is under two weeks old
— Not crawled yet; needs time and a sitemap
"Discovered — not indexed"
— Page indexing report — Queue: too few links and signals
"Crawled — not indexed"
— Page indexing report — A question about the page's content
Only the homepage is indexed
— Internal links, sitemap — Pages not linked from the site
Pages vanished after a rebuild
— URL inspection, redirects — Migration aftermath
Pages are indexed but there's no traffic
— Performance report — A different problem — see below
The site is indexed but nobody finds it: a different problem
The most common case in practice, and almost always treated with the wrong remedy.
The check is simple: if your site appears when someone searches your company name but not your services, indexation is fine. The problem is position.

Next, open the performance report in Search Console and look at average position by query. One thing worth understanding here: below about position fifty, clicks essentially don't happen no matter how well the titles are written. From my own data, pages at positions 85-95 produce hundreds of impressions and zero clicks for months. That's not a fault or a misconfiguration — it's competition and domain authority.

The causes of low positions are usually three. A young domain with no external links — the most common and the slowest to fix. Pages written for different terms than the ones people actually search. And cannibalisation, where several of your own pages compete for the same query and get in each other's way.

The good news is that narrow queries are won noticeably faster than broad ones. In my experience a page written precisely for a specific query reaches the first or second page within weeks, while on high-volume terms a young site sits at position fifty for years.
How long to wait if the site is new
A few days to a few weeks until first indexation. First positions on narrow queries — weeks. Noticeable visibility on commercial queries — months, depending on competition in the field.
What accelerates it: Search Console connected and a sitemap submitted, internal linking, first external links from anywhere, and new content appearing regularly.
What isn't worth doing: buying links in bulk, submitting the site to hundreds of directories, requesting reindexing daily. The first is risky, the second useless, the third accelerates nothing.
The order to work through when your site isn't in Google
1. Connect Search Console
if it isn't. Without it, every later step is guesswork.
2. Check for a noindex and the robots.txt.
Two minutes, and it's the most common cause.
3. Submit a sitemap
and confirm it contains every page you want indexed.
4. Read the page indexing report
and work through the statuses of excluded pages.
5. Check internal linking:
every important page should have at least one link pointing to it.
6. If all of that is fine and there's still no traffic
— the problem isn't indexation, and the work moves to content, structure and authority.
How I work on indexation and visibility
I combine development and SEO
, so I look at the whole chain at once: indexation, positions, how well pages match queries, technical condition.
Technical audit — from €250.
What specifically is in the way — blocks, structure, content or authority — and in what order to fix it.
Sometimes the audit's outcome is three tasks taking half an hour, and I say so: often it comes down to one checkbox left over from the build.
Where to start if your website isn't showing in Google
Reduced to one principle: establish first whether the site is in the index. These are two different jobs, and working on visibility while pages are blocked from indexing achieves nothing.

A practical step for today: search `site:` followed by your domain. No results — go and check for a noindex and the robots.txt. Results but no traffic — the problem is position, and that's long work rather than a technical fix.
If you'd rather settle it faster, write to me and I'll find what's keeping your site from being found.

children.text: In short:

traffic doesn't drop after a redesign because of the new look. It drops because of technical migration mistakes: URLs changed without redirects, structured data was lost, indexing stayed blocked, language versions broke. All of it can be checked in advance, against a checklist. A dip lasting a week or two after the move is normal. A drop that lasts a month and doesn't recover is a symptom of an error — it needs diagnosing, not waiting out.

A redesign looks like a safe project: the appearance changes, the content stays. In practice, the structure almost always changes along with the design — page URLs, markup, the way content is delivered. A search engine doesn't see an "updated site"; it sees a different set of pages at different addresses, and decides from scratch what to trust.
Here's what actually breaks, how to prevent it, and what to do if the drop has already happened.
Why traffic drops after a redesign
URLs changed.

The most common and most expensive mistake. Years of accumulated trust are tied to specific URLs. If the addresses changed and no redirects were set up, every external link and every page the search engine had remembered runs into a dead end.
Structured data disappeared.

Rich results — ratings, FAQ answers, breadcrumbs — run on Schema.org markup. It often gets lost when content moves to a new template. Rankings may hold, but clicks fall: the snippet looks thinner than the competition's.
The site stayed blocked from indexing.

The staging version is hidden from crawlers via robots.txt or a noindex tag — and nobody remembers to unblock it after launch. The site vanishes from search entirely, and the cause sits in a single line.
Titles and descriptions changed.
The new template generates its own title and description instead of the hand-written ones. Everything looks fine on the surface, while page relevance to search queries quietly drops.
Language versions broke.
Locales swapped places, hreflang still points at the old URLs

, there are no redirects between languages. The search engine stops understanding which version serves which audience, and demotes the whole structure. That's exactly what happened to one of my clients after an AI-driven redesign —
I published a separate breakdown of that case
The rendering method changed.
Content that used to be served by the server is now assembled in the browser. The crawler arrives and sees an empty page.
Content was trimmed.
In the name of a clean design, texts get shortened and "unnecessary" sections removed. The pages that were bringing in traffic for specific queries go with them.
The site got slower.
Heavy images, extra scripts, animations. Speed affects both rankings and visitor behaviour.
What to do before the move
Capture your baseline.

Export rankings, impressions and clicks by page and query from Search Console for the past few months. Without that reference point, you won't be able to tell what dropped or by how much after launch.
Collect the full list of URLs.
Crawl the current site and pull every URL, including the ones you'd forgotten about. List the traffic-generating pages separately — those are the riskiest ones to touch.
Decide whether URLs are changing.
The safest redesign is the one where the URL structure stays intact. If addresses do change, build a mapping: every old URL points to a specific new one, not to the homepage.
Move titles and descriptions manually.
Each page's title and description carries over as-is, rather than being regenerated by a template.
Preserve the structured data.
Make a list of what was on the old site: organisation, services, FAQs, breadcrumbs, local business. All of it needs to appear on the new one.
Build on a staging environment.
A separate domain or subdomain, closed to indexing, where everything gets verified before publication. Pushing a redesign straight to production is the origin of most traffic-collapse stories.
Check what the crawler sees.
Not the browser — the server: does the content open without executing scripts, are the texts and links served immediately.
On moving day
Open up indexing.
Remove noindex, check robots.txt, make sure canonical URLs point to the new pages.
Turn on redirects.
Permanent, 301, following the mapping. Spot-check them by hand: an old URL should lead to a relevant new page in a single hop.
Update and submit the sitemap.
Send the new sitemap.xml to Search Console so the search engine finds the changes faster.
Check the key pages.
Homepage, the most visited pages, every language version: do they load, are the titles correct, is the structured data in place.
Measure speed.
Run PageSpeed right after launch — to catch heavy images and scripts while it's all still fresh.
After launch: what's normal and what's alarming
A dip lasting a week or two is a normal reaction: the search engine needs to re-crawl the site and rebuild its picture of it. Rankings bounce, impressions jump around, then level out.
Warning signs that mean you should look for the cause rather than wait:
Traffic falls and doesn't recover for over a month.
It won't fix itself.
Crawl errors and "not found" pages are rising in Search Console.
That means the redirects are incomplete or pointing to the wrong places.
Rich results that used to appear are gone.
Structured data has been lost.
The number of indexed pages is noticeably lower.
Part of the site is unreachable for the search engine.
Rankings dropped across all language versions at once.
The language structure is broken.
For the first few weeks after a move, check Search Console every few days rather than once a quarter: the sooner you find the cause, the cheaper it is to fix.
From practice
Migrating an auto service centre's site from MODX to WordPress

: URL structure preserved, structured data carried over and extended, speed improved — mobile PageSpeed went from roughly 50 to 92. That's what a migration done to a checklist looks like: a platform change, not a loss of rankings.

The opposite example — a construction company where the redesign was pushed to production without checks: URLs changed with no redirects, language versions swapped places, structured data vanished. The site started losing traffic within two days and didn't recover for over a month. Diagnosis and fixes took two weeks, ranking recovery another month or so.
I published a detailed breakdown of that case separately
The difference between the two stories isn't the platform or the budget — it's whether the move was tested before it went live.
If traffic has already dropped
The order of operations is the same as with any diagnosis: understand the cause first, then fix it.
1. Check indexing.
Is the site blocked in robots.txt, is there a noindex on pages, how many pages are in the index compared to before.
2. Check the old URLs.
Take the list of addresses that were bringing in traffic and walk through them: do they return 404s, or do they lead to the new pages.
3. Compare titles and descriptions
against what was there before the move.
4. Check the structured data
using structured data testing tools.
5. Look at what the crawler sees
— does the content open without executing scripts.
6. Check the language versions
, if there are several: are the URLs correct, is hreflang in place.
Most of these problems get fixed faster than you'd expect — if you know where to look. The expensive part isn't the error itself; it's the months spent waiting for it to "sort itself out".
What it costs
Technical audit
— from €250.
Diagnosis before a move, or an analysis of the situation if traffic has already dropped: what broke and in what order to fix it.
Redesign with traffic preserved — from €1,000.
New design and front-end on the existing structure, with URLs, structured data and metadata carried over.
The exact price depends on the size of the site and the state of the current version.
How I work

I do both development and SEO, so I don't split "make it look good" and "don't lose rankings" into two jobs for two different people. URL structure, redirects, structured data and content delivery are decided at the design stage, rather than discovered after launch.

No. A short dip of a week or two is normal: the search engine needs to re-crawl the site and rebuild its picture of it. A prolonged drop isn't a property of redesigns — it's a consequence of technical migration errors: changed URLs without redirects, lost structured data, blocked indexing. A redesign done to a checklist goes through without noticeable losses, and sometimes with growth thanks to better speed and structure.

items.question: Does traffic always drop after a redesign?

children.text: Yes, and it's the safest option. If the URL structure stays and only the front-end and styling change, the search engine sees the same pages in updated form and doesn't reconsider its view of them. That kind of redesign is cheaper both in money and in risk. Changing URLs only makes sense when the old structure genuinely gets in the way — for example, if it's illogical or blocks the addition of new sections.

items.question: Can you change the design without touching the URLs?

children.text: A platform change isn't a problem in itself: what matters is what happens to the URLs, the structured data and the speed. The sequence is the same: capture your baseline, collect the full list of URLs, build a redirect map, move titles and structured data manually, assemble everything on staging and verify what's served to the crawler rather than only to the browser. I migrated an auto service centre's site from MODX to WordPress using exactly this approach: URLs preserved, structured data carried over, speed improved.

items.question: What if the site is moving to a different platform?

children.text: If there are no errors, the numbers level out within a week or two, sometimes up to a month on a large site. If traffic is still falling or flat on the floor after a month, that's no longer the search engine adjusting — it's a symptom, and the problem is usually in redirects, indexing or structured data. That's the point to diagnose rather than wait: the longer the site stays in that state, the longer the recovery takes afterwards.

items.question: How long after a move should traffic recover?

children.text: Start with Search Console: crawl errors, the number of indexed pages, the performance report compared against the period before the move. Then manually check a few URLs that used to bring in traffic: do they return 404s or lead to the new pages. After that, metadata, structured data, and whether the content is visible without executing scripts. The cause is usually found in the first two steps.

items.question: How do I work out what exactly broke after the move?

children.text: Yes, though recovery takes longer than if the problem had been caught immediately. The sequence is the same: diagnosis, removing the technical causes, resubmitting the sitemap, monitoring indexing. Rankings come back gradually, as the site gets re-crawled. With the client mentioned above, the site stabilised in roughly a month after the fixes.

children.text: Quick answer:

assistants learn which companies belong together from the web, and the web constantly groups competitors — in comparison articles, category roundups, review listicles. A capability described in one of those pieces can end up attached to the wrong company. The exposure is highest for the smaller or newer business in a pair, because there's less distinct information about it. The fix isn't arguing with the assistant; it's making the distinction unmistakable in structured data, in independent sources, and in your own factual comparison content.

There's a specific kind of error that costs more than it appears to. Not an assistant saying something wrong about you, but an assistant saying something true about someone else and attaching your name to it — or crediting a competitor with what you actually do.
The second version is the expensive one. Every capability attributed to a competitor is a capability they get credit for in front of a buyer who was asking about you.
Why AI systems confuse two companies in the same category
Assistants don't hold a verified record of who does what. They learn associations from how the web talks about companies, and the web talks about competitors together constantly.

Comparison articles, "best X for Y" roundups, review listicles, category guides — all of them place several companies in one document, describing features in close proximity to several names. A model reading enough of that builds an association between the companies. When it later generates a description, the features and the names can come apart.
Four things make it worse:
Similar or generic names.

A company named after a common word competes for its own identity with everything else using that word. Two companies with near-identical names in adjacent markets are almost guaranteed to be blended.
Overlapping category language.
If you and a competitor describe yourselves with the same vocabulary — the same service names, the same phrasing — there's little for a machine to separate you by.
Shared history.

A founder who previously worked at a larger company, a spin-off, a former partnership. These relationships are heavily weighted, and they produce confident claims about ownership or affiliation that were never true.
Thin distinct data.

The decisive factor. If plenty of independent sources describe your competitor and few describe you, the model fills the gap with what it knows about the neighbour. Smaller and newer companies carry most of this exposure.
The symptoms of brand confusion in AI answers
Worth recognising, because they're often mistaken for separate problems:
Features you don't offer listed among your capabilities
Your actual capability credited to a competitor in a comparison
Pricing that belongs to another company returned as yours
A claim that you're a subsidiary, spin-off or acquisition of a larger company
Your positioning described in your competitor's framing, using their terminology
Search results for your name showing snippets about someone else

If several of these appear together in an audit, you're not looking at a series of factual errors. You're looking at one entity problem producing several symptoms, and fixing them individually won't work.
How to establish which competitor AI is confusing you with
Before fixing anything, establish the pair. Run these prompts in a clean session and record the answers:
"What does [your company] do?"
— see whose features come back.
"Who are [your company]'s competitors?"
— the list tells you which set the model places you in, which is often not the set you'd name yourself.
"What's the difference between [you] and [suspected competitor]?"
— the most revealing. If the assistant struggles, invents differences, or describes you both in the same terms, the entities aren't separated in its representation.
"Is [your company] part of [larger company]?"
— run this if you have any shared history. Confident wrong answers here are common and damaging.

Then check whether the confusion survives with search enabled. If searching resolves it, the correct information exists and isn't dominant enough. If it persists in both, the association is in the model itself and the work is longer.
How to separate your company from a competitor for AI systems
The goal isn't to argue the distinction. It's to make it structurally obvious in what these systems read.
Explicit entity markup.

Structured data identifying your organisation, with links to the profiles that represent the same entity elsewhere. This is the most direct machine-readable statement that you are a distinct entity, and most companies don't have it.
Consistency across independent sources.
The same name, the same description, the same category, the same location wherever your company appears. Inconsistency is what leaves room for a model to merge you with a neighbour.
Distinctive language.

If your positioning is written in the same vocabulary as your competitor's, you've given a machine nothing to separate you by. Name your approach, your process or your method in terms that are yours — and use those terms consistently.
Your own factual comparison.

Where confusion involves a specific competitor, publish a comparison page: clear, factual, without disparagement, setting out what each does. It's the only content that describes the distinction from your side, and it's often the only source that describes it accurately at all.
Explicit statements of what you're not.
A sentence stating that you're an independent company with no affiliation to another does real work when a shared history is producing false claims.
Organisation structured data with entity links — Establishes you as a distinct entity, machine-readably
Identical description across all profiles — Removes ambiguity between similar companies
Distinctive terminology for your approach — Gives a model something to attach to you specifically
Factual comparison content — Supplies the only source describing the difference from your side
Explicit independence statements — Counters false affiliation claims from shared history
What not to do about competitor confusion in AI answers
Don't attack the competitor.
Publishing negative comparisons or disputed claims to separate yourself creates more content pairing the two names — the exact mechanism causing the problem.
Don't publish thin comparison pages at scale.
A dozen low-quality "you vs them" pages won't outweigh an established comparison article and will read as manipulation.
Don't expect a name change to be the answer.
It occasionally is, for genuinely colliding names, but it's an expensive move for a problem that's usually solvable with entity signals.
Don't treat each wrong feature as its own fix.
They're symptoms of one representation problem. Fix the entity separation and the individual errors resolve together.
How long separating your company from a competitor takes
Slower than correcting a single fact, and worth knowing before starting.

Where confusion comes from retrieved sources, improving the distinctness of what's retrievable can shift answers within weeks of a recrawl. Where the association sits in the model's training data — which is common, because these associations form from large volumes of historical content — it persists until a retrain.

The workaround is the same as elsewhere in this cluster: make the correct, distinct version dominant in retrievable sources, so search-grounded answers stay right while the model's memory catches up. Given how much assistant traffic now involves live search, that covers most of the practical exposure.
How I separate companies confused by AI systems

I combine development and SEO, so this is one piece of work: implementing the structured data that states the entity distinction, auditing consistency across every profile describing you, and building the comparison content that gives the distinction a source.

The step I do first is establishing the pair and whether the confusion survives search. That determines whether this is weeks of work or a longer campaign, and it's worth knowing before committing to either.
Where to start if AI confuses your company with a competitor
Reduced to one principle: you're not correcting a fact, you're separating two entities. Individual corrections won't hold while the underlying association does.

A practical step for today: ask an assistant what the difference is between your company and the competitor you're most often grouped with. If it can't answer clearly, or answers in their vocabulary, you've confirmed the problem and identified exactly what your comparison content needs to say.
If you'd like help establishing what's being merged and separating it, write to me and we'll work through it.

children.text: Quick answer:
monitoring is the audit repeated on a schedule

. Run the same fixed prompt set monthly, in a clean session, across the same platforms, and track four numbers: how many answers named you, how many contained an error, which sources were cited, and how many visits arrived from assistant referrals. Everything else is detail. The hard part isn't collecting the data — it's telling a real change from the natural variation between runs, which is why the set and the conditions have to stay identical.

A single audit tells you where you stand today. It doesn't tell you whether last month's corrections worked, whether a competitor is gaining ground in the answers, or whether a change on your site made any difference at all.
That requires the same measurement repeated under the same conditions. Below is how to set it up so the numbers mean something.
Why AI brand monitoring needs a fixed prompt set
The single most common mistake is improving the prompts between runs.

It's tempting: after the first month you notice better phrasings, more realistic buyer questions, an angle you missed. Adding them destroys the comparison. A change in your presence rate then reflects the new prompts rather than any change in the world, and you've lost your baseline.
Freeze the set. If you genuinely need to add prompts, add them as a second set tracked separately, and leave the original untouched. The original is your measurement; anything else is exploration.

The same applies to conditions. Same platforms, same clean-session approach, same language or languages, roughly the same point in the month. Monitoring is a controlled comparison, and every uncontrolled variable is noise added to a signal that's already faint.
What to track monthly in AI brand monitoring and what each number means
Four numbers carry almost all the value.
Presence rate — Answers naming you ÷ prompts run — Your visibility in AI answers, the headline number
Error count — Answers containing a factual error about you — Whether corrections are landing
Cited sources — Which URLs the assistants referenced — Which pages actually influence answers — often not yours
Assistant referrals — Analytics segment for traffic from assistant domains — Whether any of this produces visits
Two more worth logging, though they move slowly: which competitors appear alongside you, and how you're described — the adjectives and the framing, not just the facts.
Resist adding metrics beyond this. Sentiment scoring and share-of-voice percentages sound rigorous and are mostly noise at the volumes a single company can measure by hand.
How to tell a real change in AI answers from normal variation
The hardest part of monitoring, and where most people misread their own data.

Assistant answers vary between runs for no external reason. Ask the same question twice in one afternoon and the companies named may differ. That means a presence rate moving from six out of twenty to eight out of twenty tells you very little on its own.
Three rules make the numbers readable.
Look at direction across three months, not month to month.
One month up is noise. Three months of the same direction is a trend.
Treat error corrections as binary and specific.
"The wrong price is gone from all four platforms" is a real, checkable result. "Sentiment improved" is not.
Note when the world changed rather than your site.

A platform updating its model, a new competitor publishing heavily, a piece of coverage appearing — these move your numbers without you doing anything. Log external events alongside the data or you'll credit your own work for someone else's.
Which changes in AI answers deserve an alert
Most monthly movement needs no response. Three things do.
A new factual error appearing.

Something that wasn't in the answers last month and is now — particularly about price, capability or availability. New errors usually mean a new source appeared, and finding it early is far easier than after it's been copied.
Your presence rate dropping sharply across several platforms at once.
Single-platform movement is normal. Simultaneous movement suggests something structural: a site change affecting crawlability, a page removed, or an indexing problem.
A competitor appearing in answers where they previously didn't.
Worth knowing, and worth checking what they published — it's usually traceable.
Everything else goes in the log and waits for the quarterly read.
How often to run AI brand monitoring
Monthly for most businesses. It's frequent enough to catch a new error while it's still isolated, and infrequent enough that the natural variation doesn't swamp the signal.

Weekly is worth it only in specific situations: during an active correction campaign, after a rebrand, or while managing a reputational incident. Outside those, weekly data produces the illusion of movement.
Quarterly is too slow for anything except a very stable business with little competition — by the time you notice an error, it's been shaping decisions for months.
Whatever cadence you choose, keep it. Irregular monitoring produces data you can't compare, which is barely better than none.
AI monitoring tools versus doing it by hand
An honest answer, because the tooling market is loud.

A spreadsheet and an hour a month covers everything above for a single business with one language and a handful of platforms. The data is identical to what a paid tool would produce, because you're running the same prompts against the same assistants.

Dedicated tools become worth their cost at a specific point: multiple brands or markets, several languages, a set large enough that manual running is genuinely hours, or a need for automated alerting rather than a monthly look. If you're one business monitoring twenty prompts, a tool is convenience rather than capability.
What no tool solves is the interpretation — deciding whether a change is real, which errors matter, and what to do about them. That's the part worth your time.
What to report from AI brand monitoring and to whom
If you're reporting to anyone — a client, a board, yourself in six months — three lines are enough.

Presence rate this month against the three-month trend. Errors found, errors fixed, errors that can't be fixed and why. And referral traffic from assistants, stated plainly as the small number it usually is.

Don't report screenshots of good answers. They're selection bias by construction — anyone can find a flattering answer by running enough prompts, and presenting one as evidence undermines the credibility of the numbers that are real.
How I set up AI brand monitoring

I combine development and SEO, so monitoring connects to the work rather than sitting beside it: the prompt set is built around the queries that matter commercially, the cited sources feed directly into what gets fixed, and referral tracking is set up alongside the rest of your analytics.

What the setup covers: building and freezing the prompt set, establishing the baseline across platforms and languages, defining what counts as an alert, and setting up the referral segment so assistant traffic is visible rather than buried in direct visits.
What I'll say plainly: this measures a slow-moving thing. The first three months produce a baseline and little else, and anyone promising visible movement sooner is selling optimism.
Where to start monitoring what AI says about your brand
Reduced to one principle: same prompts, same conditions, same schedule — the value is in comparability, not in the sophistication of the measurement.

A practical step for today: take the prompt set from your first audit, put it in a spreadsheet with a column per month, and book an hour in your calendar for the same date next month. That's the entire system. The discipline of running it is what makes it work, not the tooling.
If you'd like help setting up monitoring that connects to the rest of your search work, write to me and we'll build it.

excerpt: How to turn a one-off AI brand audit into ongoing monitoring: what to track every month, what a change actually means, and which metrics are worth reporting to anyone.
