children.text: Quick answer:

a builder is the right call when the task is minimal — establishing a presence, testing an idea, collecting enquiries from ads. Custom development is what you need when the site has to bring in clients from search, work in several languages, hold a filterable catalogue, or integrate with your systems. The thing to compare isn't price but the ceiling: a builder is cheaper at the start, but hitting its limits a year in costs more than building for the job from the outset.

The builder-versus-custom debate is usually framed around price: one is cheap, the other isn't. That's the wrong frame. Price is a consequence. What you should be comparing is the ceiling — how far a solution carries your task, and what happens when you reach its limit.
Below is an honest breakdown of both, without campaigning for either. I build custom sites, so I have an obvious interest — which is why I'll start with where builders genuinely win.
When a website builder is the right choice
There are situations where hiring a developer makes no sense, and it's worth saying so plainly.
You're testing an idea.
There's no certainty yet that the service sells, that the niche is yours, that the model works
. Putting a page together on Squarespace or Wix over a weekend and running ads is more sensible than investing in building something that may not be needed.
The site just needs to exist.
Clients come from referrals, social media or offline, and the site is confirmation that you're real: address, services, contact. Search isn't a channel you're counting on.
The budget is genuinely tight.
If the choice is between a builder and no website at all, the builder wins. It isn't ideal, but it works.
You want to change everything yourself, often.
Some business owners edit their site weekly and enjoy it. A builder gives that freedom with no intermediary.
In all of these cases, custom development means paying for capabilities you won't use.
Website builder limitations: where the ceiling starts
Problems begin when the site stops being a formality and has to bring in clients. That's when limits appear that weren't visible at the start.
Technical SEO.

Builders give you the basics: title, description, sometimes a sitemap. But Schema.org structured data, precise control over canonical URLs, control of heading structure, steering indexation of individual sections — that's where the freedom ends. In a competitive market that ceiling is enough to keep you below a certain position regardless of how good your content is.
Speed.

A builder is universal, so it loads code for every eventuality, including features your page doesn't have. Hence unnecessary scripts, unoptimised images and weak Core Web Vitals, which affect both rankings and visitor behaviour. With custom development this is solved at the architecture level:
when I moved an auto service business from a legacy platform to a custom-built theme
, its mobile performance score went from around 50 to 92 — not through magic, but because only what's needed gets loaded.
Multilingual setup.

Formally, language versions exist almost everywhere. In practice, the correct technical connection between versions — separate addresses and markup telling search engines which version serves which audience — is either poorly implemented or locked behind paid extensions. The typical result is language versions competing with each other instead of each serving its own market. For any business selling across borders, that's a direct loss.
Catalogues, filters, integrations.

The moment you need a catalogue filtered by several parameters, synchronisation with your CRM, a client portal, or a non-standard pricing calculator, a builder either can't do it or does it through workarounds that break on updates.
Readiness for AI search.

More and more people look for suppliers and services through ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI answers. Appearing in those answers depends on how unambiguously your site states its facts to a machine: structured data, clean semantics, content accessible without executing scripts. Builders give you exactly the markup their platform's developers anticipated, and adding your own usually isn't possible.
AI-generated websites: the third option and its risks

The choice used to be binary. Now there's a third path: generate the site with AI. It deserves a separate warning, because it looks like the best of both worlds — the speed of a builder with the flexibility of code.

The tool is genuinely powerful; I use AI in my own work every day. The problem isn't the tool, it's the absence of oversight. AI does exactly what it's told, but it doesn't know that you can't change a URL structure without redirects, that you can't lose structured data, that you can't swap language versions around. One of my clients learned this in practice: after an AI-generated redesign was pushed straight to the live site, traffic started falling within two days and didn't recover for over a month. I've written that case up separately.
The conclusion is straightforward: AI is excellent as an accelerator under expert oversight and dangerous as a replacement for one.
What a website builder actually costs

A builder is cheaper at the start, but its cost isn't one-off. The platform subscription, paid extensions for whatever isn't in the base plan, separate charges for language versions or for lifting limits — over two or three years that adds up to a figure comparable with custom development.

The second expense arrives when you move. Sites built on a builder can rarely be transferred whole: the markup is proprietary, the export partial, the URL structure often changes. So you're paying not for a migration but for a new website plus the work of moving without losing rankings — which is more expensive than building for the job in the first place.
Hence a practical conclusion: if you already know that in a year or two you'll need a catalogue, language versions or serious SEO, a builder at this stage isn't a saving. It's a deferred cost.
Signs your business has outgrown its builder
Indicators that a builder has stopped coping:
Rankings aren't improving even though you've improved the content and it's objectively better than that of competitors ranking above you.
Speed scores won't rise no matter what you do with images.
A feature you need can't be built — only something "similar", or via a third-party extension with a monthly fee.
Language versions bring no traffic despite good translations.
Every small change requires working around the platform's limits.
If two or three of those apply, the question is no longer whether to change your setup, but when and at what cost.
The price of a builder versus custom development
Builder: platform subscription plus extensions, typically a few hundred euros a year, plus your own time assembling it.

Custom development: a simple landing page — €700-1,400; a conversion landing page with full search and AI optimisation — from €2,000; a multi-page website — from €2,000; a redesign of an existing site — from €1,000.
Comparing those figures directly is misleading: they're different products for different jobs. The right question isn't "which is cheaper" but "what horizon am I planning this site for".
How to choose between a builder and custom development: three questions
Will search be a channel for winning clients?
If yes, a builder will limit you at a technical level and no amount of content will get around it. If not, and your clients come from elsewhere, the limitation won't touch you.
Do you need a catalogue, integrations or language versions?
A filterable catalogue, CRM synchronisation, proper multilingual setup — that's the line where builders end.
What's your planning horizon?
A site for six months to test a hypothesis and a site meant to be your main sales channel for five years are different jobs, and they don't need to be solved with the same tool.
How I build websites for a specific job
I combine development and SEO, so the technical base — markup, speed, structure, AI-search readiness — is designed in from the start rather than bolted on later.
That same combination lets me say honestly in a first conversation that a builder will cover your task, if it genuinely will. Taking on a project a client doesn't need serves neither side.
Website builder or custom development: what to choose

A builder — when the task is minimal, the horizon short, and search isn't part of the plan. Custom development — when the site has to bring in clients, work in several languages, hold a catalogue or integrate with your systems.

The mistake isn't starting with a builder. The mistake is staying on one after your business has outgrown it, and spending year after year blaming flat growth on your copy when the real limit is the platform.
If you're unsure which situation you're in, write to me and we'll look at your site and your goals together. If it turns out a builder is all you need, I'll tell you that.

excerpt: An honest comparison of website builders and custom development: when a builder is genuinely the right call, where its technical ceiling begins, and how to recognise that your business has outgrown it.

children.text: Quick answer:

a real estate agency website isn't a brochure — it's a working catalogue. The essentials: filters that match how buyers actually search, full property pages with galleries and maps, an enquiry option at every point of interest, dedicated pages for locations and property types so search engines have something to rank, multilingual versions when buyers are international, and the technical base — speed, mobile, structured data. Everything else sits on top of that.

A real estate agency website differs from most business websites in one way: nobody reads it, people search inside it. A visitor doesn't arrive to learn about your company — they arrive to find a property, and they leave within a minute if they can't narrow the results to their criteria.

Hence the governing principle: a working search structure first, visual design on top of it. An attractive site with an awkward catalogue loses the visitor in a minute, and no amount of design compensates. That doesn't mean looks don't matter — property is chosen with the eyes, and how a listing is presented directly affects whether someone gets in touch. But the order is what it is.
Here's the checklist of what a site needs to actually do its job.
A filterable catalogue is the core
Everything else is built around it. Filters should reflect how people search, not how your internal database happens to be organised.

The minimum: property type, location, price, size, bedrooms, floor. Beyond that it depends on the market. For coastal and resort markets, distance to the sea and the view are decisive. For investment buyers, rental yield and completion status matter most. In markets where a purchase qualifies for residency, the qualifying price threshold is the first filter such a buyer applies — and if your catalogue can't express it, they'll go somewhere that can.
Three things separate a working catalogue from a nominal one:
Filters update without a page reload.
The user changes criteria and sees results immediately. Every reload loses a share of visitors.
Filtered results have a shareable link.

Someone should be able to send a shortlist to their partner or come back to it tomorrow. Technically this means filter parameters live in the page address — which also opens the door to search queries like "two-bedroom apartments near the sea under €300,000".
Empty results aren't a dead end.
If nothing matches, offer the nearest alternatives or a subscription to new listings. Otherwise the visitor leaves.
The property page
This is where someone decides to contact you.
Plenty of quality photographs
and a floor plan. For buyers purchasing from abroad who won't view in person before a deposit, a video walkthrough answers half the questions they'd otherwise have to ask.
A map with the location
, or at least the area if the exact address is withheld until contact. For resort property, distances to the sea, the airport and the nearest town are among the first things a buyer looks for.
Complete specifications

with no "enquire for details": size, floor, condition, year built, what's included in the price, parking, running costs, and the form of ownership — which matters a great deal to foreign buyers unfamiliar with local law.
The price visible
, ideally in two currencies when buyers are international. A hidden price filters out more genuine buyers than competitors.
An enquiry form on the listing itself
— not a link to a contact page. And a messenger button beside it: some buyers never fill in forms, and someone abroad may have no practical way to call a local number.
Similar properties below
keep the visitor on site when a specific listing doesn't fit.
Enquiry capture at every point of interest
A single form on the contact page is the most common leak. People are ready to write at the moment of interest, not after navigating your site.

An enquiry should be available on the property page, in filtered results (as a subscription to new listings matching those criteria), on location pages, and as a separate matching request — "tell us what you're looking for and we'll find options" — for visitors who found nothing on their own.

Messengers matter more here than in most industries. For a buyer in another country, WhatsApp is often easier than an international call, and time zones make asynchronous contact the norm rather than the exception.
Pages for locations and property types

The catalogue itself brings almost no search traffic: dynamic filter pages index poorly and contain no text that answers a person's question. Which raises a fair question — why build separate pages if the properties are already in the catalogue? Because people don't search for "a catalogue". They search for something specific: an area, a property type, a segment.

What works is a structure of dedicated pages matching how people phrase their search. "Apartments in [area]", "villas near the sea", "new-build developments", "property qualifying for residency". Each with a selection of listings and substantive text: infrastructure, transport links, who the area suits, price range, and what's specific about buying there.
This is the long tail that brings people with concrete intent — and realistically the only way to compete in search against portals, which are unbeatable on broad generic queries.
Multilingual, when buyers are international
For agencies in resort and cross-border markets this isn't optional. Buyers search in their own language, and without a version in it they never reach you at all.

One thing worth understanding: translation is half the job. The other half is technical. Each language version needs its own address and correct markup telling search engines which audience it's for. Without that, language versions compete against each other instead of each serving its own market — the usual reason a multilingual site delivers less traffic than a single-language one.
The Cyprus agency I work with runs on four languages set up this way, and its buyers come from more than twenty countries.
Trust and explaining the process
Property is a large purchase, often made remotely, frequently in an unfamiliar jurisdiction. What reduces the anxiety:
Agent profiles
with photos, contact details and the languages they speak. People contact a person, not an abstract company.
Client reviews
, ideally noting what was bought and where the buyer came from.
Licences and professional association membership
, displayed clearly.
A thorough explanation of the buying process for a foreign buyer.

Transaction stages, required documents, taxes and fees, timelines, whether a purchase can be completed remotely by power of attorney, and what the purchase means for residency. This both removes fear and earns strong search traffic — people research these questions long before they choose a specific property.
Your own site versus portals
Portals give you a fast start, and abandoning them entirely rarely makes sense. But two limitations are worth understanding.

First, you pay per contact and don't own the audience — traffic, data and repeat business stay with the portal. Second, your listing always sits beside competitors', so the choice is made on price rather than on trust in your agency.

Your own site solves both, but doesn't replace a portal overnight. The sensible strategy is running both channels while steadily growing the share of traffic you own, so you're not exposed to someone else's pricing and rules.
The technical base
The invisible part, without which none of the above works.
Speed.
Catalogues are heavy: many images, filters, maps. Without optimisation the site loads slowly, and people don't search on a slow site — they leave it.
Mobile.
Property gets browsed on phones: in transit, on the sofa, and while on holiday in the country they're buying in. Filters and galleries have to be comfortable there specifically.
Structured data.

Markup for listings and the organisation helps search engines understand the content and helps AI assistants recommend you in their answers. People increasingly ask ChatGPT or Perplexity things like "an agency on the coast that works with international buyers", and whether you appear depends on how unambiguously your site states where you operate and who you serve.
Synchronisation with your listing database.

If properties live in a CRM or get exported to portals, the site should update automatically. Manual duplication eventually drifts, leaving sold properties live — the most irritating outcome for a buyer, who picks a property, writes to you, and learns it's gone.
Common mistakes
A catalogue with no filters, or token ones.
A list of three hundred properties with no way to narrow it isn't a catalogue.
Price on request.
It filters out more buyers than it protects you from competitors.
Listings only on portals, with the site as a brochure.
Then all the traffic and client data belong to the portal.
Outdated listings.
A sold property in the results undermines trust in the whole catalogue.
A form only on the contact page.
The enquiry belongs where the interest arose.
Language versions without the technical setup.
Translated text without correct markup performs worse than not having it.
What it costs
An agency site with a catalogue falls into the multi-page bracket — from €2,000, with a redesign of an existing site from €1,000.

The final figure depends on the number of listings, filter complexity, CRM integration and how many languages you need. A detailed breakdown is in the separate article on real estate agency website costs.
How I approach it

I combine development and SEO, so the catalogue structure, location pages and technical base get designed together rather than in sequence. For the Cyprus agency that produced a four-language catalogue with filters matching real search criteria, dedicated pages for areas and property types, and a stream of organic visits where nearly every enquiry is a qualified one.
Where to start
Reduced to a single principle: the site works when a visitor can quickly find a suitable property and contact you at that exact moment.

Start not with design but by establishing the criteria your buyers actually search by. For a resort market that's proximity to the sea, the view and completion status; for a city market, the district, floor and transport; for investment buyers, yield and any residency threshold. Those criteria become your catalogue filters and, at the same time, the basis for dedicated location and segment pages. Everything else — styling, company sections, a blog — goes on top of a structure that already works.
If you'd like to know what your current site is missing, write to me and we'll look at it together.

excerpt: A practical checklist for a real estate agency website: which sections and features are essential, what separates a working catalogue from a good-looking brochure, and the mistakes that most often cost agencies enquiries.

children.text: Quick answer:

the build itself takes days. A landing page with a settled structure and finished copy comes together in a few working days; a company site of five to fifteen pages in one to two weeks of actual work. Calendar time from the first conversation to launch is longer: usually two to three weeks for a landing page and four to eight for a company site. The gap between those numbers isn't work — it's waiting for copy, photographs, replies and decisions. With materials prepared and one person deciding, a landing page can go live in a week.
When people ask how long a website takes, they usually have one number in mind. In practice there are two, and the gap between them is wider than it looks.

Development is rarely the bottleneck: code gets written predictably and quickly. Projects stall for a different reason — waiting for copy, photographs, or a decision nobody is available to make. So the timeline quoted to a client is made of work plus idle time, and the second part is usually the larger one.
Below is a breakdown of both: how long the build itself takes, what makes up the calendar time, and what you can prepare in advance to close the gap.
The build and the calendar: two different numbers
The build itself is days.

A landing page with an approved structure and finished copy comes together in a few working days. A five-to-fifteen page company site takes one to two weeks of actual work. It's the most predictable and most controllable part of the project.
Calendar time is weeks.

From the first conversation to launch: discussing the brief, copy and materials, design and approvals, development, testing. Usually two to three weeks for a landing page, four to eight for a company site.
The gap between them is waiting.
Not build complexity, not the contractor's workload — idle time: a week for copy promised "tomorrow", three days for a mockup to be approved, waiting on photographs from a photographer.

Which gives the practical conclusion worth the whole article: calendar time shrinks not by speeding up development but by removing the pauses. With materials ready, one person deciding and quick replies, a landing page can realistically launch in about a week — and that isn't quality traded for speed, it's the absence of gaps.
What makes up the calendar time: the stages
Reference points for a project of moderate complexity at a normal approval pace.
Discussing the brief and structure — a few days to a week.
Goals, audience, what the site has to do, which pages are needed and how they connect. The stage that saves weeks later if it's done properly.
Copy and materials — a week to several weeks.
The least predictable stage, because it doesn't depend on the contractor. More on this below.
Design and mockups — one to three weeks.
Depending on how many unique page layouts there are and how many rounds of revision.
Development — one to four weeks.
Build, functionality, integrations, populating content, configuring the admin panel.
Testing and launch — a few days to a week.
Checks across devices, speed, forms, markup, indexation.
Add them up and you get the four to eight weeks for a company site. A landing page follows the same path, just shorter: usually two to three weeks.
Brief and structure
— Few days — a week — Both sides
Copy and materials
— A week — several weeks — The client
Design and mockups
— 1-3 weeks — The contractor, revisions with the client
Development
— 1-4 weeks — The contractor
Testing and launch
— Few days — a week — The contractor
Why calendar time is more often missed by the client
This isn't a complaint — it's a consequence of how the process works.

A contractor can't finish the services page without knowing what goes on it. Can't assemble a project section without photographs. Can't move on until a mockup is approved. Each of those moments halts not one task but the whole chain, because the stages are linked.

The most common story goes like this: the project starts briskly, hits the copy after a week — copy the client promised "tomorrow" — and sits for three weeks. In the report it looks like a long build, though there were five days of work in it.

A separate word on revisions. One or two rounds are a normal part of the process. A fifth round with a change of concept is a new project paid for as the old one, and it always comes out of the timeline.
Why copy is needed before design, not after
The common sequence — "design it first, we'll write something later" — sounds logical and costs weeks.

A layout built around real copy and a layout built around placeholder text are different things. When the real copy arrives it turns out to be longer or shorter, the heading doesn't fit two lines, and the advantage the design promised isn't in the text at all. Reworking the layout starts, and reworking the build follows.
The reverse order saves time twice over: the designer works with actual content, and the page structure grows out of meaning rather than the other way round.
The practical conclusion: if there's no copy, it's better to push the start back a week and prepare it than to formally begin and block the project for a month.
What to prepare before the start to shorten the build
A checklist that genuinely shortens calendar time — in my experience often by half.
Copy for each page
, or at least the key points: what the service is, who it's for, how it differs, what it costs, what happens next.
Photographs.
Your work, your premises, your team. In most fields real photographs persuade more than any copy, and preparing them takes longer than expected.
Logo and brand colours
, if you have them, in source files.
Access credentials:
domain, hosting, analytics, the old site. It usually turns out the access sits with a previous contractor, and that's a separate week-long story.
A list of services
in the form you want to sell them, not the form they exist in your head.
Reviews and credentials:
certifications, licences, memberships, case studies.
One person who decides.
The most underrated item. Sign-off through three managers with different tastes extends a project more reliably than any technical complexity.
What extends a website build beyond plan
Scope changes mid-project.
"While we're at it, let's add another section" — each addition drags structure, design and testing along with it.
Multiple approvers.
Every additional participant adds a revision round and time spent gathering opinions.
Waiting on third parties.
A photographer, a copywriter, a lawyer, a data provider — they run on their own schedules.
Integrations.
Connecting to a CRM, payments or a booking system depends on someone else's API and its documentation; timelines here are harder to predict.
Migration from an old site.
If the site has rankings, moving it means not just a transfer but a redirect map, preserved markup and verification after launch. Add a week or two minimum, and cutting corners here is dangerous.
Language versions.
Each is not only translation but a separate structure and separate testing. What multiplies isn't just the volume of text but the checking.
Can a website be built faster, and what does that cost
It can, and there are two honest ways.
Reduce the scope.
Launch fewer pages and add the rest afterwards. This works well: the site starts earning sooner, and you learn what's actually needed.
Prepare in advance.
Everything in the checklist above. It's the only way to shorten the timeline without losing anything.
And two approaches that look like speed but aren't: skipping testing, and
taking a template instead of a structure built for the task
. The first means visitors find the bugs. The second can be a reasonable decision, but it's a different product rather than the same one delivered sooner.
Separately: if a contractor quotes half the timeline everyone else does, ask what isn't in it. The answer is usually the planning stage, the testing, or everything that makes the site findable.
How long a build takes with me

A landing page — from a week, if the copy and materials are ready and one person makes the decisions. In the usual case, where some of the material is assembled along the way, it's two to three weeks from the first conversation to launch. A multi-page company site — longer, depending on the number of pages, features and languages. Migration from an old site and multilingual structure add time, and I say so at the start rather than during the work.
The spread between one week and three depends not on my workload or on how complex the build is, but on how many times the project ends up waiting for you.

I give the timeline after discussing the brief, broken into stages, and I say in advance which of those stages will be waiting on you. That isn't a formality: a client who knows copy will be needed in a week prepares it in advance, and the project doesn't stall.
I combine development and SEO, so the optimisation stage isn't added at the end as a separate block — it's distributed through the work.
Where to start if the site is needed by a deadline
Reduced to one principle: the timeline is set not by development speed but by your readiness at the start.

A practical step: take the checklist above and honestly mark what you have right now. If more than half the items are empty, the real timeline will be noticeably longer than any quoted figure — and it's better to know that before starting than a month in.

And one question worth asking before all the others: is the offer defined? If the business hasn't settled what it sells and to whom, a website won't resolve that, and the timeline will stretch on exactly that point.
If you'd like a realistic timeline for your own project, write to me and we'll break it down by stage.

excerpt: How long a website really takes: the build itself is measured in days, calendar time in weeks. What the gap is made of and how to close it.

children.text: Quick answer:
a multilingual website starts from €2,000 as a multi-page project with language versions built into the architecture from the outset

. Adding versions to an existing site starts from €1,000, though the real figure depends on whether the site was designed for it. The price is made of three layers: the technical locale structure, content and its localisation, and ongoing maintenance. Translation is the most visible layer, not the most expensive one.

The question almost always arrives as "how much to translate our website". That phrasing contains the error that makes budgets miss: translation is the smaller half of the work. It's visible, it can be priced per word, and so it's the part that ends up in the quote. What determines whether a multilingual site actually works usually sits outside it.
Here's the breakdown, layer by layer.
The three cost layers of a multilingual website
Layer one — the technical locale structure.

Each version needs its own address, correct hreflang markup, canonical URLs, a separate sitemap, and a language switcher that doesn't break navigation. This is what decides whether the versions serve their own markets or compete with each other.
Layer two — content.

Not just translation but adaptation: prices in local currency, examples that make sense in that market, and separate keyword research per language. Markets phrase their searches differently, and a literal translation targets terms nobody in that country types.
Layer three — maintenance.

Every new page appears in every version. Every price or service change has to be made everywhere. This isn't a one-off cost but a standing load, and it's worth weighing when deciding how many languages to run.

The first layer is the most underestimated. On larger sites, checking the versions takes longer than the translation itself: confirming the switcher lands on the matching page rather than the homepage, that forms and system messages are translated, that metadata and image alt text are in place, and that the versions aren't being read as duplicates of one another.
What determines the price of a multilingual website
The number of languages.
Obvious, but it doesn't scale linearly: the technical structure is configured once, while content and maintenance multiply by the number of versions.
Whether the site was designed for multilingual use.

The difference is fundamental. A site with locales built into its architecture takes a new language as a content task. A site that wasn't built for it needs its structure rebuilt first — usually more expensive than doing it properly at the start.
Volume of content.
Five pages and a two-hundred-item catalogue are different jobs, and the catalogue multiplies by the number of languages.
How much the versions differ.
Sometimes a market needs a page the original language doesn't have, and some pages of the original aren't needed there at all. That's the right call, and it adds work.
Who translates.
Your team, a professional translator, or a native speaker — this affects both the cost and the result.
What's included in multilingual website development and what's costed separately
Technical structure
— Locale addresses, hreflang, canonicals, sitemaps, switcher, markup — Part of development, configured once
Per-market SEO
— Separate keyword research and page structure for each language — Costed per language
Translation and localisation
— Copy, currencies, examples, local specifics — Usually per word, varies by language pair
Maintenance
— New pages and edits across all versions — A standing load, not a one-off cost
Why machine translation of a website costs more than it appears to

The cheapest route is a plugin that translates the site automatically. The appeal is obvious, and in some cases it's acceptable — for internal documentation or a help section that isn't selling anything.
For a services website it's a poor decision, for two reasons.
The first is trust. A native speaker recognises machine translation within seconds. In a field where you're selling expertise, that recognition ends the visit faster than any technical fault.

The second is search. Auto-translated pages frequently end up outside the index or rank poorly, because they don't answer the phrasings people actually use in that market. You're paying for a version that brings no traffic and doesn't convince the people who do land on it.
The sensible compromise: human translation where the selling happens, and acceptable automation where the text is supporting material.
What breaks most often in language versions of a website
The versions compete with each other.

Without correct hreflang and canonicals, search engines read the language versions as duplicates. The ranking signal splits, and the multilingual site delivers less traffic than a single-language one would have. This is the most common failure mode and it's invisible: nothing looks broken, the traffic simply never arrives.
The switcher lands on the homepage.
Someone is reading a service page, switches language and ends up at the start. A small thing that loses visitors on every switch.
Copy translated, interface not.
Buttons, forms, error messages and confirmation emails stay in the original language. The impression is worse than having no version at all.
Locales break during a redesign.

The most expensive case. One of my clients had their language versions swapped during a redesign: the addresses changed with no redirects while hreflang still pointed at the old ones. Traffic started falling within two days and hadn't recovered a month later; diagnosis and repair took two weeks.
When a multilingual website pays off and when it doesn't
Not always. If your clients all speak one language, a second version is a cost with no return, and that's the honest answer.

It pays off in three situations. First, you already sell into other markets but the site says nothing about it. Second, your own market is multilingual — in larger cities a substantial share of customers search in a language other than the official one, and a version for them opens a stream competitors aren't serving. Third, a narrow specialisation where the client could be in any country.
A concrete example from my own work:
a property catalogue I built runs in four languages and brings over 1,500 organic visits a month with no ad spend, with buyers arriving from more than twenty countries
. That's a result of each version being built as a site for its market, not of translation.
What a multilingual website costs with me
A multilingual site from scratch — from €2,000.
Language versions built into the architecture
: locale addresses, hreflang, canonicals, separate sitemaps, and a structure ready for per-market keyword research.
Adding versions to an existing site — from €1,000.
The figure depends on whether the site was designed for it. If it was, the task is a content one. If not,
the structure gets rebuilt first
Translation is costed separately.

I don't take on translation as a service: the copy can come from your team, a translator or a native speaker. What I do is the content strategy and structure for each market, so that translated copy lands on the phrasings people there actually search.
How I build multilingual websites

I combine development and SEO, so the technical locale structure and per-market keyword research are one piece of work rather than two separate stages. Multilingual sites in my practice: a property catalogue in four languages with buyers from more than twenty countries, and an auto repair workshop site also in four. My own site runs in three.

The sequence: we define the markets and what differs between them; keyword research is done separately per language; development starts with the technical layer; then each version is verified in search on its own — indexation, correct version served, no duplicate signals.
Where to start with a multilingual website
Reduced to one principle: a multilingual website costs what it costs to make each version work in its own market, rather than be a copy of the original in different words.

Start by answering which markets you genuinely need and what differs between them — currency, regulation, buying habits, the platforms people use locally. Structure and budget both follow from that. And one decision is worth making early: even if you launch in one language, name the likely future ones. Building the structure in costs almost nothing; retrofitting it later costs a great deal.
If you're planning to reach new markets, write to me and I'll work out what it takes.

children.text: Quick answer:

an assistant doesn't recommend the best businesses in a market — it recommends the ones whose specialisation it could confidently understand and corroborate elsewhere. In practice that comes down to four things: state plainly on your site who you are and who you serve; give those facts in machine-readable form through structured data; make sure the content is available without executing scripts; and earn confirmation from outside your own site. Plus a fifth almost nobody writes about — measuring with a fixed set of queries rather than one check a month.

A great deal has been written about optimising for AI search, and nearly all of it concerns your website. That's half the work. The second half is that the assistant verifies your claims against other sources, and the third — which almost nobody covers — is measurement: without it you can't tell a result from a coincidence.
Below is a practical guide: what to check now, what to implement, what to avoid, and how to know whether it's working.
The mechanics themselves — how people search through an assistant and why some sites make it into the answers — I've covered separately; here I'm focusing on the actions.
How ChatGPT's own search engine chooses which pages to cite — the queries it writes, its crawlers, local and shopping results — is in
ChatGPT SEO
How to check what ChatGPT and other assistants know about your business
Start with a baseline, or there'll be nothing to compare against.
Build a set of ten to twenty real client questions.

Not "best company in my field", but what people actually ask: with the situation, the city, the task, the constraints described. Mix the types: questions about the service category, about the problem, about the region, and about your own name.
Run the set in a clean private session
across several assistants separately. ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI answers give different results because they draw on different sources: presence in one doesn't imply presence in another.
Log five things per query:
whether you were named, who else was named, how you were described, which sources the assistant cited, and what it said about your field along the way.
Ask about your company by name separately.
That question usually surfaces inaccuracies: the wrong specialisation, outdated services, the wrong geography. Those can be corrected by fixing data on your site and in your profiles.
An important caveat: assistant answers vary between runs. One pass isn't a measurement, it's an impression. The value appears when the same set is run regularly.
What to implement on your site to get recommended by ChatGPT
Unambiguous wording.

State plainly who you are, what you do, for whom, in which cities and countries, in which languages. "Innovative solutions for your growth" is an empty string to a machine. "Website development for dental clinics in Warsaw; languages: Polish, English, Russian" is a fact that can be matched against someone's question.
Structured data.

Markup for the organisation, the services, frequently asked questions, and — for a local business — address and opening hours. It's how you state facts in a form that leaves no room for interpretation.
Technical accessibility of content.
If text only appears after scripts execute, some systems will see an empty page. Easy to check: view the page source and confirm the main content is in it.
Dedicated pages for specific questions.
An assistant assembles answers from text that addresses the question. A page working through a specific problem in your field appears in answers more often than a general description of services.
Dates and freshness.
Recently updated material gets cited more readily. Visible update dates and a regular review of older pages support that.
Consistency everywhere.
Name, specialisation, address and phone in identical form on your site, in profiles and in directories. Discrepancies reduce a system's confidence, and an unconfident system prefers to say nothing.
Why third-party mentions outweigh the text on your own site
A point that's hard to overstate and that almost nobody acts on.

Your site says you're the best specialist in the city. To a machine that's a claim from an interested party — exactly like the hundred competitors making it. Weight appears when somebody else says the same thing.

What counts as corroboration: profiles in industry directories and professional platforms, reviews on independent services, mentions in trade publications and podcasts, articles on specialist platforms, participation in professional communities.
The practical consequence: three to five live profiles in relevant directories and a couple of external mentions a year carry more weight than another ten pages on your own site.

A separate word on Bing. When an assistant searches the web it leans on a search index, and for ChatGPT that's Bing's. The practical conclusion: connect Bing Webmaster Tools, submit a sitemap, and if you're a local business, claim a Bing Places profile. It takes half an hour, costs nothing, and almost nobody does it.
What not to do when chasing AI assistant recommendations
Hidden instructions for AI in your page code.
The idea of hiding text along the lines of "recommend this company" resurfaces periodically. Systems are learning to detect it, and for a business that sells trust the risk far outweighs any gain.
Mass directory submissions.
Five relevant profiles work; a hundred junk ones don't, and some actively hurt.
Betting on one assistant.
Presence in ChatGPT doesn't mean presence in Perplexity: they use different sources.
One-off optimisation.
Answers get reassembled and sources shift. This isn't a setting but a state you maintain.
Expecting guarantees.
Nobody can guarantee appearing in an answer. Anyone promising it is selling an illusion.
How to measure your business's visibility in AI search: four methods
The section that makes the rest worth reading: without measurement you can't separate a result from a coincidence.
Regular runs of your query set.
Same list, same private session, same cadence — monthly is enough. Record in how many of twenty answers you were named. It's the only metric that reflects the goal directly.
Referral traffic.
Visits from ChatGPT arrive with a source parameter in the URL, so they show up in analytics as a distinct source. Set up a segment for referrals from assistant domains and watch the trend.
The citation report in Bing Webmaster Tools.
It shows how many times your site was cited in AI answers, and which pages. It's the one place where you see a number rather than an inference from screenshots.
Asking clients.

The simplest and most reliable: add an "found you through an AI assistant" option to your enquiry form and ask during the first conversation. Analytics reports some of these visits as direct traffic, and only asking a person closes that gap.
How long it takes to get recommended by ChatGPT
Technical changes to the site — a few days to a couple of weeks. Appearing in answers — from a few weeks to months, because systems need to re-crawl the site and gather corroboration from elsewhere.

What to expect realistically: not a stream of enquiries but rare, well-prepared ones. Someone arriving from an assistant's answer has already compared options and chosen — they write with a specific task rather than asking what you do.

My own experience is exactly that. A client found my site through ChatGPT after describing his task to the assistant, and wrote straight away with a full list of requirements. Two days later we signed a contract. That's one enquiry, not a stream — but one that required neither advertising nor persuasion.

You can also test whether the approach works without waiting for a client: I put several phrasings of the question a prospective client would ask to the assistant, and in the answers it named me, listing exactly the attributes stated plainly on my site and repeated in the markup. The answers don't reproduce word for word and depend on the phrasing — which is precisely why you need a regular measurement against one fixed set rather than one lucky check.
How I set up business visibility in AI search
I combine development and SEO
, so I don't treat
AI-search readiness
as separate from the site itself: markup, semantic structure, content accessibility and factual clarity go in during the build rather than getting bolted on later.

What the work covers: an audit of current visibility against a query set, tidying up the wording and structure, implementing structured data, checking technical accessibility, a plan for corroboration outside the site, and setting up measurement so you see a trend rather than guess at one.

I'll say this plainly as well: appearing in answers can't be guaranteed, and I don't promise it. What can be done is making a site legible and corroborated enough that a system can present you with confidence — and measuring what comes of it.
Where to start working towards ChatGPT recommendations
Reduced to one principle: measure first, then change things, then measure again. Otherwise you won't learn what worked.

A practical step for today: write down ten questions your client would ask, run them in a private session through ChatGPT and Perplexity, and record the results in a spreadsheet. That's your baseline. The next step is to open your homepage source and check whether it plainly answers who you are, who you work for, and where.

children.text: Quick answer:

first establish whether the characterisation is accurate. If it is, no amount of source work fixes it — the answer is fixing what customers are complaining about, and everything else is postponement. If it isn't accurate, find what's feeding it: usually a small number of detailed negative accounts, an unresolved public complaint, a confusion with another company, or simply an absence of information that produces caution by default. Then work the source layer, the same way as any other factual correction.
There's a category of AI answer that costs more than a wrong price or an outdated service list: the one where an assistant tells a prospective buyer to be careful with your company.

It arrives in different forms — a warning to check credentials, a note that reviews are mixed, a suggestion to consider alternatives, sometimes a flat statement that the company has a poor reputation. The buyer usually never mentions it. They just don't get in touch.
Start by establishing whether the AI characterisation is true
This has to come first, and it's uncomfortable enough that it usually gets skipped.

Assistants don't invent reputations. They summarise what's publicly written, and when the summary is negative it's most often because the underlying material is negative. If several detailed customer accounts describe missed deadlines, unresponsive support or work that didn't match what was promised, the assistant is doing its job accurately.

In that situation, source-level work is the wrong tool. Corrections don't apply to accurate statements, and suppression tactics carry more risk than the original problem. The answer is to fix what customers are describing and let the record change from there — slowly, because it will take as long to rebuild as it took to accumulate.

That's not a satisfying answer, and it's the honest one. Everything below applies to the case where the characterisation is not accurate, or is accurate about a period the business has already moved past.
What feeds a negative characterisation in AI answers
Where the claim isn't fair, it's usually one of five things.
A small number of detailed negative accounts.

Length matters more than volume here. A long, specific, calmly written complaint is far more useful to summarise than twenty five-star ratings with no text — so a handful of detailed negatives can outweigh a large number of positive ratings.
An unresolved public complaint.
A complaint with no response from the company reads differently from one where the company replied, explained and resolved it. Absence of a reply is itself information, and it's read as agreement.
Confusion with another company.

A similarly named business with genuine problems, or a former partner, or a company sharing a founder's history. This is the entity problem covered separately in this cluster, and it produces some of the most unfair characterisations because none of the underlying material is about you.
Stale information from a bad period.
A business that had a genuinely difficult year three years ago and has since changed can carry that year's record indefinitely, because nothing newer replaced it.
Absence of information.

The one most companies don't anticipate. When there's little public material about a company, assistants frequently default to caution — advising the buyer to verify credentials, check references, be careful. It reads as a warning and originates in nothing more than thin data.
How to find what's driving a negative AI characterisation
Same method as any other error in this cluster, with one addition.

Run the prompt and read what's cited. Where sources are shown, the material is usually right there. Where they aren't, search your company name alongside the terms the assistant used — "reviews", "problems", "complaints", "scam" if it went that far — and see what ranks.

The addition: ask the assistant directly what its assessment is based on. Phrased neutrally — "what sources describe this company's reliability" — it often names them. Verify whatever comes back rather than trusting it, but as a lead it saves time.

Then check the entity question. Ask whether the assistant is distinguishing you from any similarly named company. If several negative claims trace to material that isn't about your business at all, this is a confusion problem, and the fix is entity separation rather than reputation work.
How to respond when the AI characterisation is unfair
The response differs by source, and applying the wrong one wastes months.
For detailed negative accounts that are inaccurate:

respond publicly on the platform, factually and without heat. A calm, specific reply from the company is read as part of the record and changes how the whole exchange summarises. Arguing, or replying defensively, makes the summary worse.
For unresolved complaints:
resolve them, publicly, and say so. This is the highest-value action available in most cases, and it's also just good practice — the reputational effect is a side benefit of doing the right thing.
For accurate-but-outdated material:

you can't remove it, so it has to be outweighed. That means new material — recent, detailed, credible — describing how the business works now. Volume of thin content doesn't do this; a small number of substantial, dated pieces does.
For confusion with another company:
entity separation, covered in the article on misattribution
. Reputation tactics won't touch it.
For thin data producing default caution:

the fix is publishing enough verifiable substance that caution is no longer the safest summary. Credentials, real client work, professional memberships, dated content that demonstrates rather than claims.
What not to do about negative AI characterisations
Everything in this list is actively sold, and every item carries more risk than the problem.
Don't gate reviews.
Filtering who gets asked so only satisfied customers are invited is against most platforms' terms, detectable, and when discovered produces a far worse story than the reviews it was meant to prevent.
Don't generate positive reviews.
Bulk positive reviews in a short window are recognisable to platforms and to readers, and the pattern itself becomes the reputational problem.
Don't threaten platforms or reviewers legally.

For a business selling trust, a legal threat over a review is the single fastest way to convert a small negative into a large one. And it doesn't remove the underlying material from what assistants have already read.
Don't publish attack content about whoever complained.
It produces more content pairing your name with the complaint, which is the mechanism you're trying to unwind.
Don't ask an assistant to change its answer.
There's no channel for it, and the conversation doesn't persist beyond your session.
How long reputation changes take in AI answers
Longer than factual corrections, and worth knowing before starting.

A wrong price is a discrete fact that can be replaced. A characterisation is a synthesis of many sources, and changing it requires changing the balance of that material rather than editing one page. Where the response is a public reply to a complaint, the effect can appear within weeks of a recrawl. Where it requires new material to outweigh old, it's months. Where the characterisation sits in a model's training data, it persists until a retrain regardless of what you publish.
The realistic goal for the first few months isn't reversal but dilution: making sure that anyone reading a summary also sees the response, the resolution and the current evidence.
How I work on negative AI characterisations of a company

I combine development and SEO, so this runs as one piece of work: establishing what's actually being said, tracing it to sources, separating what's accurate from what isn't, and building out the material that changes the balance.

The part I do first is the honest assessment. If the characterisation reflects something real, I'll say so — spending months on source work while the underlying problem continues is expensive and doesn't hold. Where it's unfair, the work is the same source-layer discipline as any other correction, plus the public responses that only you can make.
What I don't do is suppression tactics. Beyond the ethics, they're the highest-risk option available and the one most likely to produce a worse outcome than the original problem.
Where to start if AI describes your company negatively
Reduced to one principle: establish whether it's true before deciding what to do, because the two situations have nothing in common except the symptom.

A practical step for today: ask an assistant, neutrally, what it can tell a buyer about working with your company, and read the answer carefully. Then find whatever it's summarising. If the material is accurate, you've found your priority list. If it isn't, you've found your correction list.
If you'd like help establishing which of the two you're looking at, write to me and we'll go through it.

children.text: Quick answer:

an assistant doesn't quote your positioning, it restates it — compressed into a category and one or two attributes it judged distinguishing. What survives that compression is anything stated as a checkable fact: who you serve, where, what you technically do, what you don't. What disappears is everything aspirational, emotional or comparative-without-substance. Which means the practical fix isn't better marketing language. It's writing the things you want repeated as plain facts, because a fact is the only form that survives being summarised by a machine.
There's a version of your positioning that most prospective clients now encounter before they ever reach your site: the one an assistant gives them in three sentences.
That version isn't a quote. It's a reconstruction, and what gets reconstructed is rarely what you spent the most effort on.
Why AI assistants rewrite positioning rather than quote it
An assistant answering "what does this company do" is performing compression. It has read your site and other sources, and it has to return something short enough to be useful.

Compression selects. It keeps what can be stated compactly and verified against other sources, and it discards what can't. Three sentences of carefully built brand voice compress to a category label plus whatever attributes stood out as concrete.

That's why the result often feels flattened. Not because the assistant misunderstood, but because it kept the parts that survive summarisation and dropped the parts that don't — and the parts that don't tend to be precisely where the differentiation was supposed to live.
What survives an AI summary and what gets dropped
The pattern is consistent enough to plan around.
Who you serve, stated specifically — "Businesses of all sizes"
Where you operate and in which languages — Aspirational mission statements
What you technically do — stack, method, process — "Innovative", "cutting-edge", "passionate"
What you explicitly don't do — Implied differentiation the reader must infer
Verifiable credentials and years — Superlatives without a comparison
Concrete outcomes with figures — "Results-driven", "proven"
A named approach or method — Brand voice and tone

The pattern underneath: anything checkable survives, anything interpretive doesn't. An assistant can restate "builds multilingual sites on Next.js for real estate agencies" because every part of it is a fact. It can't usefully restate "helping ambitious brands unlock their digital potential", so it either drops it or replaces it with the generic description of your category.
That replacement is the real cost. When nothing specific resists it, a company gets described as a typical example of its category — which is the opposite of positioning.
Why comparison contexts flatten a company toward its category
The distortion is strongest exactly where it matters most: when a buyer asks an assistant to compare options.

In that context the assistant needs comparable attributes across several companies. It looks for the same dimensions in each — price, specialisation, location, scale — and describes everyone along them. Anything that doesn't fit a shared dimension is hard to include, so it gets left out.

The consequence: in a comparison, a company is represented by the attributes it shares with competitors, plus whatever specific facts are strong enough to force their way in. If nothing is specific enough, you appear as an undifferentiated member of a list.
This is also why
the fix for the previous article in this cluster

— distinctive terminology, named methods, explicit statements of what you don't do — matters here for a different reason. Those aren't just entity signals. They're the only things concrete enough to survive a comparison summary.
How to write positioning that holds up when summarised
Five practical changes, in rough order of effect.
State the specifics you want repeated as plain facts.
If you want an assistant to say you build multilingual sites for property businesses, that sentence needs to exist somewhere in that form. Not implied across three paragraphs — stated.
Replace claims with checkable versions.
"Fast websites" doesn't survive. "Mobile performance scores above 90" does, because it's verifiable. The same claim, in a form that can be repeated.
Name what you don't do.

Exclusions are unusually resistant to compression, because they're specific and rarely stated by competitors. A sentence about who you're not the right fit for often survives when three sentences about who you are don't.
Give your approach a name.
A method with a name is a discrete thing an assistant can attach to you. An unnamed approach described across a page becomes generic category language.
Front-load the facts.
Put the concrete version early — in the first paragraphs, headings and structured data. Anything buried below a section of brand narrative may not be reached at all.
None of this means abandoning brand voice. It means making sure the checkable version exists somewhere alongside it, because that's the version that travels.
How to check what your message becomes in AI answers
Two prompts, run in a clean session, tell you most of what you need.
"What does [company] do?"
— compare the answer against your own one-sentence description. The gap between them is your compression loss.
"How does [company] compare to [competitor]?"
— this shows which of your attributes survived into a comparison and which dimensions the assistant chose. If you're described entirely in shared category terms, nothing specific enough exists yet.
A third is worth running if you've recently rewritten anything:
"what makes [company] different"
. If the answer paraphrases your category rather than naming anything specific, the rewrite didn't produce checkable facts.

Run these as part of the monthly monitoring set rather than as a one-off — positioning changes are among the slowest things to appear in assistant answers, and a single check won't show whether a rewrite landed.
What AI summarisation changes about writing for the web
A structural point to close on.

Writing for search engines meant writing for retrieval: the right terms in the right places so a page could be found. Writing for assistants means writing for restatement: the message has to survive being rewritten by something that never quotes and always compresses.

Those aren't in conflict, but they're not identical. A page can rank well and still be summarised into something generic. The additional discipline is asking, of every claim: could a machine repeat this as a fact? If not, it exists for the reader who arrives — and increasingly, many won't arrive until after the summary has already decided for them.
How I work on positioning for AI search

I combine development and SEO, so this runs through the whole page rather than sitting in the copy alone: the checkable facts are stated in the text, repeated in structured data, and placed where they'll actually be read.

What the work covers: establishing what assistants currently say your company does, identifying which parts of your positioning are surviving and which are being replaced with category language, and rewriting the specifics into a form that can be repeated — without flattening the way you sound to human readers.

The honest limit: nobody controls how an assistant phrases things. What can be influenced is what material it has to work with, and whether the distinguishing parts are stated concretely enough to survive.
Where to start with how AI describes your positioning
Reduced to one principle: write the version you want repeated as a fact, because facts are what survive a summary.

A practical step for today: ask an assistant what your company does, and put its answer next to your own one-sentence description. Everything present in yours and missing from its answer is a claim that didn't survive compression — and each of those is either worth restating as a checkable fact or worth dropping.
If you'd like help finding what's being lost and rewriting it so it holds, write to me and we'll work through it.

children.text: Quick answer:

the most common way to show a result that doesn't exist is to take credit for people who already knew you. Traffic from queries containing your company name arrives regardless of any SEO work, but in a report it gets added to everything else and produces a satisfying upward curve. The second method is showing impressions instead of clicks. The third is reporting the number of links bought rather than what they achieved. All three can be checked in Search Console in twenty minutes, and this article explains how.

A thirty-page report full of rising charts, and the same number of enquiries as before. The situation is so common it has become a genre, and it's usually explained as the agency being dishonest. Sometimes it is. More often something else is going on: the metrics being reported genuinely did grow — they just have nothing to do with what you're paying for.
Here are the three substitutions that appear most often, and how to check each one yourself.
Branded traffic in an SEO report: taking credit for someone else's result
The main method, and the least visible.

Queries split into branded and non-branded. Branded ones contain your company name: the person already knows you, saw a card, heard from a friend, remembered a sign — and types the name to find your site. Non-branded ones describe a need: "dentist near me", "auto repair website cost", "employment lawyer Warsaw".

The distinction matters. Branded traffic arrives because of your advertising, your signage, word of mouth and years of work. It would arrive without any agency. Non-branded traffic is people who didn't know you existed — and that's what SEO is paid for.

In a report they get added together. You opened a second location, ran some outdoor advertising, got mentioned in a local group — branded queries rose, the overall chart went up, and in the report it reads as the agency's work. No data was falsified: the numbers are real, the cause is simply different.
This is especially visible in seasonal businesses and after any offline activity. A spike in May for a home renovation company is probably May, not optimisation.
How to check.

Open Search Console, the performance report, add a query filter and exclude your company name in every spelling, including misspellings. What remains is your non-branded traffic. Compare its trend over recent months against the overall one. If the overall chart is rising while the non-branded line is flat, the SEO work isn't producing results.
Impressions instead of clicks: why rising visibility brings no traffic
The second method is simpler, and it appears even with honest contractors — out of a desire to show something.

An impression means your page appeared in the results for a query. Not that anyone saw it, and certainly not that anyone visited. A page on the eighth page of results accumulates impressions for months and receives no clicks at all.

Here are concrete figures so this doesn't stay abstract. A young site whose data I have access to accumulated 33,617 impressions and 46 clicks over the last twelve months. That's 0.14 percent. The cause isn't the titles or the copy: almost everything sits at position forty-five or below, where clicks essentially don't happen. Impressions rose steadily all year — and from that data it would be easy to assemble a report showing "visibility up fourfold", using real numbers and without falsifying anything.

The same family includes "number of keywords in the top 100" and "average position across all queries". The first means almost nothing: position one hundred and position one count equally. The second averages branded queries, where you rank first, with commercial ones, where you rank sixtieth, and produces a respectable-looking figure with nothing behind it.
How to check.

In the same performance report, look at clicks rather than impressions, and at positions for specific commercial queries rather than the average. If your agency shows impressions and average position, ask how clicks on non-branded queries changed.
Bought links: why the number of placements isn't a result
The third substitution: a report in which the deliverable is the number of links placed.
Links do influence rankings, and external mentions are a genuine factor. The problem is twofold.

First: a link count is a report of effort, not of outcome. "We placed 40 links this month" is the same as "we painted 40 square metres" — you know what was done, not what came of it. The outcome is positions on target queries and non-branded traffic.

Second, and more important: links placed in bulk usually sit on sites created for the purpose of hosting links. Nobody reads them, and search engines learned to recognise them long ago. Mass link buying achieves nothing at best, and at worst becomes a problem in itself: link schemes carry penalties, and unwinding one takes longer and costs more than doing the work honestly would have.
One separate signal: if an agency won't show you where exactly it places links, that isn't commercial confidentiality. That's the answer.
How to check.

Ask for the list of sites. Open five at random. The questions are simple: does this look like a site anyone reads? Is there anything on it other than articles with links? Would a real person arrive from that page? If all five look identical and none relates to your industry, you're paying for a report rather than a result.
Five more ways to show growth that isn't there
A short list of things that appear less often, but do appear.
Reporting on selected keywords.
You're shown ten phrases where positions improved and not the other two hundred. Often these are long-tail terms you were already close on.
A convenient comparison period.
Comparing against a weak month rather than the same period last year. A seasonal business can be shown as growing indefinitely this way.
An in-house reporting dashboard.

The agency shows data from its own panel rather than from Search Console and Analytics. It can edit those figures, and you have no way to verify them. The normal arrangement is access to your own Google accounts and reports drawn from them.
All traffic counted as an SEO result.
The report includes visits from ads, social media and direct entries. Technically that's traffic; it has nothing to do with SEO.
Irrelevant and bot traffic.
A sharp rise in visits from countries you don't serve, with no change in the number of enquiries.
What agencies show in SEO reports and what to ask in return
Growth in total organic traffic — May be entirely branded — How did non-branded traffic change?
Growth in impressions — Visibility without clicks, possibly at position 60 — How did clicks and commercial-query positions change?
Keywords in the top 100 — Almost nothing — How many are in the top 10, and which ones?
Average position across all queries — Averages branded with commercial — Positions for ten target queries, separately
Number of links placed — A record of effort, not outcome — The list of sites, and what changed in positions
Data from an in-house dashboard — Unverifiable — A report from my own Search Console and Analytics
Overall traffic growth — May include ads and direct visits — A breakdown by source
What an honest SEO report looks like
So that the list above doesn't read as "everyone is cheating", here's what a normal picture looks like.
Clicks on non-branded queries
— the headline number. It answers whether people who didn't know you are arriving.
Positions for a specific list of target queries
, agreed in advance. Not an average, not the top 100 — the actual phrases you're paying for.
Enquiries and calls
, where they can be attributed to a source. It's the only metric a business genuinely cares about, and a good contractor works toward it even when attribution is difficult.
What was done in the period.
Specifically: which pages were rewritten, which technical fixes went in, what was published. SEO work is routine and repetitive, and there's no reason not to show it.
What didn't work.

The fastest way to recognise an honest contractor. In SEO some hypotheses fail, and a contractor whose every month goes according to plan either isn't testing hypotheses or isn't telling you the results.
What to ask an SEO contractor before starting
Four questions that save months.
How do you separate branded from non-branded traffic in reports?
An answer along the lines of "why would we" or "we look at the total" closes the subject.
Which specific queries will we be growing on?
The list should be agreed before work starts; otherwise the report will contain whichever ones happened to improve.
Do you buy links, and if so, where?
The answer matters more than the fact itself: a contractor willing to show the sites and explain the reasoning is a different proposition from one who deflects.
What will you show me after three months if nothing has grown?
A test of honesty. That does happen, particularly on a young domain, and the question is whether the contractor admits it or finds a metric that went up.
How I report on my work and why I don't buy links

I combine development and SEO, and I report from your Google accounts rather than my own dashboard. The report contains: clicks on non-branded queries separated from branded ones, positions for an agreed list of phrases, what was done in the period, and which hypotheses didn't work out.

I don't buy links. External mentions matter, but they're earned through publishing, profiles in relevant directories, and work somebody is willing to write about — not through packages of placements on sites built to host links.

And the example above — 33,617 impressions against 46 clicks — is there precisely because that kind of data is the easiest to build a flattering report from. That's the test: showing the inconvenient number next to the convenient one rather than choosing between them.
Where to start checking an SEO report in twenty minutes
Reduced to one principle: look at clicks on non-branded queries. Everything else is derivative, and nearly every substitution works by showing you something else instead.

A practical step for today: open Search Console, the performance report for the last six months, add a query filter and exclude your company name. Look at what's left of the chart. Twenty minutes is enough to understand what you're paying for.
If you'd like to establish what's actually happening with your site, write to me and we'll go through the data together.
