children.text: This is a diary of my own project, not a retelling of someone else's statistics. On 18 September 2026 I opened
tatsianabandziuk.com

to indexing — a trilingual site for a retail analytics consultant that I designed and built myself. 160 pages, no backlinks, no domain history, no branded demand. I have access to its Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools and Clarity accounts, so the exports below are published in full and with screenshots.

The short answer first: the first impressions in Google appeared on day two after I opened the site to indexing, 70 of its 160 pages were indexed within nine days, and three weeks in half the site was still outside the index — 71 pages in
"Discovered — currently not indexed"

. The first clicks came on day ten. The totals for the 28-day measurement window, 18 September to 15 October: 1,068 impressions and 6 clicks. The day-by-day data runs to 11 October — Search Console is still settling the final days.

Where the numbers come from. Impressions, clicks, CTR and positions — the Performance report in Google Search Console for 18 September to 15 October, all devices and all countries, no filters applied. The state of the index — the Page indexing report as of 14 October. Sessions and referrers — Microsoft Clarity for the same period, with its own bot filter. Bing impressions — Bing Webmaster Tools for 20 September to 11 October. Nothing is recalculated, rounded or averaged: every section carries a screenshot of the report its numbers come from.

Two things come without a screenshot: the query table and the reason breakdown in the indexing report. Both show specific URLs and queries I am not publishing, so those numbers appear as text — and you have as much reason to take them on trust as anyone else's. Everything else is attached as exported.
Indexing and traffic numbers from the first 28 days
1,068 impressions and 6 clicks, 0.56% CTR — Search Console, Performance report for 18 September to 15 October
Average position 14.9 across devices — the same report, with no device split applied
81 pages indexed and 79 outside the index, 71 of them "Discovered — currently not indexed" — Page indexing report as of 14 October
43% of all impressions came from one country where nothing is being sold, the Russian-speaking cluster together 59% — country breakdown in Performance
250 impressions at positions 3–8 produced zero clicks — query breakdown in Performance, no screenshot
7 real sessions from ChatGPT against 11 from Google — Clarity, referrers report
56 impressions and no clicks in Bing — Bing Webmaster Tools for 20 September to 11 October
Zero backlinks: not one was bought or placed by hand at any point

picture.alt: Daily Google impressions of a new site: growth from 3 to 110 a day and a fall to 17

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: Why these indexing and traffic numbers are real, and why they are not bad

It is easy to find posts about a thousand visits in two weeks and rankings for everything at once. None of it can be checked: no export, no date range, no domain. So this goes the other way — the domain is named at the end of the article, the exports are published, and nothing is rounded in my favour.

Now about "not bad". The site is three weeks old. It has no backlinks, no domain history and no branded demand. In those conditions 1,068 impressions, 70 pages indexed in nine days and first clicks in week two are a working start. A failure looks different: zero impressions and an empty index after a month. A thousand visits to a fresh domain with no links in two weeks is either paid traffic, someone else's screenshot, or fiction.

The uncomfortable parts are here too: 71 pages unindexed, no clicks at all from positions 3–8, and 40% of everything that reached the counter is bots. A diary is only worth reading with those included.
Starting position of the new site: three languages, 160 pages, zero backlinks

The site went live on 18 September 2026 with six service pages, six case studies, 54 articles, five calculators and the usual supporting pages, in English, Polish and Russian, with localised section paths.

Everything that normally gets postponed was done before launch: a sitemap with real last-modified dates, schema.org on every page type, IndexNow pings on publish, FAQ answers served in HTML without JavaScript, Core Web Vitals in the green.
What the site did not have, and still does not: backlinks, mentions, domain history, branded demand. Without that context the numbers below read wrong.
Daily Google impressions of a new site: up to 110, then down to 17
Across the 28 days Google showed the site 1,068 times and sent 6 people. The chart below covers the days whose data is already complete.

cells: 18–27 a day; indexed pages grew from 17 to 70
Plateau at 60–110 a day, first clicks

children.text: Reaching a hundred impressions a day inside two weeks is a normal start. The drop at the end is the interesting part: it looks like the end of the short-lived boost Google gives new sites to sample how users react to them. That is a hypothesis, not a fact, and next month's export will test it. If impressions do not recover, the cause is something else.

picture.alt: Search Console, 28 days: 1,068 impressions, 6 clicks, 0.6% CTR and an average position of 14.9

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: "Discovered — currently not indexed": 71 pages out of 160
The worst number of the period. As of 14 October: 81 pages indexed, 79 not, and 71 of those in "Discovered — currently not indexed".

The status means Google learned the URL — from the sitemap or a link — and decided not to spend a crawl on it. It is not a markup error, not a robots rule, not a slow server: all of that was checked and is fine. It is a trust deficit. Crawl budget goes to domains with external signals, and a three-week-old site has none.
The conclusion follows directly, and people rarely like it: while half the pages sit outside the index, rewriting the text on those pages changes nothing. First they have to be read.

picture.alt: Page indexing report: 81 pages indexed, 79 not indexed

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: Google impressions came from the wrong markets: 43% from one non-target country
The country breakdown was the biggest surprise.

The top ten of 63 countries, sorted by clicks. Russia alone produced 458 impressions — 43% of the period's total — and not one click. The Russian-speaking cluster together with Kazakhstan, Ukraine, Belarus and Uzbekistan accounts for 628 impressions, almost 59%, and a single click between them.

The target English-speaking markets, the US and the UK, produced 155 impressions at positions 40.3 and 35.4 — effectively absent. The one market where everything lines up is Poland: 129 impressions, 3 clicks, 2.3% CTR and an average position of 9.5.

This is what happens when one language version lands in a less contested SERP: positions 3–8 arrive quickly there, while the same topics in English are held by sites with a decade of history. Aggregate numbers end up looking healthier than the actual situation.

picture.alt: Impressions and clicks by country: Poland, Kazakhstan, India, Mexico, Russia, the US, Ukraine, the UK

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: Positions 3 to 8 in search produced zero clicks: a zero-click search, measured
The most useful finding of the period. A cluster of definitional queries — "what is this metric" — collected roughly 250 impressions at positions between 3.5 and 8 and produced not a single visit.

The cause is the query type, not the ranking. Someone asks for a definition, gets it in the snippet, in People Also Ask, in the AI overview, and never leaves the results page. A good position on a definitional query now means participating in the answer, not receiving a visit.

Practical consequence: either promise something the AI answer does not contain — a calculator, a table of benchmarks, a template, a worked example — or stop treating those pages as a traffic source and judge them by citations instead.
ChatGPT referral traffic to a new site: 7 visits against 11 from Google

Clarity counted 161 sessions for the period and excluded 107 bot sessions on top of that. Referrers: Google 11 sessions, ChatGPT 7, other search engines 5, and 4 more from the site's own domain. The rest arrived with no referrer at all: direct visits and whatever the browser did not pass on.
The bot filtering is not mine: Clarity does it and states it in the dashboard as "107 bot sessions excluded". That filter is not perfect, so 161 is "real according to Clarity", not proven humans.

At that volume it is not statistics yet, but the ratio is telling: for a three-week-old site with no links, an AI assistant delivers two thirds of what search delivers. And getting into an assistant's answer turned out to be faster than getting into Google's top ten.

One more number from the same export: the 107 excluded bot sessions are 40% of everything that reached the counter. Unfiltered, the report would have shown 268 sessions instead of 161, and the picture would look markedly healthier than it is.

picture.alt: Clarity referrers: google.com 11 sessions, chatgpt.com 7, other search engines 5

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: Technical optimisation at launch did not speed up indexing
For completeness: LCP 1.8s, INP 110ms, CLS 0.003, performance score 93 out of 100. The site is fast, stable and fully marked up — and none of that helped with indexing or rankings.

This is not an argument against technical work. It is a reminder of what it does: it removes obstacles, it does not create demand or substitute for authority. When 71 pages sit in "Discovered — currently not indexed", shaving 0.3 seconds off LCP is not the lever.

picture.alt: Clarity dashboard: 161 sessions, 107 bot sessions excluded, 146 unique users

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: Indexing in Bing and IndexNow: 56 impressions and no clicks

A separate thread: 56 impressions and zero clicks in Bing between 20 September and 11 October, with IndexNow submissions wired up from day one. That is low even for a new domain, so next month goes partly into diagnosing it — whether the sitemap was accepted and whether key verification passes.
Bing matters beyond its own share: its index feeds Copilot and parts of other AI answers. A site that is weak in Bing quietly loses AI visibility too.

picture.alt: Bing Webmaster Tools: 56 impressions and no clicks between 20 September and 11 October

contentBlocks.title: Image Full

children.text: The page exists and may even have been crawled, but Google has not added it to the index, so it cannot appear in results. Search Console splits this into reasons: "Discovered — currently not indexed" means the URL is known but was never fetched; "Crawled — currently not indexed" means it was fetched and left out anyway.

items.question: What does "not indexed" mean?

children.text: Nothing visible: the page stays live, keeps its links, and simply never appears in search. In practice it usually means Google found the page thin, duplicated elsewhere, or not worth storing yet — on a new domain the last reason dominates, because the whole domain is still unproven.

items.question: What happens if a page is crawled but not indexed?

children.text: On this site the first pages entered the index within a week of opening it to indexing, 70 of 160 within nine days, and half the site was still outside the index after three weeks. The spread depends less on the site's speed than on how much the domain is trusted.

items.question: How long does it take to get a website indexed by Google?

children.text: Not by rewriting those pages. Remove from the sitemap what does not need indexing, link the important pages from pages that already rank, submit the priority URLs manually, and earn the first external signals. That is the order I am following in month two, and the next instalment will show whether it worked.

items.question: How do you fix "Discovered — currently not indexed"?

children.text: Published estimates vary and depend on the query mix, so instead of quoting one, here is a measured instance from this site: a cluster of definitional queries collected around 250 impressions at positions 3–8 and produced zero clicks.

items.question: What percent of searches end without a click?

contentBlocks.title: Indexing a new site: common questions

children.text: The plan for month two: indexing, snippets, external signals
Four priorities, in order.
Indexing. Work through the unindexed list, drop from the sitemap what should not be indexed, add internal links to important pages from the ones already ranking, manually submit twenty priority URLs.
Snippets. Rewrite titles and descriptions for ten pages already sitting at positions 3–15, around a promise the AI answer cannot fulfil.
External signals. First mentions: profiles, professional communities, two guest pieces. Without this, priority one hits a ceiling.
AI visibility baseline. Run 30–40 control questions through ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overview and Copilot, record where the site appears, repeat monthly.
Which site this is, and where to see how it was built
How
tatsianabandziuk.com
is built and why it was built that way — section structure, page templates, markup and speed — is covered in the
case study in my portfolio
. This diary covers only what happens to the site after launch, month by month.

children.text: Quick answer: SEO gets a page ranked in a list of results so people click it. GEO (generative engine optimization) gets a business or a fact named inside an answer that an AI writes — in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or Google's AI Overviews. AEO (answer engine optimization) gets your exact wording chosen as the answer to one question. They share most of their foundations: Google says there are no extra requirements to appear in its AI features beyond being indexed and eligible for a snippet. They differ in the result (a mention instead of a click), in where the evidence comes from (each AI engine reads different sources), and in how you measure success. In practice you do not choose between them: you do SEO, and then you check, engine by engine, whether the work shows up in AI answers.

Most articles on GEO vs SEO compare two definitions and stop. This one compares them with data: the original research that named GEO, Google's own documentation, click studies from Pew Research Center and Ahrefs, my analysis of
141 AI answers to buying questions
, and a live test I ran on 23 October 2026, asking ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google the same question and comparing what each of them cited.
What is GEO vs SEO: the short definitions
SEO (search engine optimization)

is the work that gets a page to appear high in the list of results of a search engine — Google, Bing — for the queries its audience types, and to be clicked. Its unit is the page, its result is a position, its proof is a visit.
GEO (generative engine optimization)

is the work that gets a business, a product or a fact included in an answer generated by an AI model. The term comes from a 2023 research paper by a team from Princeton University and IIT Delhi, presented at the KDD 2024 conference. Its unit is the claim, its result is a mention or a citation, its proof is the answer itself.
The full definition — where the term comes from, how AI engines pick their sources and what the research says works — is in
what is generative engine optimization
AEO (answer engine optimization)

is narrower: the work that gets your wording selected as the answer to a specific question — in a featured snippet, an AI Overview, a voice assistant or a chatbot. It is older than GEO and grew out of featured snippets.
How answer engines choose one answer, with a live test and a step-by-step method, is in
what is answer engine optimization
AIO

is used in two senses: "AI optimization" as an umbrella term for all of the above, or Google's AI Overviews as a product. When you see "SEO vs GEO vs AEO vs AIO", the fourth letter usually means the umbrella.

cells: Being the chosen answer to one question
Any of the above, in AI systems

picture.alt: SEO, AEO and GEO as layers: SEO decides which pages can be found, AEO which wording answers a question, GEO whether a business is named in a generated answer

contentBlocks.title: SEO, AEO and GEO as layers: SEO decides which pages can be f

children.text: GEO vs SEO side by side: twelve differences that matter

The differences are less about technique than about what the system on the other side does with your page. A search engine ranks documents and lets the person choose. A generative engine reads documents, compresses them and decides for the person.

cells: One answer with two or three names
A spoken-style question, often a full sentence with context
The fact or claim about you
Mostly your own site plus links to it
Your site, plus listings, reviews, forums, video and the press
A mention, often without a click
Answers can change between two runs
Share of answers, citations, accuracy of the description
Fixed question sets run across engines
You are not named, or named with wrong facts

children.text: The most practical difference is the last row. In SEO, the bad outcome is invisibility. In GEO there is a second bad outcome SEO never had: being named with an old price, a service you stopped offering, or a competitor's feature. I wrote about that separately:
where AI gets outdated information about your company
Where SEO and GEO overlap: Google says there is no separate checklist

For Google's own AI features the overlap is close to total, and Google says so directly. Its documentation for site owners states that there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no special optimizations necessary: a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet. The same page says there is no special schema.org markup to add, that structured data should match the visible text, and that clicks from AI features are reported inside the normal Performance report in Search Console.

The documentation also explains a mechanism that matters for strategy: both features may use "query fan-out" — the system runs several related searches across subtopics and then assembles the answer. One question from a user becomes many searches in the background. A page that ranks for none of those sub-queries has no way in.

So for Google, the foundation of GEO is SEO: crawlable pages, an index, relevance, and a snippet-eligible answer. Everything that follows in this article is about what changes on top of that foundation — and about the engines that are not Google.
Where GEO and SEO differ: the result is a mention, not a click
The biggest change is in what the user does after the answer. Two independent measurements:
Pew Research Center

analysed the March 2025 browsing of 900 US adults — 68,879 Google searches. An AI summary appeared on 18% of them. When it did, people clicked a regular result on 8% of visits, against 15% when there was no summary. They clicked a link inside the summary on 1% of visits, and ended their browsing session on 26% of pages with a summary, against 16% without one.
Ahrefs

compared 300,000 keywords in Search Console data before and after AI Overviews launched in the US. For keywords that show an AI Overview, the click-through rate of the first position was 34.5% lower than expected without it.

picture.alt: With an AI summary on the page, clicks on regular results fall from 15% to 8% of visits (Pew Research Center, March 2025 data); position one loses 34.5% of its clicks on keywords with an AI Overview (Ahrefs, 300,000 keywords)

contentBlocks.title: With an AI summary on the page, clicks on regular results fa

children.text: The scale is no longer a niche. In July 2026 Alphabet reported more than 1 billion monthly users of AI Mode, Google's conversational search, and 950 million monthly users of the Gemini app; in February 2026 OpenAI said ChatGPT had more than 900 million weekly users.

What follows from this is not "SEO is dead" — the AI answer is still built from pages that rank. What follows is that a ranking alone no longer guarantees a visit, and that the answer itself has become a place where a buyer forms an opinion about you before seeing your site.
SEO vs GEO in one live test: the same question in Google, Perplexity and ChatGPT

On 23 October 2026 I asked all three engines the same question: "what is the difference between GEO and SEO" — Google in US English, Perplexity and ChatGPT with web search on. Then I wrote down which sites each of them used.

picture.alt: Google's AI Overview for "what is the difference between GEO and SEO": a structured answer that cites Medium, SEO.com, Semrush, Informa TechTarget, eSEOspace and YouTube

The organic results under it were led by a Reddit thread, then Informa TechTarget, Contentful, Semrush, a property-marketing blog, a digital agency and SEO.com. The AI Overview cited a different mix: a Medium post, SEO.com, Semrush, TechTarget, an agency blog and a YouTube video.

children.text: Perplexity built a comparison table from ten sources: TechTarget, Semrush, Search Engine Land, Ahrefs, SEO.com and five smaller sites.

picture.alt: ChatGPT's answer with web search: it cites Google's developer documentation and the original GEO paper on arXiv, and personalizes the example with "SEO consultant in Warsaw" from the account's memory

contentBlocks.title: ChatGPT's answer with web search: it cites Google's develope

children.text: ChatGPT cited primary sources instead of marketing blogs: Google's developer documentation and the original GEO paper on arXiv. It also did something the other two did not: its example for SEO was "your website ranks in Google's top 3 results for 'SEO consultant in Warsaw'". That came from the memory of my own account, which knows what I do. The answer you see is not the answer your buyer sees.

picture.alt: Which sites appeared where: of seven organic results, only TechTarget, Semrush and SEO.com were also cited by both the AI Overview and Perplexity; the first organic result, Reddit, was cited by neither

contentBlocks.title: Which sites appeared where: of seven organic results, only T

children.text: Three things are visible in one question:
Ranking helps, but does not decide.
Three of the seven organic results — TechTarget, Semrush and SEO.com — were used by both the AI Overview and Perplexity. The first organic result, a Reddit thread, was used by neither.
AI answers reach past the first page.
Medium, YouTube and agency blogs that were not among the organic results ended up in the AI Overview.
Each engine has its own habits.
Perplexity read widely, Google mixed its index with video and blogs, ChatGPT went to primary sources and to the user's memory.
One question is an illustration, not a study. The pattern, though, matches what I measured on a much larger set.
How ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode pick sources: data from 141 answers

In September 2026 I put 47 buying questions — "which web developer should I hire for…", "who does SEO for…" — to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode and counted every source in all 141 answers. The full method is in the
study
; the numbers that matter for GEO vs SEO are these:

picture.alt: How many sources each assistant cites per answer: Perplexity 16.7, Google AI Mode 3.7, ChatGPT 1.6

contentBlocks.title: How many sources each assistant cites per answer: Perplexity

cells: Reads the open web widely and shows its work
A tight selection close to what ranks in Google
Selects before reading; mostly sources other than your site

children.text: Two findings change how GEO differs from SEO:
Work on your own site pays off unevenly.
It shows up in Perplexity first, in Google's AI features through ranking, and least in ChatGPT, where the businesses named were mostly found through third-party pages.
Entity ambiguity outranked page quality.

When a company's name was shared with others or described inconsistently, assistants skipped it or mixed it up with someone else, however good its pages were. In SEO a confusing name costs you some clicks; in GEO it can cost you the mention entirely.

When the subject was GEO itself, the assistants cited YouTube, LinkedIn and Reddit more often than the trade press — while Google's first page for the same commercial terms was held by agency listicles. Two channels, two different sets of winners.
What the GEO research actually found

The paper that introduced the term is "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" by Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan and Ameet Deshpande, presented at KDD 2024. The authors built GEO-bench — 10,000 queries from 25 domains — and tested nine ways of rewriting a source page to see which made a generative engine use it more.

picture.alt: Change in visibility in generative answers by rewriting method, from the KDD 2024 GEO paper: adding quotations +41%, adding statistics +31%, citing sources +27%, keyword stuffing −8%

contentBlocks.title: Change in visibility in generative answers by rewriting meth

columns: What was changed in the source

cells: The same content, written more fluently

children.text: Visibility is measured as position-adjusted word count: how much of the answer comes from the source, weighted by where in the answer it appears. The percentages are calculated from Table 1 of the paper, against a baseline of 19.3.
Two results deserve more attention than they usually get:
Keyword stuffing made things worse.
The classic SEO reflex — repeat the query — reduced visibility in generated answers. What helped was evidence: quotations, numbers, citations.
The gains went to lower-ranked pages.

For sources in the fifth position, citing sources raised visibility by 115%; for sources in the first position, the same method lowered it by 30%. GEO is not a reward for those who already win at SEO — it is a chance for those who do not.

picture.alt: The same rewriting methods help pages ranked fifth and hurt pages ranked first: citing sources +115% vs −30%, quotations +100% vs −23%, statistics +98% vs −21%

contentBlocks.title: The same rewriting methods help pages ranked fifth and hurt

children.text: The limits matter too. The experiments ran on a test engine built by the authors and on Perplexity, where visibility improved by up to 37%. The engines of 2026 are not the engines of 2023, and the effect of each method varied by domain. Treat the numbers as directions, not as a recipe.
SEO vs AEO: ranking for a question vs being its answer

SEO and AEO aim at the same results page, but at different parts of it. SEO aims at the list; AEO aims at the box above the list — the featured snippet, the AI Overview, the voice answer — and at the chatbot reply that answers the question directly.

cells: One question with one direct answer
Better relevance and authority of the page
The answer stated in the first lines, in a format that survives extraction
Must match the visible answer exactly
Whether your wording was the one used

children.text: The practical method of AEO is simple to describe and hard to do well: build a map of real questions, give each question one owner page, answer it in the first two sentences, then add the detail. That is the work described on the
answer engine optimization
page.
GEO vs AEO: being named vs being quoted
GEO and AEO are often used as synonyms. They overlap, but they answer different questions:
AEO asks: is my wording the answer?
It works question by question, mostly on your own pages.
GEO asks: am I in the answer at all, and described correctly?
It works on how a business is represented across every source an engine reads — including the many that are not yours.

A law firm can win AEO for "how long does a residence permit take in Poland" and still be absent when someone asks an assistant "which immigration lawyer in Warsaw should I contact". The first is a fact the engine quotes; the second is a recommendation the engine assembles from listings, reviews and articles. Both matter; they are fixed in different places.
SEO vs GEO vs AEO in one map
Put together, the three are layers, not alternatives:
SEO is the foundation.
Without crawlable, indexed, relevant pages, nothing else can happen — Google's AI features draw on its index, and other engines search the web too.
AEO works on the answer.
It makes the facts on your pages extractable: one question, one clear answer, consistent markup.
GEO works on the representation.
It makes sure the engines can tell your business apart from others, find the same facts about you on sites they trust, and repeat them correctly.
That is also why "SEO vs GEO" is a slightly wrong question. The useful question is how much of each layer your situation needs.
Is SEO dead? Will GEO replace SEO?

No — and the evidence is in the systems themselves. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on its search index and require nothing beyond being indexed and snippet-eligible. Perplexity cited companies' own websites 667 times in 47 answers. ChatGPT searches the web before naming providers. Every one of these engines depends on documents that someone optimized to be found.

What is dying is a narrow version of SEO: chasing positions for informational queries that an AI now answers on the page, and reporting traffic as if a click were the only outcome. When the Pew data shows clicks halving under an AI summary, the value of being the source of that summary goes up, not down.
Will SEO exist in five years? The discipline of making content findable, readable and trustworthy for machines will. The reports will look different: share of answers next to share of clicks.
How to measure SEO and GEO: different KPIs, one plan

cells: Share of answers that name you, per engine
Accuracy of how you are described
Which sources each engine cites for your questions
Leads that mention AI, branded searches, AI referral traffic
A fixed set of buyer questions, run on a schedule

children.text: Three rules make GEO measurement honest:
Freeze the question set.
Write down 20–50 questions your buyers actually ask, in their words and languages, and run the same set every month. Changing the questions changes the result.
Run clean sessions.
As the ChatGPT example above shows, memory and conversation history change the answer. Log out, use a fresh session, and note the date, engine, model and language of each run.
Record sources, not only names.
Whether you are named matters less than why. The cited sources tell you where to work next.
How to do this step by step is in
how to check what AI assistants say about your company
and
how to monitor brand mentions in AI answers
GEO and SEO strategy: what to do first, by type of business

cells: Local SEO and a complete business profile first; then consistent listings and reviews, which assistants read
Entity clarity and third-party mentions; clear service pages; articles with original data
Technical SEO and product data first; then comparison and buying-guide content with real numbers
Publisher or SaaS with informational content
Google, where AI Overviews absorb simple answers
Fewer generic explainers, more original research, tools and data that answers have to cite

children.text: And the checklist that works for most of them, in order:
Make sure the site is crawlable and indexable, and that your server does not block the AI crawlers you want — for ChatGPT search that is OAI-SearchBot.
Fix entity clarity: one name, one description of what you do, for whom and where, the same on the site, in structured data and on every profile.
State the facts that set you apart as plain sentences — services, markets, prices, numbers — not slogans.
Give each important question its own page and answer it in the first lines.
Back claims with numbers and named sources; quote experts where it adds evidence.
Keep structured data identical to what the page says.
Get listed and described correctly on the directories and review sites that actually appear in answers for your industry.
Earn mentions in articles and comparisons on sites the engines already use.
Publish something only you can publish: data, cases, measurements.
Freeze a question set and run a baseline in each engine.
Repeat monthly; fix what the sources tell you.
Report SEO and GEO side by side, so neither is judged by the other's metric.
Common GEO myths
"GEO needs a separate website or special markup."
For Google's AI features it explicitly does not. For other engines, clear content and consistent facts matter far more than any tag.
"llms.txt will get us into ChatGPT."
It is a proposed convention that no major assistant has confirmed using. It is cheap to add and harmless, which is all it is. Details:
does your site need an llms.txt file
"Repeat the question as many times as possible."
The original GEO research measured keyword stuffing as the one method that reduced visibility.
"Write it with AI, the AI will like it."
Engines quote what is distinctive and verifiable. Text that says what a thousand other pages say gives them no reason to pick yours.
"Once we're in the answer, we're in."
Answers change between runs and between users. Inclusion is a share over many runs, not a state.
Where to start

If you are starting from zero, do the SEO foundation first and run a GEO baseline at the same time, so you know what the AI engines say about you before you change anything. The four ways I can help are on the
generative engine optimization
page; Google and AI answers as one ongoing job are on
AI SEO services
; ChatGPT on its own and all models measured one by one are on
ChatGPT SEO services
and
LLM SEO services

Aggarwal et al., "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization", KDD 2024 (arXiv 2311.09735) · Google Search Central, "AI features and your website", updated 10 December 2025 · Pew Research Center, browsing data of 900 US adults, March 2025, published 22 July 2025 · Ahrefs, "AI Overviews reduce clicks by 34.5%", 17 April 2025 · TechCrunch, 23 July 2025 (AI Overviews, AI Mode) and 6 October 2025 (ChatGPT) · own study of 141 AI answers, September 2026 · own live test, 23 October 2026.

Yes. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode draw on its index and need nothing beyond normal indexing and snippet eligibility, and other AI engines search the web before they answer. What has changed is that a ranking no longer guarantees a click, so SEO is now measured together with presence in AI answers.

items.question: Is SEO still relevant in 2026?

children.text: GEO is a layer on top of SEO. SEO makes pages findable and ranked; GEO makes sure that, when an AI writes an answer from those and other pages, your business is included and described correctly.

items.question: What is GEO relative to SEO?

children.text: No. Generative engines depend on documents that are crawlable, indexed and relevant — which is what SEO produces. GEO changes the outcome you aim for and adds sources outside your site to the work.

items.question: Is GEO replacing SEO?

children.text: You need separate measurement and a few separate tasks — entity clarity, third-party sources, a question set per engine. The content and technical work is largely shared with SEO.

items.question: Do I need a separate GEO strategy?

children.text: Changes on your own site can appear in answers within weeks, once pages are recrawled. New mentions on other sites and a change in how assistants describe you usually take two to four months.

items.question: How long does GEO take to show results?

children.text: AEO works on being the quoted answer to one question, mostly on your own pages. GEO works on being included and correctly described in generated answers, across all the sources an engine reads.

items.question: What is the difference between GEO and AEO?

children.text: Partly: keep the business profile and listings complete and consistent, state your facts plainly on the site, and ask the same buyer questions in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google every month. The harder part is tracing which sources each engine uses and changing them.

title: SEO vs GEO vs AEO: How Search Engine Optimization and Generative Engine Optimization Really Differ

children.text: Quick answer: GEO, short for generative engine optimization, is the work of getting a business, product or fact included — and described correctly — in answers that AI systems write: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Copilot and Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode. The term comes from a 2023 research paper by Princeton University and partners. It works on three things: whether AI crawlers can read your site, whether the facts about you are consistent everywhere, and whether other sites mention you, because AI engines cite third-party sources far more often than a company's own pages. Its result is a mention or a citation in an answer, not a position in a list of links.

Most definitions of GEO are one paragraph long and borrowed from each other. This article starts from primary sources: the paper that coined the term, two large studies of where AI engines take their sources, the documentation Google, OpenAI and Microsoft publish for site owners, my own analysis of
141 AI answers to buying questions

, and a live check on 23 October 2026 of how Google and Perplexity answer the question «what is generative engine optimization» itself. That last check turned out to be the best example of GEO in this article.
What is GEO? Generative engine optimization defined
Generative engine optimization (GEO)

is the practice of making a company, its products and the facts about it easy for AI systems to find, trust and repeat when they write an answer. A search engine shows a list of pages and lets the reader choose. A generative engine reads those pages itself, picks a few passages and writes one answer, usually with two to fifteen sources attached. GEO is about being one of those sources, or at least one of the names in the answer, and about the answer describing you accurately.
Three things set GEO apart from earlier kinds of optimization:
The unit is a claim, not a page.
The engine does not show your page; it repeats something your page, or someone else's page, says about you.
The result is inclusion.
You are either in the answer or not. There is no page two.
Accuracy is part of the job.
An answer can name you with an old price, a service you dropped or a feature that belongs to a competitor. I describe those cases in
where AI gets outdated information about your company
Where the term generative engine optimization comes from

The name comes from a research paper, «GEO: Generative Engine Optimization», by Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan and Ameet Deshpande, from Princeton University, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi. It was published on arXiv in November 2023 and presented at KDD 2024, one of the main data-mining conferences.

The authors built a benchmark of 10,000 queries across 25 domains, rewrote source pages in nine different ways and measured how much more often each rewrite was used in the generated answer. Their headline result: the right changes to a page raised its visibility in generative answers by up to 40%, and on Perplexity, tested live, by up to 37%. That paper is why the field has a name. Its findings are summarised further down, in the section on what works.
What counts as a generative engine
A generative engine is any system that answers a question by writing text from sources it retrieves. In 2026 the ones that matter for most businesses are:

cells: Google AI Overviews and AI Mode
AI Mode: more than 1 billion monthly users (Alphabet, 22 July 2026)
more than 900 million weekly users (OpenAI via TechCrunch, 27 February 2026)
Microsoft Copilot and Bing AI answers

children.text: Each of them reads the web differently, which is the most practical thing to know about GEO and the subject of a whole section below.
What GEO means in marketing, and the other meanings of «GEO»
Search «what is geo» and Google mixes several meanings, so it is worth separating them before anything else.
GEO in marketing before 2023
meant geographic targeting: showing ads or content by location (geotargeting, geofencing, geo-modified keywords such as «dentist Warsaw»). Many marketing glossaries still use it that way.
GEO in SEO and marketing since 2024
almost always means generative engine optimization, the subject of this article.
Outside marketing
, GEO is a geostationary orbit in satellite engineering, a common abbreviation for geography, and Georgia's country code in sport.

The two marketing meanings meet in one place: local businesses. When someone asks ChatGPT for «a dentist in Warsaw who speaks English», the answer depends both on location data and on generative engine optimization. In my study, ChatGPT referenced Google Maps in 23 of 47 answers to such buying questions.
A second naming problem: GEO,
AEO
(answer engine optimization),
LLMO
(large language model optimization) and
AIO

(AI optimization) are used interchangeably by many writers, and both Google's AI Overview and Perplexity repeat that in their answers. They overlap but they are not identical: AEO is narrower and is about your wording becoming the answer to one specific question. The differences, with examples, are in
GEO vs SEO vs AEO
Answer engine optimization on its own — how one answer is chosen and how to become its source — is covered in
what is AEO
The same work seen from the models' side — training data, each model's search index and its crawler — is in
LLM SEO
How generative engine optimization works: from a question to a cited answer
To optimize for something you need to know what it does. Every generative engine with web access goes through the same five steps, although each one does them differently.

picture.alt: How a generative engine answers: question, query fan-out, retrieval from an index, passage selection, synthesis, answer with cited sources

contentBlocks.title: How a generative engine answers: question, query fan-out, re

children.text: The question.
Usually longer and more specific than a search query: a full sentence, often with context from earlier in the conversation and, in ChatGPT, from the user's saved memory.
Query fan-out.
The engine splits the question into several searches. Google documents this directly: AI Overviews and AI Mode may issue multiple related searches across subtopics to build one response.
Retrieval.

Those searches run against an index: Google's own for AI Overviews and AI Mode, Bing's and the engine's own crawl for others. A page that is not indexed, or that blocks the engine's crawler, cannot be retrieved.
Selection.
From dozens of retrieved pages, the engine keeps a handful of passages that answer a sub-question clearly and that it judges trustworthy.
Synthesis.

The model writes the answer from those passages, merges them, shortens them and attaches citations. This is also where mistakes happen: two sources get blended, an old figure survives, a feature is attributed to the wrong company.

GEO acts on steps 3 to 5. Step 3 is mostly technical and the same as SEO. Steps 4 and 5 are where GEO differs: a page can be retrieved and still not be used, because no single passage on it answers the question on its own, or because other sources say something different about you.
Why being indexed is necessary but not enough

Google states that there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode: a page needs to be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet. That is the entry ticket. Selection then depends on whether a passage can be lifted and still make sense, and on what the rest of the web says. Google's own 2026 guide for marketers puts it the same way: meeting the technical requirements covers you «for search generally, including AI formats», and the rest is unique, useful content.
Where AI engines get their sources: third-party sites vs your own website
The most useful finding about generative engine optimization so far is not about how to write a page. It is about whose pages get cited.

A University of Toronto team (Mahe Chen, Xiaoxuan Wang, Kaiwen Chen and Nick Koudas, September 2025) compared the sources behind Google results and AI search answers for the same product questions, sorting every source into three types: the brand's own site, social platforms and «earned» media, meaning independent reviews, publishers and comparison sites.

picture.alt: Source mix, Google vs AI search, Canada: earned media 31–54% of Google sources and 69–78% of AI search sources; social platforms 14–23% in Google and almost none in AI search

contentBlocks.title: Source mix, Google vs AI search, Canada: earned media 31–54%

children.text: The United States data point the same way, only more strongly: earned media made up 81.9% of AI search sources for cars, 92.1% for consumer electronics and 72.7% for software. Two more findings from the same paper matter for any business that works in more than one language:
AI answers and Google results share few sources.
For smartphones only 20% of the domains in the top 10 overlapped; for local services such as auto repair, 2.5%.
ChatGPT changes its sources with the language of the question.

The overlap between the domains it cited for the same question in different languages was close to zero. Claude was the most stable across languages. A company visible in English answers is not automatically visible in Polish or German ones.

Ahrefs reached the same conclusion from another direction. Studying 75,000 brands (Louise Linehan, May 2025), it measured which signals correlate with a brand being mentioned in Google's AI Overviews.

picture.alt: What correlates with brand mentions in Google AI Overviews: branded web mentions 0.664, branded anchors 0.527, branded search volume 0.392, Domain Rating 0.326, backlinks 0.218

contentBlocks.title: What correlates with brand mentions in Google AI Overviews:

children.text: Mentions of the brand on other websites correlated at 0.664; the number of backlinks, the classic SEO signal, at 0.218. Brands in the top quarter by web mentions averaged 169 AI Overview mentions, the next quarter 14, and the bottom half next to none. Correlation is not proof of cause, and Ahrefs says so, but two independent studies pointing the same way is a strong signal:
in GEO, what others write about you weighs more than what you write about yourself.
The type of question changes the sources

There is one important exception, and my own data shows it. In September 2026 I asked ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode 47 questions of the type «who should I hire for…» and counted every citation in the 141 answers.

For service questions, Perplexity and AI Mode built their answers largely from the providers' own websites, while ChatGPT leaned on its own search and on map listings. So the rule is not «your site doesn't matter». It is:
for product categories, independent reviews and publishers dominate; for services, your own pages count, but only if they answer the buyer's question directly.
The full breakdown is in the
study of 141 AI answers
What GEO research says works on a page

The KDD 2024 paper tested nine ways of rewriting a source page and measured the change in how visible that page became in generated answers. Here they are, translated into what you would actually change in your text.

columns: What it means in your text

cells: Quote a named, relevant person: a client, an engineer, an official document
Name and link the source of every claim
Use the precise term your field uses
Shorter sentences, one idea per sentence
State things plainly instead of hedging

children.text: Two details from the paper are more useful than the table itself. First, the gains were much larger for pages that started lower in the source list: a page in fifth position gained 115% from citing sources, while the page in first position lost 30% with the same change. GEO helps the underdog more than the leader. Second, the effects differed by subject: statistics helped most in law and government topics, quotations in people and society topics. There is no universal recipe, only a direction:
concrete, attributable, checkable statements get reused; vague ones do not.
Generative engine optimization strategy: five layers
Everything above reduces to five layers of work. They are listed in the order I do them for clients, because each one depends on the one below.

picture.alt: GEO strategy in five layers: access, facts, pages, mentions, measurement

contentBlocks.title: GEO strategy in five layers: access, facts, pages, mentions,

children.text: 1. Access: let the AI crawlers read your site
Each engine has its own crawler, and a robots.txt written years ago may block it. OpenAI documents three of them, and they do different jobs:
OAI-SearchBot
finds pages for ChatGPT search. OpenAI states that sites which opt out of it will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, apart from plain navigational links.
GPTBot
collects content for training future models. Blocking it does not remove you from ChatGPT search.
ChatGPT-User
visits a page when a user asks ChatGPT to open it; robots.txt may not apply to it.
So a business can keep its content out of model training and still be visible in ChatGPT answers:

content.code:
User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /

User-agent: *
Allow: /

children.text: Changes take about a day to reach ChatGPT search. Google's AI features use Googlebot, so nothing extra is needed there, but the snippet controls do apply: «nosnippet» or a short «max-snippet» limit how your content can appear in AI Overviews and AI Mode. If you want to check your setup quickly, I describe it in
how to prepare a website for AI search
2. Facts: one version of the truth about your company

Generative engines merge sources. If your website says you were founded in 2015, LinkedIn says 2017 and an old directory lists a previous address, the answer may contain any combination. The work here is unglamorous: list the twenty facts that define your business — name, services, prices or price ranges, locations, languages, founders, years, key clients you can name — and make them identical on your site, Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, directories and any review platforms. The most common sources of wrong answers, and how to fix them, are in
how to correct wrong information in ChatGPT
3. Pages: written so a passage can be lifted
The selection step favours passages that answer a sub-question on their own. In practice that means:
a heading that names the question in the words a customer would use;
the answer in the first one or two sentences under it, with the subject named, not «we» or «it»;
numbers, dates and names instead of adjectives;
one page per service, not one page listing ten. In my study, the providers named most often had a page whose whole subject was the service being asked about.
4. Mentions: be present where engines read

Because earned media dominates citations, part of GEO happens off your site: reviews on the platforms your industry uses, inclusion in comparison articles, interviews and guest pieces in trade media, a correct entry in the directories that rank for your service. For a sole trader or a small firm this is less about volume and more about being present in the five or ten places that the engines actually cite for your type of question. The way to find those places is to ask the engines and record their sources.
5. Measurement
Without measurement, GEO is guesswork. It gets its own section below.
GEO best practices checklist

cells: OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Googlebot are not blocked
Read robots.txt; test the key URLs
Key pages are indexed in Google and Bing
Main content is in the HTML, not loaded only by scripts
Name, services, prices, locations and dates match everywhere
Compare site, Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, directories
An «About» page states who is behind the business, with verifiable details
Read it as a stranger would
Each service has its own page
Each heading names a question; the answer follows immediately
Read the first sentence under each heading
Claims carry numbers, dates and named sources
Structured data matches what is visible on the page
You appear on the review and comparison sites that engines cite for your service
Ask the engines; record the sources
Industry and local directories have current data
A fixed set of 20–50 customer questions is checked monthly in each engine
AI referral traffic is tracked separately

children.text: Generative engine optimization examples
The best examples of GEO are the answers to questions about GEO itself, so on 23 October 2026 I asked Google and Perplexity «what is generative engine optimization» and looked at what they cited.
Example 1: Google's AI Overview takes its definition from the third result

picture.alt: Google AI Overview for «what is generative engine optimization», 23 October 2026: the definition is attributed to Coursera; Seer Interactive and Mailchimp are cited alongside

contentBlocks.title: Google AI Overview for «what is generative engine optimizati

children.text: The organic results for this query were led by Moz, then a Reddit thread, then Coursera. The definition at the top of the AI Overview, however, is attributed to Coursera, not to the first result. Coursera's article opens with a «Key takeaways» block whose first line is a one-sentence definition. The Overview then cites Seer Interactive for the comparison with SEO and lists AEO, LLMO and AIO as alternative names.
The lesson is the core of GEO:
the passage that can be lifted whole wins, even from third place.
A page that ranks first but opens with a story is retrieved and passed over.
Example 2: Perplexity starts from Wikipedia

picture.alt: Perplexity answer to «what is generative engine optimization», 23 October 2026: Wikipedia is the first source, followed by a practitioner's playbook

contentBlocks.title: Perplexity answer to «what is generative engine optimization

children.text: Perplexity opened with Wikipedia and a practitioner's guide, then used Business.com, HubSpot, Coursera, the Cambridge Dictionary, Moz and the original paper on arXiv. Its answer, like Google's, repeats Wikipedia's framing that GEO is «also known as» answer engine optimization. That is the second lesson:
for definitions, engines lean on reference sources, and whatever those sources say becomes the default answer
— including simplifications. If an encyclopedia, dictionary or industry glossary describes your product category wrongly, that error will travel.
Example 3: rewriting one paragraph for AI answers
A typical paragraph from a clinic's home page, before (the clinic is invented for the example):
We are a passionate team with many years of experience, offering top-quality dental care for the whole family. Our tailored approach ensures great results at competitive prices.
Nothing in it can be quoted: no name, no place, no fact, no number. After:

Nova Dental is a dental clinic in Warsaw's Mokotów district, open since 2014. It places implants on the day of the consultation, has English- and Ukrainian-speaking dentists, and a single implant with a crown costs from 4,900 zł.

The second version names the business, the city and district, the year, the service, the languages and the price. Each of those is a separate claim an engine can match to a question such as «English-speaking dentist in Warsaw for an implant, how much». That is the method from the research table — statistics, precise terms, plain statements — applied to a paragraph you already have.
How to measure generative engine optimization
There is no Search Console for most AI engines, so measurement is built from four sources.
1. A fixed question set.

Write 20 to 50 questions a buyer would ask, phrased the way they would ask them, including the city and the language. Ask each one in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and Gemini once a month, in a clean session. Record three things: whether you are named, whether you are cited with a link, and whether the description is correct. The method is described step by step in
how to check what AI says about your company
2. Share of answers.
From that set, the main figure is the share of questions in which you appear, per engine. Expect it to move slowly and differently by engine.
3. Bing Webmaster Tools.

Microsoft's AI Performance report, in public preview since February 2026, shows how often your pages are cited in Copilot, Bing's AI answers and some partner experiences, which pages, and the «grounding queries» the AI used to find them. Since June 2026 it also groups those queries by intent and topic and shows your citation share. It is the only first-party citation report any engine provides so far, and it is free.
4. Referral traffic.

ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini send visitors whose sessions can be grouped into an «AI» channel in GA4 by source (chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com, copilot.microsoft.com). ChatGPT normally adds «utm_source=chatgpt.com» to its links. One caution from this month: after the GPT-6 rollout on 7–8 October 2026, many ChatGPT links arrived without the tag and without a referrer, so GA4 counted those visits as Direct; on 15 October practitioners reported the tags returning, and OpenAI has not commented. A sudden drop in «ChatGPT traffic» may be a tracking change, not a visibility change.
Google does not report AI Overviews or AI Mode separately: their clicks and impressions are included in the regular Web performance report in Search Console.
Generative engine optimization tools: what they measure and where they stop
The tools market has grown fast, and «generative engine optimization tools» is now searched as often as the term itself. They fall into four groups.

Trackers earn their cost when the question set is large, when several markets or languages are involved, or when you need to show trends to a board. No tool can make an engine cite you; they only show whether it does.

children.text: Common GEO myths
«You need an llms.txt file.»
Google states its Search systems don't use it, and no study has found that it increases citations. It has a use, but not that one; the details are in
does your site need llms.txt
«There is special markup for AI.»
Google says no special schema is required for its AI features. Structured data helps understanding when it matches the visible page, exactly as it did before.
«Repeat the keyword so the AI picks it up.»
It is the only method in the GEO paper that made visibility worse: −8%.
«GEO replaces SEO.»

Google's AI features are built on Google's index; ChatGPT and Copilot search run on web indexes too. A site that is not found by search engines is rarely found by generative engines. The relationship is covered in
GEO vs SEO
«Someone can guarantee you'll be recommended by ChatGPT.»
Nobody controls the answer. Answers change between sessions, users and model versions. What can be promised is the work and the measurement, not the outcome.
Does a small business need GEO?
It depends on how your customers choose. GEO is worth doing now if:
your customers ask for recommendations before they buy: professional services, clinics, software, education, relocation, anything with a high price and a long decision;
you already get some AI referral traffic and want to know why it comes and how to get more;
an AI assistant describes your business wrongly — that costs you whether or not you «do GEO».
It can wait if your customers buy by walking past, by price comparison on marketplaces, or by calling the first local result. In that case local SEO and the Google Business Profile matter more.

For most small businesses GEO is not a separate budget line but a layer on top of SEO: the access and pages layers are the same work, and the facts and mentions layers are a few hours a month. In my practice, monitoring of AI answers on a fixed question set starts at 250 € a month, a one-off AI visibility audit at 250 €, and continuous work on Google and AI answers together at 800 € a month. What each option includes is on the
generative engine optimization services
page, and the audit on the
AI visibility audit
page.
Where to start with generative engine optimization

Start with the question your customers ask before they call you. Ask it today in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode, in the language your customers use, and write down who is named and which sites are cited. That list is your GEO plan: the cited sites are where you need to be present, and the named competitors show what the engines consider a good answer.
If you would rather have that done properly — 30 or more questions, four engines, every source recorded and a plan for the gaps — that is what my
AI visibility audit
does. Or
write to me
with the question your customers ask, and I'll tell you what the engines answer today.

In SEO and marketing, GEO stands for generative engine optimization: optimizing to be included and correctly described in AI-generated answers. In older marketing texts GEO can also mean geographic targeting.

items.question: What is GEO short for?

children.text: They overlap, and many people use the terms interchangeably. Strictly, AEO (answer engine optimization) is narrower: it aims to make your wording the direct answer to one question, while GEO covers being named and cited anywhere in a generated answer. See
GEO vs SEO vs AEO

items.question: Is GEO the same as AEO?

children.text: An AI engine splits the question into several searches, retrieves pages from an index, keeps a few passages and writes an answer from them. GEO makes your site readable for the engine's crawler, your facts consistent across the web, your pages easy to quote, and your business present on the third-party sites the engine trusts.

items.question: How does generative engine optimization work?

children.text: Access fixes show within days: ChatGPT search picks up robots.txt changes in about a day. Page changes show when the page is recrawled, usually within weeks. Mentions on other sites and corrections of wrong facts take one to several months, and facts that live only in a model's training data change only when the model is updated.

children.text: No. Answers vary by session, user, language and model version. A trustworthy provider promises the work and a measurement method, and reports the share of answers you appear in over time.

title: What Is Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)? Definition, How AI Engines Choose Sources and What Works

children.text: Quick answer: AEO, short for answer engine optimization, is the work of making your page the source of the direct answer to a specific question — the answer box in Google, the first sentence of an AI Overview, the line ChatGPT or Perplexity quotes, or the reply a voice assistant reads out. It is a part of SEO: the page still has to be indexed and trusted. What AEO adds is the form of the content: the question named in a heading, a complete answer in the first sentence or two below it, and the details, numbers and sources after that. Since 7 May 2026 Google no longer shows FAQ rich results, so AEO today is about the text itself, not about markup.

Search used to answer a question with ten links. More and more often it answers with one sentence: in the US, 58.5% of Google searches end without a click to any website. Answer engine optimization is about whose sentence that is. This article covers what AEO means, where answers appear, how Google and AI tools choose them — shown on a live test from 23 October 2026 — and how to do AEO step by step, with examples, a checklist and the tools that measure it.
What is AEO? Answer engine optimization defined
Answer engine optimization (AEO)

is optimizing content so that a search engine or an AI system uses it as the answer to a question, instead of just listing it among results. An «answer engine» is any system that replies with an answer rather than a list: Google's answer box and AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot, Gemini, and voice assistants such as Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant.
The unit of AEO is one question and one answer. The success you can see is concrete: your sentence appears in the answer box, opens the AI Overview, or is quoted with a link to your page.
Where the term comes from

The term is older than ChatGPT. It spread in 2017–2018, when Google's featured snippets and voice assistants began answering with a single result read out loud; the SEO consultant Jason Barnard is usually credited with coining it. Generative AI did not create AEO — it multiplied the places where one answer replaces a list.
AEO and GEO in one paragraph
AEO and GEO (generative engine optimization) overlap, and many writers use them as synonyms. The useful difference: AEO is about
your wording becoming the answer to a question
; GEO is about
your business being named, and named correctly, anywhere in an AI-generated answer
, including when nobody asked about you directly. A page can win at AEO for «how long does it take to build a website» without the company behind it ever being recommended. The full comparison is in
GEO vs SEO vs AEO
, and GEO itself is explained in
what is generative engine optimization
What AEO stands for in marketing and SEO, and the other «AEO»

In SEO and digital marketing, AEO stands for answer engine optimization. «AEO in SEO» means the part of search optimization aimed at answers rather than rankings; «AEO marketing» usually means content marketing planned around the questions buyers ask.
Two other meanings share the acronym and fill a large part of the search results for «what is AEO»:
Authorised Economic Operator

— a customs status in the EU and many other countries that speeds up border clearance for trusted companies. «What is an AEO certificate» is searched as often as «what is AEO» itself. It has nothing to do with search.
American Eagle Outfitters
— a US clothing retailer whose stock ticker is AEO.
If you landed here looking for the customs certificate, the place to ask is your national customs authority.
Where answers appear: answer boxes, AI Overviews, chat assistants and voice
Each answer surface takes its answer in a different way, and what your site gets in return differs too.

141 AI answers to buying questions

How answer engines choose an answer: a live test

To show how this works in practice, on 23 October 2026 I asked Google (US English) and Perplexity the same question: «how long does it take to build a website». Then I compared whose text each one used with who ranks in Google's ordinary results.

Wix's page summarises the whole answer in its first lines — AI tools take minutes to hours, DIY builders days to weeks — before any detail. Forbes, third in the ordinary results, is not among the visible sources at all.

contentBlocks.title: Perplexity answer to the same question, 23 October 2026: the

children.text: What the winners have in common is not their ranking. Every page used for a visible answer:
names the question in its title or first heading, in the same words people search with;
gives the answer as a range of time in the first lines, then explains it;
breaks the answer down by type — builder, template, custom — so a table can be built from it.
Forbes ranks well and is trusted, but its article does not give a ready answer at the top. That is answer engine optimization in one example:
ranking gets a page considered; a quotable answer gets it used.
My own article on this question,
how long does it take to build a website

, is not among the sources either. It opens with a quick answer, but it does not rank in Google's US top ten for this query, so neither engine retrieved it. That is the other half of AEO: a quotable answer that search cannot find is never considered.
AEO in SEO: where answer engine optimization fits

AEO is not a separate channel next to SEO; it is a layer of it. An answer engine can only use a page that it can find, read and trust, so everything SEO does — crawlability, indexing, links, reputation, speed — is the precondition. What AEO adds is the form of the content.

children.text: A useful rule: if a page answers a question but nobody can quote it without reading three paragraphs, it is SEO-ready and not AEO-ready.
How to do answer engine optimization: step by step
Step 1. Find the questions people actually ask
Collect real questions, not keywords:
People Also Ask
boxes in Google for your main topics; each answer opens more questions.
Search Console:
filter queries containing «how», «what», «why», «how much», «can», «which» in the Performance report.
Assistants:
ask ChatGPT and Perplexity your topic and note the follow-up questions they suggest.
Your inbox:
the questions customers send before buying are the best AEO list you have.
Group them by intent. One page should answer one main question and its close variants, not ten unrelated ones.
Step 2. Put the answer first
Under the heading that names the question, write the answer in the first one or two sentences, so that it makes sense if it is the only thing someone reads:
name the subject instead of «it» or «we»;
give the number, range, yes or no, or the definition straight away;
add the condition that changes the answer («for a five-page site», «in Poland», «as of 2026»).
The rest of the section explains, qualifies and proves. This is the inverted pyramid of news writing, applied to every section of a page.
Step 3. Structure the page so parts can be lifted
one question per H2 or H3, phrased the way people ask it;
lists for steps and options, tables for comparisons and prices;
short paragraphs, one idea each;
the main content in the HTML, not loaded later by scripts.
A table of «type → time → price» was turned almost directly into Perplexity's answer in the test above.
Step 4. Prove the answer

Answer engines prefer answers they can trust. Numbers with dates, named sources with links, an author with real experience and a visible «updated» date all help. The research behind GEO measured this: adding statistics, quotations and sources raised a page's use in generated answers by 27–41%, while repeating the keyword lowered it by 8%.
Step 5. Use markup where it still counts
Structured data does not win answers by itself, and two formats that were once AEO staples are gone from Google's results: HowTo rich results were removed in 2023, and
since 7 May 2026 FAQ rich results no longer appear in Google Search for any site.

FAQ markup does no harm, but it no longer produces anything visible. What remains useful is markup that describes what the page and the business are — Organization, LocalBusiness, Article, Product, BreadcrumbList — and only when it matches what is visible on the page.
Step 6. Keep answers current

An answer that was right in 2023 and is wrong now is worse than no answer: engines may keep quoting it. Put a visible date on pages with prices, timelines or statistics, and review them at least once a year.

children.text: Answer engine optimization examples
Example 1: the same answer, before and after
A typical answer on a web studio's FAQ page, before:
Great question! Every project is unique, and timelines depend on many factors. We always work closely with our clients to deliver the best possible result within a reasonable timeframe.
Nothing here answers the question. After:

A five-page business website takes four to six weeks with a developer: one week for structure and content, two to three for design and development, one for testing and launch. A one-page site can be ready in a week; an online shop with payments takes eight to twelve weeks.
The second version gives the range first, then the breakdown and two alternatives — exactly the shape of the answers Google and Perplexity used in the test.
Example 2: a heading that can be matched to a question

Before: «Our process». After: «How long does it take to build a website with a developer?» The first heading describes the company; the second names the question that someone types or says. Only the second one can be matched to a query.
Example 3: a definition that can be quoted

Before: «In today's fast-changing digital landscape, businesses face new challenges…». After: «Answer engine optimization (AEO) is optimizing content so that a search engine or an AI system uses it as the answer to a question.» Definitions that start with the term and finish in one sentence are the ones answer engines quote — the AI Overview for «what is generative engine optimization» took its definition from exactly such a sentence, as I show in

How to measure AEO
Share of questions answered.

Take your list of 20–50 key questions. Once a month, check who provides the answer box, the opening of the AI Overview, and the sources in ChatGPT and Perplexity. The share of questions where it is you is the main AEO figure.
Search Console.

AI Overviews and AI Mode are not reported separately; they are included in the Web performance report. Watch question-type queries: falling clicks with stable impressions often mean that an answer is now shown above you.
Bing Webmaster Tools.

The AI Performance report, in preview since February 2026, shows how often your pages are cited in Copilot and Bing's AI answers, which pages, and the «grounding queries» used to find them; since June 2026 it groups them by intent and topic.
AI referrals in GA4.

Visits from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com and copilot.microsoft.com can be grouped into their own channel. After the GPT-6 rollout on 7–8 October 2026, part of ChatGPT's links arrived without a tag or referrer and were counted as Direct, so treat short-term drops with care.

children.text: Common AEO mistakes
Building an FAQ section for the markup.
Since May 2026 FAQ markup produces no rich result in Google. An FAQ is still useful when the questions are real and the answers are complete; a list of questions written to fill markup is not.
Answering at the end.
A long introduction before the answer is the most common reason a well-ranked page is passed over, as Forbes was in the test above.
Cute headings.
«Our approach», «The secret», «Why it matters» describe nothing that anyone asks.
One page for every question.
Thirty thin pages, each with one short answer, compete with each other and look like low-value content. Group close questions on one page.
Measuring only rankings.
A page can hold position three and lose most of its clicks to an answer shown above it. Track who gives the answer, not only where you rank.
Does your business need AEO?

Answer engine optimization pays off when your customers ask questions before they buy: how much, how long, which option, is it legal, what is needed. Professional services, clinics, software, education and any purchase with research behind it fall here. It matters less for impulse purchases and for businesses that customers find by walking past.

For most sites AEO is not a new project but a rewrite of existing pages: the key service pages and the five to twenty articles that answer real questions. In my practice, measuring where a site stands in answers starts at 250 €, preparing a site for AI search at 800 €, and ongoing monitoring at 250 € a month. What is included is on the
answer engine optimization services
page.
Where to start with AEO

Take the one question your customers ask most often before they contact you. Search it in Google and ask it in ChatGPT and Perplexity. If the answer they give comes from someone else, look at that page: it almost certainly names the question in a heading and answers it in the first sentence. Then do the same on your page — and if you want this done for your whole site, with the questions, the rewrites and the measurement,
write to me
or see the
answer engine optimization services
