children.text: Quick answer: Small business SEO is the work that makes a business findable when someone searches for what it sells — in Google's map, in the regular results and in AI answers. For a small business it comes down to five things: a complete and correctly named Google Business Profile, one page for each service you actually sell, a steady flow of genuine reviews, pages that answer the questions customers ask before buying, and a site that loads fast and is easy to contact from a phone. Most of it is decisions rather than technical work, and Google's own documentation says a small local business «can probably do much of the work yourself».

Every few months someone announces that SEO is dead. This time the reason is AI: Google answers the question at the top of the page, ChatGPT answers it without a page at all, and the clicks that used to reach small websites go somewhere else. Some of that is true and measurable. Most of what a small business needs to do about it is not what the headlines suggest.

This guide goes through the work in the order I would do it, with the data behind each decision and the rules that actually get profiles suspended. It is written for an owner who will do this themselves, or who wants to know what they are paying for. If you would rather hand it over, the
SEO services for small business
page describes how I work; the guide is meant to be useful either way.
What small business SEO is, and how it differs from SEO for a large site
Small business SEO

(also called SEO for small business, small business SEO marketing or SEO optimization for small business) is search engine optimization scaled to a business that has a handful of services, one or a few locations, and nobody whose full-time job is marketing.
The method is the same as for any site, but four things are different in practice:
The map matters more than the website.
For «[service] in [city]» searches, the three businesses in Google's map block get the attention, and that block is won through the Google Business Profile, not through the site.
Reviews are part of the ranking, not just the sales pitch.
They influence both what Google shows and what a customer clicks.
You are competing with directories, not only with competitors.
Yelp, Yell, Panorama Firm and their equivalents outrank individual businesses for many searches, which changes where it is worth fighting.
There is no team.
A plan with forty tasks is a plan that will not happen. The order of work matters more than its length.
One thing is not different: Google's documentation for small businesses is short, free and specific, and almost nobody reads it. Several of the rules below come straight from it.
Is SEO dead now that AI answers the question?
This is the most-asked question in the topic, so it deserves data rather than reassurance. The honest answer has three parts, and they point in different directions.

picture.alt: Three measurements about AI in search: AI Overviews appear on 15% of local searches but 92% of informational ones; click-through at position one is down 58% on keywords with an AI Overview; Google's documentation says no special optimization is needed for AI features

contentBlocks.title: Three measurements about AI in search: AI Overviews appear o

children.text: What the data says about AI answers and clicks
The clicks are really going. Two independent measurements agree:
Pew Research Center
followed the actual browsing of 900 US adults across 68,879 Google searches in March 2025. When an AI summary appeared, 8% of visits led to a click on a result, against 15% when there was none. Only
of users clicked a link inside the AI summary itself, and 26% ended their browsing session on that page instead of 16%.
Ahrefs
compared 300,000 keywords — half with an AI Overview, half without — using Search Console data from December 2023 to December 2025. Click-through at position one fell
on keywords where an AI Overview appeared. Ahrefs is careful to call this correlation rather than proof of cause.

Google's own position, stated by Liz Reid in August 2025, is that «total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year» and that the clicks are of higher quality. Google publishes no numbers to go with that, so you are weighing an unquantified claim from an interested party against two measurements with published samples. Note that the two are not strictly in conflict: Google is talking about total volume across the whole web, the studies about the chance of a click on a given query.
Why local searches are the exception that matters here
Now the part that decides whether any of this applies to your business.
Whitespark

ran 540 searches by hand across three US cities and six industries in May 2025 and sorted them by intent. For searches of the «[service] in [city]» kind — the ones that bring customers ready to buy — an AI Overview appeared
of the time, and the local map block appeared
of the time. For informational questions the numbers almost exactly reverse: AI Overview 92%, map block 6%.
Ahrefs

, looking at 56 million AI Overviews in May 2025, found the same pattern from the other end: AI Overviews are less likely on local and branded queries, and local queries made up only 6.85% of the keywords that triggered them.

So the AI answer is eating the informational search — «how often should I service a boiler» — and mostly leaving the buying search alone. For a plumber, the first is traffic and the second is customers.
The caveat is that this is moving.
Semrush
, tracking 400 US commercial keywords monthly, found AI Overviews on 45.75% of them in September 2025 and
by August 2026 (reported by PPC Land; I could not find Semrush's own post). Commercial searches are being pulled in fast, even if local ones are not yet.
What Google says about optimizing for AI features
There is a direct answer, and it is in Google's documentation, last updated 10 December 2025:
«There are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary.»

The same page adds that «the best practices for SEO remain relevant for AI features in Google Search» and that «all existing SEO fundamentals continue to be worthwhile». There is no AI text file to add, no special markup, no separate technical setup.

That is worth knowing before you buy anything described as AI optimization. There is real work in AI visibility — checking what assistants say about your business, fixing wrong information at its source, measuring it over time — and I cover it below and in
What is generative engine optimization
. But it is not a new set of technical requirements, and anyone selling it as one is selling a page Google says does not need to exist.
How customers actually find a small business in 2026
Before the tactics, the behaviour. The numbers below come from surveys and SERP studies published in 2025 and 2026.

picture.alt: How a customer picks a small business: 97% read reviews, 68% will not consider under four stars, the median business in Google's top three has 47 reviews, and Google's share as a review source fell from 83% to 71%

contentBlocks.title: How a customer picks a small business: 97% read reviews, 68%

children.text: Almost everyone reads reviews.
In BrightLocal's Local Consumer Review Survey 2026, published in February 2026 from a sample of 1,002 US adults,
said they read online reviews for local businesses.
require at least four stars, 31% will only consider 4.5 and above, and 10% only five.
There is a visible review threshold.
Local Falcon analysed 50.4 million US search results across 1,993 business categories in January 2026: the median business appearing in Google's local three-pack has
47 reviews
, with ratings clustered between 4.5 and 4.9. Competition in cities runs three to five times higher than in rural areas.
Google is still the main review source, but less so.
In the same BrightLocal survey,
named Google as the place they read reviews — down from 83% a year earlier.
Most small businesses have a website, and SEO is their main lead source.
Clutch surveyed 406 US small business owners in August 2025:
have a website, and of those,
name SEO as their top source of leads. Among the 17% without a site, a third say a website is not relevant to their industry and 16% cite the cost.
One older number is worth citing with its age attached, because nothing newer exists: BrightLocal's study of Google Business Profile data found that

of profile views came from discovery searches — people looking for a service, not for the business by name — against 16% who searched for the business directly. That data is from 2017–2018 and no equivalent study has been published since, so treat it as a direction rather than a current figure.
About that «46% of searches have local intent» statistic
You will meet this number in almost every article on local SEO, usually attributed to Google. Its trail is worth following, because it shows what a lot of marketing statistics are made of.

The figure comes from a Google representative speaking at the Secrets of Local Search conference at Google's headquarters in Mountain View in October 2018. It reached the industry through a tweet by the SEO Nick Wilsdon on 10 October 2018, which Barry Schwartz reported at Search Engine Roundtable a week later with an unusually honest caveat: «I do trust the source but all I have is a tweet from this SEO on this stat.» He also wondered aloud whether Google was defining «local intent» in its own way.

Google has never published the research or the method behind it. The wording drifted in the retelling — some sources say «local searches», others «local intent», which are not the same thing — and the number has been repeated unchanged for eight years, through a period in which mobile use, Maps and the shape of the results page all changed considerably.

The practical point is not that local search is unimportant; Whitespark's 93% map-block finding above is measured, recent and says it is. The point is that a single remark at a conference, relayed by a third party, is not evidence — and a statistic that nobody has updated in eight years tells you nothing about today.
Small business SEO strategy: the order to do the work in
A small business cannot do everything, and does not need to. This is the sequence I would follow, each step building on the last.

picture.alt: The order of work: first the targets and the Google Business Profile, then service pages and reviews, then content and links, then measurement

contentBlocks.title: The order of work: first the targets and the Google Business

children.text: Choosing the searches a small business can realistically win

The most common waste in small business SEO is aiming at the most obvious phrase. «Plumber» in a capital city is contested by franchises and directories with budgets you cannot match. You win first where the competition is thinner and your experience is real:
A narrower service
: «boiler replacement» rather than «plumbing», «commercial lease review» rather than «legal services».
A smaller place
: the district or town where you actually work, not the whole metro area.
A language
: if you serve customers in a second language, a page in that language faces a fraction of the competition.
A question nobody answers well
: look at the results for what customers ask you on the phone. If the top results are thin directory pages, that is your opening.
Write down three to five combinations of service and place. Everything below is built around them.
Small business SEO keywords: what customers type before they buy

Owners describe their work in trade terms; customers describe their problem. Nobody searches «HVAC preventative maintenance contract» — they search «my air conditioner smells bad». Good keywords come from three places:
Your own enquiries.
The exact words people use when they call or write. These are your best keywords and no tool has them.
Google's own suggestions.
Start typing a customer's question and read the autocomplete, the «People also ask» box, and the related searches at the foot of the page. This costs nothing.
A keyword tool, for comparison only.
To decide between two phrasings, any tool will do. Volumes for small towns are often reported as zero, which does not mean nobody searches — it means the tool cannot measure that low.
Group phrases by the problem they describe, not by the words. «Emergency plumber», «burst pipe» and «water coming through ceiling» are one problem and belong on one page.
Google Business Profile: the rules that get profiles suspended
For local searches this matters more than anything on your site, and Google's guidelines contain specific rules that are broken constantly:
The name is your real name, nothing else.

Google: «Your name should reflect your business's real-world name, as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery», and «Including unnecessary information in your business name isn't permitted». «Smith Plumbing — Emergency 24/7 London» invites a suspension; «Smith Plumbing» does not.
The address must be real.
A virtual office «isn't eligible for a Business Profile», PO boxes are not acceptable, and a desk in a co-working space does not qualify «unless that office maintains clear signage».
If you travel to customers, say so properly.
A service-area business keeps one profile, hides its address, and sets a service area that «shouldn't extend farther than about 2 hours of driving time».
Use few categories.
Google asks you to «use as few categories as possible to describe your overall core business» and warns against using them «solely as keywords».
Fill in the rest.
Hours, phone, a link to the right page of your site, languages, real photographs, and answers to the questions customers actually ask.

Then make the name, address and phone identical on the site, the profile and every directory you appear in. Inconsistency here is one of the few purely mechanical things that still holds local results back. The profile is only half of the local picture — the
local SEO for small business
page covers how the map results and the website work together.
One page for each service you actually sell
A single «Services» page listing eight things ranks for none of them. Each service a customer searches for needs its own page, and that page has to do more than confirm you offer it:
Name the problem the way the customer does
, in the title and the first sentence.
Answer the first question immediately
: how the job works, how long it takes, what happens on the first visit.
Say what it costs
, or at least how pricing works. Customers compare on this, and it is exactly the kind of fact AI answers quote.
Show who does the work
— a real name and a real photograph beat any stock image.
End with one clear step
: a phone number that dials on tap and a short form.

If you work in several towns, the same logic applies to places: one page per town you genuinely serve, with content actually about that town. Copies of one page with the name swapped are what Google's spam policies now call
doorway abuse
, and they drag down the rest of the site.
Reviews: how to ask without breaking Google's rules
Reviews move both the ranking and the decision, so they need a routine rather than luck. Google's rules on what you may and may not do are explicit, and two common tactics are prohibited:
No incentives.
You may not «offer incentives – such as payment, discounts, free goods and/or services» for reviews, or for changing or removing a bad one.
No review gating.

You may not «discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers». Asking only the customers you expect to be happy is against the rules, however many tools offer to automate it.
No pressure on the premises.
You must not «require or pressure users to leave ratings or write reviews while on the premises», or set staff review quotas.

What is allowed is the straightforward version: Google permits you to «solicit or encourage the posting of content that does represent a genuine experience». Ask every customer at the moment the job ends well, send a direct link, and ask by text message rather than email. Given the median three-pack business has 47 reviews, a steady trickle beats a campaign.
Reply to the bad ones without arguing. A calm, specific reply is read by everyone who comes after, and it is the only part of a negative review you control.
Content that answers what customers ask before they buy

Content for a small business is not news about the business. It is answers to the questions people ask before they choose anyone: «how much does it cost to replace a boiler», «do I need planning permission for this», «what happens if I cancel». Each good answer is a chance to rank, to be quoted in an AI answer, and to save you the phone call.
Rules that make it work:
One question per page
, answered in the first two sentences and then explained properly.
Specific to where you work
— the local rule, the local price range, the local process. General national content is what the directories already publish.
Written or checked by the person who does the job
, with the date it was last reviewed.
Linked to the service page
where the reader can act.

Two thorough answers a month will do more than daily posts written to fill a calendar. And note what Google's spam policies say about volume: scaled content abuse covers «using generative AI tools or other similar tools to generate many pages without adding value for users». The test is the value, not the tool.
Links and mentions a small business can actually earn
Links from other sites remain a strong signal, and for a small business the realistic ones are not bought:
suppliers and manufacturers whose products you install, who often list approved installers;
trade associations and certification bodies you belong to;
local press, when you are the person who can explain something;
organisations, teams and events you sponsor;
partners you already work with, where a genuine credit makes sense.
Avoid link packages and bulk guest posts. They are against Google's spam policies, and the sites selling them are precisely the ones Google discounts.
Technical SEO for a small business website: checks you can run yourself
You do not need to read code to find the common problems:
Speed on a phone.
Run your main pages through PageSpeed Insights on mobile. Sliders, video backgrounds and stock-photo carousels are the usual culprits.
The phone number dials on tap
on every page, and the form actually sends to an inbox somebody reads. Test it yourself from a phone.
Every important page is indexed.
In Search Console, open the Pages report; or type site:yourdomain.com into Google and see what comes back.
One address per page.
The site answers on one version — with or without «www», always https — and the others redirect to it.
Basic structured data
with your name, address, phone and opening hours, kept consistent with what is visible on the page.
No star ratings from your own reviews.
Google does not show rating stars in results for reviews a business collects and displays about itself, so markup for them does not help.
If the list above turns up more than you want to fix one item at a time, it is usually the site itself rather than the settings — what a site built for this looks like is on the
small business website design
page.
Small business SEO in AI search: ChatGPT and AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)
Being visible to assistants is mostly the same work, plus a few specifics that are easy to get wrong.
Let the right crawlers in.
OpenAI runs several, and they do different jobs — this is from OpenAI's own documentation:

cells: Builds the index behind ChatGPT's search
You are not shown in ChatGPT search answers
Fetches a page when a user's question needs it
Visits are user-initiated, so robots.txt «may not apply»
Collects content that may train OpenAI's models
Your content is not used for training — ChatGPT search is unaffected

children.text: The practical consequence: blocking GPTBot does
not
remove you from ChatGPT. Blocking OAI-SearchBot does. Many security plugins and hosting firewalls block unknown bots by default, so this is worth checking rather than assuming.
Write facts as text.
Prices, service areas, opening hours, languages and qualifications belong in the page's text, not in an image or a PDF. Assistants quote what is written.
Expect to be invisible at first, and measure it.
Local Falcon analysed 189,905 ChatGPT results for restaurant searches in February 2026 and found that

of the restaurants it tracks never appeared in ChatGPT's local recommendations, against 14% invisible on Google. That is a vendor study of one industry and a non-random sample, so treat the exact figure carefully — but the direction is consistent with what anyone testing this finds. The way to know is to ask: take five questions your customers would ask, put them to ChatGPT and Google's AI Mode while logged out, and write down who gets named and which sites get cited.
How ChatGPT chooses what to cite is a subject of its own, and I go through it in
ChatGPT SEO
SEO or Google Ads for a small business: cost and timing
They are not alternatives; they work on different clocks.

cells: Across 13,474 US campaigns in LocaliQ's 2026 benchmarks, the average click cost **$5.42** and the average lead **$66.69**. Stops the day the budget does
Your time, or a monthly fee
First movement in about six weeks
Keeps working when you stop paying; slower in contested services and cities
Within days of being complete and correct
The highest return of the three for a local business, and the most often neglected

children.text: For most small businesses the sensible mix is a complete profile first, because it is free and fast; then SEO for the services you want more of; and ads only for the gaps that are urgent.
How long small business SEO takes
Honest expectations, from the only large study of this I trust:
Ahrefs looked at 1.3 million US keywords and found that
of pages in the top ten are more than three years old, that the average page at position one is about five years old, and that only
of top-ten pages are under a year old. Of a million URLs first seen in September 2023,
reached the top ten within a year — but of the pages that did get there,
managed it within the first month.

That last number is the useful one. Ranking is not a slow grind for every page: it either happens fairly quickly for a page aimed at something winnable, or it does not happen at all for a page aimed at something that was never within reach. Which is the argument for choosing narrow targets at the start.

Google's own guidance agrees on the shape: «Some changes might take effect in a few hours, others could take several months», and «you likely want to wait a few weeks to assess whether your work had beneficial effects».
In my own work the pattern is consistent: first movements at about six weeks, meaningful growth between three and six months, longer in contested markets.
How much small business SEO costs
There is no standard price, but there is a distribution. Ahrefs polled 439 SEO providers and verified their sites: the most common monthly retainer was
, and

charged $2,000 a month or less. The most common hourly rate was $75–$100, and the most common project price $2,501–$5,000. That poll was run in 2023 and updated in 2024, so read it as the shape of the market rather than today's exact numbers.
For comparison, my own: an audit from €250 one-off, ongoing work from €800 a month. The
pricing page
lists what each includes, and
how much SEO costs
goes through what drives the number up or down.

Three things are worth paying for even on a small budget: an audit that tells you whether search is a realistic channel for your business at all, the one-off technical fixes it finds, and someone to write the service pages properly if writing is not your strength. Everything else in this guide you can do yourself.
Myths: the 80/20 rule, the three C's, and «SCO»
Three things people search for in this topic that deserve a straight answer:
«What is the 80/20 rule in SEO?»

This is the Pareto principle — the general observation that a small share of causes produces most of the effect — applied to SEO by marketers. It appears nowhere in Google's documentation and rests on no SEO-specific study. As a reminder to do the few things that matter it is fine. As a law about search it is not one.
«What are the three C's of SEO?»

Usually given as content, code and credibility. The framing is traceable to Kent Lewis of Anvil Media, writing in SEMA News in September 2011. It is a useful way to organise a conversation and it is not a Google concept.
«What does SCO mean in business?»
In searches about websites, it is almost always a typo for SEO. On its own, SCO usually refers to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, or to the Unix software company of the 1990s.
None of this matters much, except as a way to judge whoever you are reading. An article built on named frameworks and round-number rules is usually repeating other articles.
Small business SEO mistakes that cost customers
Keywords stuffed into the Google profile name.
Works briefly, then the profile is edited or suspended, and a suspension takes weeks to resolve.
A virtual office used to appear in another town.
Not eligible under Google's rules.
Town pages that differ only by the town name.
Doorway abuse under the spam policies.
Review gating
— asking only customers you expect to be happy. Explicitly prohibited.
Bought reviews.
Against Google's rules and, in most of Europe, against consumer law.
One page for everything you do.
It ranks for nothing.
A contact form nobody has tested since the site launched.
More leads are lost here than to any ranking problem.
Paying for AI optimization as a separate technical product.
Google's documentation says there are no additional technical requirements.
What to do yourself and when to hire someone

Google's own guidance on this is more direct than most consultants would like. From its page on whether you need an SEO, updated in June 2026: if you run a small local business, «you can probably do much of the work yourself».

That matches what I see. The profile, the reviews, the directory listings, the service pages and the answers to customer questions are decisions about your own business, and nobody knows them better than you. An evening a week for a couple of months covers most of it.

Outside help earns its money in four places: an audit that says plainly whether search can work for your business, technical fixes that need someone who can edit the site properly, writing in competitive services, and measurement that connects search to actual enquiries rather than to rankings. For a business this size that is usually one person rather than an agency — what that looks like in practice is on the
SEO consultant
page.
If you do hire someone, ask these:
Who exactly will do the work, and will you speak to that person?
What will be done in the first three months, page by page?
What do they measure — positions, or calls and enquiries?
Who owns the site, the content and the Google profile if you part ways?
Do they build links, and from where?
Be wary of guaranteed first places, year-long contracts signed before anything is shown, and anything that keeps your Google profile under an agency account.
Where to start with small business SEO this week

Open your Google Business Profile and compare the name with your signage; remove anything that is not your business's real name. Check the categories, the hours and the address. Then write down the three services you most want more of, search for each one with your town on your phone, and note who appears in the map and in the results.
Then ask your last five satisfied customers for a review, with a direct link, by text message.
Those three steps cost nothing and take an evening. They also tell you where you stand, which is more than most audits do. If you want someone to look at the rest,
write to me
with your site, your main service and the area you cover, and I will tell you what I would do first — including, if that is the honest answer, that search is not your channel.

Customers who find you through search are looking for what you sell at the moment they need it, and they keep arriving after you stop paying — unlike ads, which stop the day the budget ends. In Clutch's 2025 survey of 406 small business owners, 40% of those with a website named SEO as their top source of leads.

On local buying searches the map still dominates — Whitespark found an AI Overview on 15% of «[service] in [city]» searches against a map block on 93%. title: Small Business SEO: A Step-by-Step Guide You Can Do Yourself

children.text: Quick answer: A small business website in 2026 costs anywhere from almost nothing to tens of thousands, and the spread is not a mystery — it tracks who does the work and how much of it there is. Doing it yourself on a website builder costs a subscription and your weekends. One freelancer or a small studio building a custom site for a small business usually starts in the high hundreds of euros and runs into the low thousands. An agency starts where that ends. On top of whatever you pay once, every website has a running cost that nobody puts in the quote: a domain, hosting, email, and whatever you pay someone to keep it working. My own starting price is €700 with design included, and the rest of this article is about why the same site can cost ten times that somewhere else.

The honest problem with this question is that most answers to it are written by someone selling the answer. Website builders publish articles concluding that websites are cheap. Agencies publish articles concluding that cheap websites are expensive. Both are right about the other and wrong about themselves.

I build small business websites for a living, so I am not neutral either. What I can do instead is show you the whole structure of the cost — including the parts that appear a year later — and tell you my prices plainly, so you can measure everything else against something concrete.
What a small business website costs in 2026: the four price bands
There are four ways a small business ends up with a website, and they cost very different amounts for reasons that are not arbitrary.

picture.alt: Four ways to get a small business website — do it yourself on a builder, a template set up for you, one developer building a custom site, an agency — with what each includes, what it costs once, and what it costs every year after

contentBlocks.title: Four ways to get a small business website — do it yourself o

children.text: Building it yourself on a website builder: a subscription plus your weekends

You pay a monthly subscription and nothing else, apart from your own time. The real cost here is the time: a first website takes most owners several weekends, and the second half of that time goes on things that have nothing to do with design — writing the text, deciding what the pages should be, finding photographs that are yours to use.

This band is genuinely the right answer for some businesses, and I would rather say so than sell you something you do not need. If your customers all find you through a map listing and a social account, and the website only has to exist so that there is somewhere to send them, a builder does that job for the price of a coffee a month.
Having a template installed for you: the cheapest way to look professional
A freelancer, often found on a marketplace, installs a theme, puts your logo and text in and hands it over. This is the cheapest way to get something that does not look homemade.

It is also where most of the disappointments live, and the reason is specific rather than snobbish: what you bought was an installation, not a design. Nothing in it was decided for your business. The pages are the ones the theme came with, which is why so many of these sites have a «Team» page with one person on it and a «Portfolio» page with stock photographs — the structure was built for somebody else and nobody adjusted it to you.
One person building a custom site: where the price starts to mean something

A freelancer or a very small studio works out what pages you need, writes or edits the text with you, designs it around your actual services, and builds it. This is my band, and it starts at €700 with design included.

The number varies with how many pages there are and whether anything has to be connected to anything else, not with how impressive the invoice looks. The thing you are really buying is that someone decided what the site should be before building it, and that the person who decided is the person who built.
An agency building it: a team, and the cost of coordinating one

You get an account manager, a designer, a developer, sometimes a copywriter and a project manager. For a company with a marketing department and a brand to protect, that structure earns its money: it has capacity, it covers for illness, and it does not depend on one person's week.

For a business with eight services and one owner, you are paying for coordination between people who could have been one person. That is the trade, stated plainly, and it is worth making deliberately rather than by default.

The bands overlap at the edges, and a good freelancer can cost more than a bad agency. But the shape holds: what you are mostly buying as you move up the scale is not quality of code. It is how many people are involved and how much of the thinking is done for you.
What you are actually paying for when you buy a website
A website quote looks like a price for a thing. It is really a price for a stack of decisions, and the decisions are where the hours go.
Working out what the site has to do.

How a visitor is supposed to become an enquiry, which services deserve a page, what someone needs to know before they call. An hour of this changes the whole build; skipping it is why some sites look good and bring nothing.
The pages themselves.
A service page that answers a customer's first three questions takes real work. A page that says «we offer this service» takes none, which is why cheap sites have so many of them.
The text.
The most underestimated line in any quote. If the price seems low, check whether you are expected to supply every word.
The design.
Not decoration — the decisions about what the visitor sees first, what the buttons say, how it behaves in one hand on a phone.
The build.
Making it fast, making the phone number dial on tap, making the form actually arrive somewhere a human reads.
Setting it up to be found.
Titles, descriptions, a sitemap, the technical basics so Google can read it. Not a marketing campaign — the groundwork without which the rest is invisible.
Handover.
Whether you can change a price or add a page without paying someone.
When two quotes differ by a factor of five, the difference is almost always in the first and third items: who decides what the site should be, and who writes it.
Is $1,500 a fair price for a website?
This question comes up so often that Google lists it among the things people also ask, and it deserves a straight answer rather than «it depends».

At that level you are buying one person's time, roughly a working week of it. That is enough for a well-made small site: a handful of pages, your own text edited rather than written from scratch, a design built around your services rather than picked from a gallery, and a proper technical setup. It is not enough for a shop, a booking system, three languages, or a site where someone researches your market for you.

So $1,500 is a fair price for the thing it buys. It becomes a bad price in two situations: when it buys a template installation that was dressed up as a design, and when it buys a custom build that genuinely needed twice the hours, in which case the corners come out of the parts you cannot see — the text, the speed, the setup.

The useful question is not whether the number is fair. It is what is inside it. A quote that lists the pages it covers, says who writes the text and names what happens after launch can be judged. A quote that says «website — $1,500» cannot be judged at any price.
What a five-page website costs, page by page
«What is the average cost of a 5 page website?» is another of those questions, and the framing is where it goes wrong: websites are not priced by the page, because pages are not the same size.

A home page is the most expensive thing on a small site — it has to say who you are, what you do, where you work and why someone should call, in the space of one screen on a phone. A contact page is the cheapest. A service page sits in between and varies enormously: «window cleaning» and «commercial lease review» are both one page, and one of them needs a lawyer's worth of explanation.

In practice a five-page site means a home page, two or three service pages, an about page and a contact page. That is the standard shape of a small business site and it is what a starting price like mine covers. Where it stops being five pages is the moment someone says «and could each city have its own page» or «and could clients log in» — both reasonable, neither five pages.
If a quote prices per page, ask what happens when one page turns out to need three times the text. The answer tells you whether the price is a price or an opening position.
The costs that are not in the quote: domain, hosting, email and certificates
Every website has running costs that exist whoever built it, and the most common unpleasant surprise in this whole topic is a renewal invoice for something the owner thought was included.

picture.alt: What you pay once versus what you pay every year — the build on one side, and on the other the domain with its renewal price, hosting, business email and the certificate that costs nothing

contentBlocks.title: What you pay once versus what you pay every year — the build

children.text: The domain.

Rented yearly, never bought. The thing to watch is that first-year prices and renewal prices are usually different, sometimes very different, and the gap is wider on local extensions than on .com. Before you register anything, look up the renewal price, not the offer price — it is on the same page, usually in smaller type. Register it in your own name, with your own email. A domain in a contractor's account is the single most expensive mistake in this list, because you cannot negotiate with someone who holds it.
Hosting.

Shared hosting is cheap and slow. Managed hosting for a specific platform costs more and takes the maintenance off you. Modern platform hosting of the kind I build on has free tiers that genuinely cover a small business site, which is why hosting is sometimes a line that honestly reads zero.
Email on your own domain.
Not the same thing as hosting, and worth paying for: a contact address at your own domain, not a free webmail address, is read differently by customers and by spam filters alike.
The certificate that makes the padlock appear.

Free, from Let's Encrypt, and automatic on any serious host. If a quote has a line item for an SSL certificate, ask about it — not because paid certificates are a scam, but because a small business site almost never needs one.
Backups.
Often included, occasionally not, and you will only find out which on the day you need one.
Laid out as a budget, the running side of a small business site looks like this:

cells: No — and watch the renewal price, not the first-year offer
Sometimes, on a modern platform's free tier
Possible, but a free webmail address costs you credibility
Often included; confirm rather than assume
Yes, and on a simple site it often is

children.text: The first line is the one to get right on day one. The rest can be changed later; a domain in someone else's account cannot be, except on their terms.
How much a website costs per month after launch
«How much does a website cost per month» is one of the biggest questions in this topic by search volume, and the answer splits into two very different halves.
The first half is the running costs above — domain, hosting, email. These are real, small, and unavoidable.
When a monthly support fee is worth paying, and when it is not
The second half is whatever you pay a person, and here I will say something against my own interest:
for a well-built small business site, this is often zero.

A site that does not run plugins, does not run an outdated content system and does not do anything complicated can go for months with nothing needing to be done to it. Support is worth paying for when something actually needs doing, not as a standing charge against the possibility.

A monthly fee is worth it when the work is real: regular changes, a shop with stock, staff and prices that move, a site that genuinely breaks. It is also worth it when the alternative is that nothing ever gets changed — plenty of small business sites are three years out of date because every edit meant an email, and a small retainer would have kept them current.

A monthly fee that buys «updates and monitoring» on a five-page brochure site is a different thing. It is buying the absence of a problem you did not have, and the honest version of it is an arrangement where you are billed when there is work and not billed when there is none.
Why the maintenance cost depends on what the site was built on
The reason two identical-looking sites can cost very different amounts to keep alive is underneath them.

A site built on a content system with a dozen plugins has a dozen things that update, occasionally break each other, and need somebody watching. That is genuine ongoing work and it is fair to charge for it. A site built as plain, modern pages with nothing bolted on has almost nothing to go wrong, which is why its maintenance line can honestly read zero.

This is worth asking about before you commit, not after: what is this built on, what has to be kept updated, and what happens if nobody updates it for a year. An answer of «nothing much» is a real feature with a real monetary value, and it rarely appears in the quote as one.
What is a different thing entirely, and what does need a monthly commitment, is getting found — that is ongoing work with a clock on it rather than maintenance, and
how much SEO costs
goes through it separately.
Website builder, freelancer or agency: what each costs over three years
One-off prices make builders look free and custom sites look expensive. Three years is a fairer frame, because that is roughly how long a small business site lives before it needs reworking.

columns: What you own at the end

children.text: The row that surprises people is the first one. A builder subscription is small, but it never stops, it goes up with every feature you turn out to need, and at the end of it you cannot take the site with you. That is not an argument against builders — for a business whose customers all come from Instagram and a map listing, a builder is the right answer and I will say so. It is an argument against comparing a subscription to a one-off price as though they were the same kind of number.
Why the same website costs €700 from one person and €7,000 from an agency
Not because one of them is lying. Because the money is doing different things.

In a one-person build, nearly all the money is the work. In an agency build, a large share is coordination: the account manager who talks to you, the project manager who talks to the designer, the designer who talks to the developer, and the time lost in the gaps between them. That structure buys real things — capacity, cover when someone is ill, a process that does not depend on one person's mood — and for a company that needs those things it is worth paying for.

For a small business with a handful of services, it mostly buys the translation layer between you and the person doing the work. That is why I work the way I do: the person who quotes is the person who builds, which removes the step that costs the most and loses the most meaning. What it looks like in practice is on the
small business website design
page, and the trade-off I will not pretend away is capacity — one person has a queue, and an agency does not. The same comparison applied to search work rather than building is on the
SEO consultant
page.
What you cannot buy back later: the domain, the text and the code
There is a category of cost that never appears in any quote and only arrives when you try to leave, and it is worth more attention than the price itself.

If the domain is registered in the builder's name, you do not own your address. If the site was built on a platform you cannot export, the three years of text you paid for come out as a copy-paste job. If nobody wrote down where the hosting account is, the day you need to move it becomes an archaeology project.

None of this is sinister — most of it happens by accident, because nobody asked at the start. Ask at the start. The three questions are: whose name is on the domain, can the site and its content be exported, and who holds the hosting account. A straight answer to all three costs nothing and is worth more than a discount.
What pushes the price up: languages, bookings, payments and integrations
Most of the spread above the starting price comes from a short list of things, and each one is a genuine multiplier rather than a markup.
A second or third language.

Not translation — a second set of pages that has to be written for that market, kept in step with the first, and told apart by search engines. This is the single most common reason a small site stops being a small site, and it is usually worth it when the second audience is real.
Booking or appointments.
Taking a time slot is simple. Taking a time slot that respects staff schedules, holidays, buffers and cancellations is not.
Payments.
A link to pay is easy. A checkout with stock, delivery options and invoices is a different product.
Connecting to something you already use.
A calendar, a CRM, an accounting system, a supplier's catalogue. The cost depends entirely on the other system's willingness, which nobody can tell you until they look.
A lot of similar pages.
Services across many towns, a catalogue, a team of fifteen. Each page is cheap; a hundred of them is not.
Content you do not have.
Photographs, texts, case descriptions. If you cannot supply these, someone has to make them, and that is a separate job with a separate price.

When a quote is higher than you expected, the fastest way to understand it is to ask which of these is in there. If none of them is, the number is about hours, not features — and then the question is what those hours are being spent on.
Can ChatGPT or an AI builder make your website for free?
People genuinely ask this now — it sits in Google's own list of related questions — and the answer has changed enough in two years to be worth stating carefully.

An AI tool will produce you a website. It will be structurally fine, generic in its text, and indistinguishable from the thousands of others produced the same way that week. For a side project or a page that exists so a link has somewhere to point, that may be all you need, and I would not argue with it.

Two things make it a poor foundation for a business that wants customers from search. The first is that the text is the part that makes a page worth finding, and generic text is exactly what a search engine has no reason to rank. The second is explicit in Google's spam policies, last updated on 28 August 2026, which name as
scaled content abuse

the practice of «using generative AI tools or other similar tools to generate many pages without adding value for users». The test there is not which tool was used — it is whether the page is worth reading.

Where AI genuinely saves money on a website project is in the middle of it, not instead of it: first drafts, structure, rewriting your own rough text into something publishable. That is the part owners find hardest and it is the part these tools are actually good at.
How much a website costs in your industry

Price depends on trade more than people expect, because different businesses need different things from a site before it works at all. A restaurant needs a menu that can be changed from a phone; a clinic needs doctors, licences and a booking flow; a construction company needs projects with photographs and a way to be found in the towns it builds in.

picture.alt: What changes the price from one trade to another — a salon needing bookings and a price list that changes weekly, a clinic needing credentials and a careful first contact, a builder needing projects and service areas, a developer needing stage-by-stage material

If your trade is not there, the structure in this article still holds; what changes is which of the multipliers above applies to you.
How to read a website quote and what to ask before you sign

picture.alt: A website quote with five things marked as present — the named pages, who writes the text, who owns the domain and code, what you can change yourself, what happens after launch — and the same quote with those lines missing, reduced to one line and a number

contentBlocks.title: A website quote with five things marked as present — the nam

children.text: A quote you can judge has five things in it. Ask for whichever are missing, and treat reluctance as information.
The list of pages.
Named, not counted. «Five pages» and «home, two services, about, contact» are different promises.
Who writes the text.
The most common gap between a cheap quote and a cheap-looking result.
Who owns what afterwards.
The domain, the hosting account, the code, the content. All of it should end up in your name, and the time to establish that is before, not after.
What you can change yourself.
Prices, opening hours, a new service — can you, or is each one an email and an invoice?
What happens after launch.
What is covered, for how long, and what costs extra.
Two more worth asking out loud: can I see something you built that is still live and still being used, and what happens if we stop working together. Both answers tell you more than the price does.
What I charge for a small business website and what is included
My own numbers, so you have something fixed to measure the rest against.
A small business website starts at
€700, with design included

— I do not sell design as a separate line, because a site designed by one person and built by another costs more and fits worse. That covers the standard shape: a home page, service pages, about and contact, written with you rather than handed to you as a form to fill in, built to load fast and to be contacted from a phone in one tap. A business-card site is normally ready in two to three weeks.
The price moves with the multipliers above, and I will tell you which one is moving it before you commit to anything.
An
SEO audit is €250
, one-off — worth doing before a rebuild rather than after, because it tells you which pages already have value worth keeping.
Ongoing search work starts at €800 a month

, and that is a different service with a different clock: first movements at about a month and a half, meaningful growth between three and six months. Invoices are in euros, or another currency by agreement. The
pricing page
lists what each includes.
What I do not charge for is a monthly fee on a site that does not need one. If nothing needs doing in a given month, nothing is billed.
What to do before you ask anyone for a price

Write down the services you want more of, in the words your customers use. Write down what someone needs to know before they call you. Find out who currently holds your domain, if you have one — the answer is sometimes a surprise.

With those three things, any quote you get becomes comparable, because you are asking everyone the same question. Without them, you are collecting numbers for different things and lining them up as though they were the same.
If you want a number from me,
write to me

with your services, the towns you work in and a link to whatever you have now — a site, a social profile, a map listing. I will tell you what I would build, what it would cost and what I would leave out, including the cases where the honest answer is that you need a map listing and a phone number rather than a website.

For a small business with a handful of services, a custom site from one person starts in the high hundreds of euros — mine from €700 with design included — and rises with languages, bookings, payments and the number of pages. An agency for the same brief starts several times higher, because a share of that price is coordination rather than work.

children.text: It is about a week of one person's time, which is enough for a well-made small site with your own text edited and a design built around your services. It is not enough for a shop, a booking system or three languages. Judge the quote by what it lists, not by the number.

children.text: The unavoidable part is a domain, hosting and email, and it is small. Beyond that, a well-built small site often needs nothing monthly at all. Pay for support when there is work to do, not as a standing charge.

children.text: Yes, every year, and it should be registered in your name. Check the renewal price rather than the first-year offer — they are often very different, and the gap is wider on local extensions.

items.question: Do I have to pay for the domain separately?

children.text: Over three years, usually not as much cheaper as it looks, because the subscription never stops and rises as you need more. The real difference is ownership: you can move a custom site; a builder site has to be rebuilt to move.

items.question: Is a website builder cheaper than a custom site?

children.text: Most small business sites run three to five years before the design starts working against them. A rebuild driven by a date rather than a problem is usually money spent to feel current.

items.question: How often should a website be redesigned?

children.text: You can get a page that exists. What costs money is the part that makes it bring customers: deciding what it should say, writing it, and setting it up to be found. That part does not have a free version, only a do-it-yourself one.

items.question: Can I get a website for free?

children.text: Not by being cheap. It hurts when the corners were cut in the invisible parts — thin or generic text, slow loading, no technical setup. What to do about that is in the
small business SEO guide
, and most of it you can do yourself.

children.text: Quick answer: an SEO audit is a measurement of a website against its own search data and its own market, ending in a written plan. A useful audit contains four things for every problem it reports: the measurement with the source and the date it was taken, the cause, the action, and the result to expect with the condition that result depends on. It is not a list of everything wrong with the site, and a good one often removes planned work instead of adding it. A full audit takes two to five days and costs around 250 euro for a small site.

Most people meet the SEO audit as a PDF full of red warnings from a crawler, with no indication of which warning matters or what to do first. That document costs the same as a real audit, which is why it is worth being precise about what the money buys. You are not paying for the list of problems — a free tool produces that in four minutes. You are paying for someone to measure your site against your own data, decide which of the problems is worth your time, say what each fix should change and by when, and tell you which of the work you were planning not to do. This article goes through each of those, shows what the finished report has to contain, and ends with the cases where you should not buy one at all. Everything is illustrated with a real audit of a live site with 645 pages in three languages,
which you can download in full
What an SEO audit is, and what it is not

An SEO audit is a measurement of one website against three things: the search data the site already generates, the pages it actually has, and the live search results it competes in. The output is not a diagnosis. The output is an ordered plan in which every line says what was measured, why it is that way, what to do about it, and what should happen afterwards.

A website audit is the broader name for the same thing, and the words are used interchangeably. Where they differ in practice is scope: a technical audit stops at crawling and code, while an SEO audit has to include demand and intent, because a technically perfect page aimed at the wrong searcher still earns nothing.

Three things an audit is not. It is not a crawler report: a crawler finds broken links and missing tags, which is maybe a tenth of the work and the only tenth a machine can do alone. It is not a keyword list: volume says how many people search, not who they are or whether they would ever buy from you. And it is not a ranking promise: anyone who commits to a position in a month is selling you the first visible movement twice.
What is included in an SEO audit: the six things that get measured
Every number in a real audit has a source and a date, so the client can open the same place and check it. In the sample audit shipped with this article, six sources were used.
Search Console, a full quarter.
Impressions, clicks, average position and the exact query text, per page and per language. In the sample site: 19,440 impressions, 3 clicks, and 559 of 645 pages with any impressions at all.
Every page, read from the content system.

Title, meta title, meta description, H1 and every H2 and H3 of all 645 pages, plus the block structure of each. This is what makes statements like «62 headings are labels» countable rather than impressionistic.
The site's own keyword plan, reconciled against reality.

Each query the site intends to answer, checked against the page that is supposed to answer it. In the sample: 1,328 assignments, of which the head query of the entire niche pointed at an unrelated page.
Live search results, read for intent.

The top ten for each query family the site targets, read to establish one thing: is the searcher a business owner looking for a contractor, or their own customer? This is the step that decides what gets written and what does not.
Presence in AI answers.
Whether an AI answer appears for the queries the site targets, and whether the site is anywhere in the pool those answers are assembled from — the question an
AI visibility audit
exists to answer. In the sample: an AI answer showed on 304 of 321 query families, and the site was in the top ten of none of them.
Internal links and reachability.
Whether the pages can be reached and are actually being shown, and whether the links between them resolve.
Notice what is missing from that list: a tool score. No audit worth paying for reports a number out of 100, because that number is a weighted average of things that do not share a unit.
How an SEO audit is performed, step by step
The order matters more than the thoroughness, because early steps decide what later steps are even worth looking at.
Take the baseline.

Export the quarter of search data and write down the handful of numbers the whole audit will be measured against later. In the sample those were 19,440 impressions, 3 clicks and an average position of 53.6 on the single most-shown page.
Read the site as a machine reads it.

Pull every title, heading and meta field into one table. Patterns show up immediately at this stage that no page-by-page review would surface: the same six label headings repeated across dozens of pages, seventeen pages whose meta title repeats their H1 word for word.
Reconcile demand against pages.
For every query the site means to win, find the page that is supposed to win it. The gaps found here are the real work; the mismatches found here are usually the cheapest fix in the whole report.
Check intent in the live results, not in the tool.
For each query family, look at who ranks. Four or more shared domains across a family means one page can serve all of it; zero or one means these are different searches wearing similar words.
Separate what you measured from what you concluded.
The impression count is a fact. «The page ranks badly because its headings do not use the query wording» is a hypothesis. A report that prints both in the same typeface is hiding the difference.
Rank by expected effect and attach a date.
Not by severity, and not by how easy the fix is: by what the fix should change, and when you will be able to see whether it did.
What an SEO audit report looks like: a real example you can download

An SEO audit report is the deliverable, so it is fair to judge the whole service by it. A sample audit report is attached to this article as a PDF, sixteen pages, covering a real trilingual site whose address is withheld. Rather than describe it, here is what each page of it has to contain.

picture.alt: The five parts of one audit finding: measurement, cause, action, expected result with its condition, and the date to check it

contentBlocks.title: The five parts of one audit finding: measurement, cause, act

children.text: Every finding gets a page of its own, and that page has five parts: the measurement with its source and date, the cause as the author reads it, the action with the hours it costs, the expected result with the condition it depends on, and the date on which the client may check it. If any one of those five is missing, the finding cannot be acted on or verified.

The report also contains three things that most templates leave out. A section on what the site already does right, because knowing which defects are absent is worth as much as knowing which are present. A section on what was deliberately not recommended and why, which in the sample covers four items including a migration that an audit script flagged as a defect and the live pages proved harmless. And a section on where the audit was wrong before it was right: three claims that the data corrected before they reached the client, and three measuring instruments that produced false results until they were calibrated.

That last section is the one worth insisting on when you commission an audit. An auditor who cannot name a place where their first reading was wrong either did not check their own work or is not telling you about it.
Can ChatGPT do an SEO audit?
It can do the reading, and it cannot do the measuring. That distinction is the whole answer.

An assistant can read your pages and tell you that a heading is vague, that a meta description is too long, that a paragraph buries its point. That is genuinely useful and it is roughly the top tenth of an audit. What it cannot do is open your Search Console and see that one page collected 2,613 impressions at position 53.6 and earned nothing from them, because it has no access to your data. It cannot tell you that a query family with 2,900 monthly searches is worthless to you, because that requires looking at who currently ranks and deciding who the searcher is. And it cannot attach a date and a condition to a prediction, because it is not going to be there in six weeks to be wrong.

There is a sharper version of this problem. Ask an assistant to audit a site and it will produce a plausible, well-organised document, because producing plausible, well-organised documents is exactly what it is good at. The failure mode is not nonsense, it is confident generality: advice that is true of every website and therefore decides nothing about yours. The test is simple. Open any claim in the document and ask where the number came from and on what date. If there is no answer, you are holding a very good essay about SEO.

Used properly, an assistant is an instrument inside the audit rather than a substitute for it, and like every instrument it needs calibrating before you trust it. In the sample audit, a link checker reported all 29 internal links broken because the phrase it searched for appears on every page of that site, and a results reader reported the same domain for every result because the results were wrapped in redirects. Both were caught by testing them against a case with a known answer first.
Is an SEO audit just a list of what is wrong with the site?
That is what a scan produces, and it is why audits have the reputation they have. The difference is that a finding is not a defect, it is a defect plus a consequence plus a price.

Take the strongest finding in the sample audit. A service page was shown 2,613 times in a quarter at an average position of 53.6 and received zero clicks. The scan version of that finding is «page ranks poorly». The audit version is: 64 queries are already matched to this page, position 53 is page six where the click-through rate is effectively zero, the headings name the service but not the city, the price or the question people actually typed, rewriting them is three to four hours of work with no development, and the page should move into the 25 to 30 range within six to eight weeks, which is where the first clicks begin. If it has not moved by week eight, the text was not the ceiling and the next step is a different one.
Everything in that second version can be argued with, which is the point. A list of what is wrong cannot be argued with, and that is its weakness, not its strength.
Is an SEO audit a way to create work for the consultant?
It is a fair suspicion, and there is a test for it: look at whether the audit ever recommends less.

picture.alt: An audit that removed work: of 978 planned pages, 623 were cancelled and 41 survived; 176,000 of 182,410 monthly searches were struck out

contentBlocks.title: An audit that removed work: of 978 planned pages, 623 were c

children.text: In the sample audit, the plan it inherited contained 978 pages to create, covering 3,190 monthly searches. Checking the live results for the query families behind them showed that nine of those clusters were aimed at the wrong person entirely. «Website for a restaurant» sounds like a restaurant owner looking for a developer; the top ten is restaurant sites and ordering platforms, so the searcher wants dinner. Real estate agents, plumbers, manufacturers and therapists all failed the same way. Nine clusters and 176,000 monthly searches were struck out, 623 of the 978 planned pages were cancelled, and what remained was 41 pages worth about 6,400 searches a month.

The work that audit removed is larger than the work it recommends. An audit that cannot do that for you — that returns a longer task list than the one you walked in with, every single time — is not measuring anything.

There is a smaller version of the same test. Ask what the auditor chose not to recommend. In the sample, the largest single block of impressions on the entire site, 2,487 of them at an average position of 77.7, was deliberately left alone: at that position and that breadth, the competition at the top is national and established, the text is not what holds the page back, and rewriting it would change nothing the auditor could promise in advance.
What an SEO audit costs and how long it takes
A full audit of a small site
costs around 250 euro and takes two to five working days. The range is driven by page count and by how many languages the site runs, because every language multiplies the reading, not the thinking.

What the price should include: the measurement with sources, the ordered plan, the expected result per action, and a follow-up conversation once you have read it. What it should not include is implementation — those are different jobs with different prices, and bundling them is how an audit turns into a sales document for the work it recommends.

A free automated audit has its place: it will find broken links and missing tags in a few minutes, and if that is all your site needs, you have saved yourself the fee. It will not tell you which of its findings matters, and it will never tell you not to write 623 pages.
When you do not need an SEO audit
Four situations where the honest answer is to spend the money elsewhere.
The site is brand new and has almost no pages.
There is nothing to measure yet. Write the pages for the queries you already know you serve, give it a quarter, then audit against real data.
You already know what is broken and have not fixed it.
If three people have told you the site is slow and the product pages have no text, an audit will tell you the same thing with better formatting. Fix the known things first; audit what remains.
Nobody is going to do the work.
An audit whose plan nobody has time to implement is an expensive document. If there is no implementation budget and no in-house hands, buy a smaller piece of actual work instead.
Your problem is not search.
If the enquiries arrive and do not convert, or the pricing is wrong, or the product is not wanted, more search visibility makes the loss larger, not smaller.

There is a fifth, less obvious case: you have had an audit in the last six months and acted on none of it. A second audit of the same site measures the same things and recommends the same actions, which is why a serious auditor will ask what happened to the first one before quoting for a second.
What to ask for before you pay for an SEO audit
Five questions that separate a measurement from a template.
Where does each number come from, and on what date was it taken?
If the answer is not a named source and a date, it is not a measurement.
Which findings are measurements and which are your interpretation?
Both are legitimate. Mixing them silently is not.
What result do you expect from each action, and by when?
Including what would prove the prediction wrong.
What are you deliberately not recommending?
A report with no such section has not made any choices.
Will you tell me where your first reading was wrong?
This is the one that cannot be answered with a template.

If the answers are good, you will be able to act on the document alone, including with someone else doing the implementation. That is the actual test of an audit: it should be useful even if you never hire the person who wrote it.

children.text: (Kompleksowy przewodnik dla właścicieli stron i przedsiębiorców)

SEO to nie tylko optymalizacja techniczna strony. To strategia pozyskiwania ruchu organicznego, zwiększania widoczności i generowania wartościowych kontaktów (leadów). Dobrze wykonane SEO może stać się kluczowym źródłem wzrostu biznesu. Natomiast złe SEO to często wydawanie budżetu bez realnych efektów.

Wielu właścicieli firm nie potrafi odróżnić rzetelnej pracy SEO od powierzchownych działań, które wyglądają na aktywność, ale nie prowadzą do wzrostu ruchu ani leadów. Ten artykuł pomaga jasno zdefiniować sygnały ostrzegawcze i dać praktyczne wskazówki, jak ocenić jakość specjalisty SEO.
Na czym polega dobra praca SEO?
Aby rozpoznać, kiedy wykonawca jest kiepski, najpierw warto zrozumieć, jak wygląda praca profesjonalisty.
Dobry specjalista SEO:
Przeprowadza analizę konkurencji i szerokie badanie słów kluczowych
Tworzy strategię słów kluczowych obejmującą zapytania o dużym, średnim i niskim wolumenie
Optymalizuje aspekty techniczne, treści i doświadczenie użytkownika
Łączy działania SEO z realnymi celami biznesowymi
Raportuje wyniki za pomocą konkretnych KPI
Kluczowa różnica:
rezultat > wykonane działania
Dlaczego niektórzy specjaliści SEO zawodzą?
Błędny SEO-owiec często skupia się na czynnościach zamiast efektach:
tworzy raporty oparte na wykonanych zadaniach, a nie wyniku,
obiecuje TOP w wyszukiwarkach bez uzasadnienia,
ignoruje metryki biznesowe takie jak leady czy konwersje,
nie dopasowuje pracy do Twoich celów.
Przyjrzyjmy się temu bliżej.
Główne sygnały, że masz do czynienia z kiepskim SEO-specjalistą
1. Raporty pełne technicznych działań, bez wyników
Często raporty zawierają opisy wykonanych prac, np.:
„zastosowano pogrubienie tekstu”,
„wysłano stronę do ponownej indeksacji”,
„zaktualizowano meta-tagi”.
Takie informacje mogą być poprawne technicznie, ale same w sobie nie pokazują postępu.
Prawdziwy raport SEO powinien zawierać:
Trendy ruchu organicznego
Pozycje w wyszukiwarce dla kluczowych zapytań
Dane o konwersjach i leadach
Informacje o zachowaniu użytkowników
2. Brak jasnych KPI i metryk biznesowych
Jeśli raporty to tylko lista zadań bez powiązania z wynikami (np. wzrostem ruchu, liczbą leadów czy konwersji), to znak, że praca nie jest skuteczna.
Najważniejsze KPI, które specjalista SEO powinien monitorować:
liczba odwiedzin organicznych,
widoczność w wyszukiwarkach,
konwersje z ruchu organicznego,
czas spędzony na stronie i inne zachowania użytkowników.
3. Obietnice „gwarantowanego TOP-u” w Google
Żaden ekspert SEO
nie może zagwarantować konkretnych pozycji
w wynikach wyszukiwania — algorytmy są zbyt złożone i dynamiczne.
Profesjonalista:
wyjaśnia strategię i działania,
prezentuje realistyczne cele,
opiera się na wynikach i danych.
POZYCJA to środek, cel to
ruch i leady
4. Ignorowanie słów kluczowych o niskiej częstotliwości (long-tail)
Wysokie słowa kluczowe są ważne, ale te o mniejszej częstotliwości często przynoszą bardziej sprecyzowany i wartościowy ruch.
Dobra strategia SEO obejmuje:
słowa o dużym wolumenie,
średnim wolumenie,
niskim i komercyjnym wolumenie.
Jeśli specjalista pomija ten ostatni obszar — traci szansę na konwersje.
5. Brak analizy konkurencji i strategii
SEO bez analizy konkurencji to praca na oślep. Profesjonalista powinien znać:
grupę docelową,
kontekst rynkowy,
strategie rywali online.
Brak tych analiz to sygnał braku kompetencji.
Jak ocenić usługę SEO — praktyczny check-list
Oceń, czy specjalista:
Posiada dobrze udokumentowaną strategię słów kluczowych.
Raportuje wyniki ruchu i pozycji.
Uwzględnia konwersje i leady w raportach.
Analizuje konkurencję.
Komunikuje się regularnie i konkretnie.
Jeśli te elementy są pominięte, prawdopodobnie płacisz tylko za zadania, a nie wyniki.
Najczęstsze pytania o wybór specjalisty SEO
Zwykle już po 1–3 miesiącach współpracy powinieneś widzieć:
raporty z KPI,
wyjaśnienia działań,
pierwsze sygnały wzrostów (nawet minimalne).
Jeśli dostajesz tylko listy zadań — to znak ostrzegawczy.

items.question: Jak szybko można stwierdzić, że SEO-owiec pracuje źle?

children.text: Tak. Badanie słów kluczowych to fundament pracy SEO i powinno być transparentne.

items.question: Czy SEO-owiec powinien udostępniać listę słów kluczowych?

children.text: Nie. Nikt nie może zagwarantować pozycji, ale można obiecać strategię i realistyczne cele związane z ruchem i leadami.

items.question: Czy można obiecać pozycje w TOP10?

children.text: Raporty wartościowe to takie, które pokazują:
wzrost organicznych odwiedzin,
zmiany w pozycjach słów kluczowych,
wzrost leadów i konwersji,
zachowania użytkowników.

items.question: Jakie raporty są wartościowe?

children.text: SEO to proces długoterminowy, ale brak transparentnych danych i analiz to problem. Jeśli nie ma żadnych wyników — warto rozważyć audyt zewnętrzny.

items.question: Co jeśli wyników nie ma?

children.text: SEO powinno wspierać realne cele biznesowe, takie jak:
sprzedaż produktu,
wypełnienie formularza kontaktowego,
umówienie wizyty.
Na przykład: jeśli Twoja strona oferuje zakup nieruchomości, kluczowy KPI to liczba zakupów i zapytań, a nie tylko ranking.

items.question: Dlaczego SEO musi być powiązane z celami biznesowymi?

children.text: Co powinno się liczyć w SEO
SEO
to nie zadania do odhaczenia — to struktura pracy prowadząca do realnych rezultatów.
Kiepski SEO-owiec:
skupia się na raportach i zadaniach,
ignoruje KPI i biznesowe cele,
obiecuje TOP bez realnych planów.
Dobry SEO-owiec:
buduje strategię zgodną z celami Twojej firmy,
raportuje efekty, nie czynności,
tłumaczy każdy krok i decyzję.
Jeśli widzisz, że twoje SEO nie przynosi ruchu, leadów ani wzrostu konwersji i nie możesz tego przełożyć na konkretne liczby — warto rozważyć zmianę wykonawcy.

title: Jak rozpoznać kiepskiego specjalistę SEO

children.text: W dobie zaawansowanych modeli sztucznej inteligencji (AI) — takich jak ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing Copilot, Gemini czy Perplexity — coraz więcej informacji o firmach i ekspertach pojawia się nie poprzez tradycyjne linki, lecz bezpośrednio w odpowiedziach generowanych przez system. To ogromna szansa, ale też nowe ryzyko: AI może „wymyślić” nieprawdziwe informacje o Twojej marce, które następnie trafiają do wyszukiwarek, asystentów głosowych i narzędzi analizujących dane.
Ten przewodnik wyjaśnia:
dlaczego tak się dzieje,
jakie to niesie konsekwencje dla Twojej firmy/brandu,
oraz jakie konkretne działania podjąć, by wykrywać, zapobiegać i korygować błędne odpowiedzi AI.
Czym są odpowiedzi generowane przez AI i dlaczego to ważne
Odpowiedź AI to fragment tekstu wygenerowany przez model językowy w odpowiedzi na zapytanie użytkownika. W przeciwieństwie do tradycyjnych wyników wyszukiwania, AI często prezentuje:
bezpośrednie odpowiedzi,
podsumowania informacji,
sugestie i rekomendacje.
Wyniki te mogą pojawiać się w:
sekcjach odpowiedzi w wynikach wyszukiwania (np. Google SGE),
chatowych interfejsach wyszukiwania,
narzędziach desktopowych i mobilnych.
Ponieważ użytkownicy często ufają takim odpowiedziom, błędne informacje o Twojej marce mogą stać się powszechnie postrzegane jako prawda, nawet jeśli Twoja strona zawiera poprawne dane.
Dlaczego AI czasem generuje błędne informacje o marce
AI nie weryfikuje faktów — opiera swoje odpowiedzi na analizie statystycznej danych, które poznał podczas treningu. Główne przyczyny błędów to:
Nieaktualne lub błędne dane treningowe
. Modele mogą bazować na stronach zawierających przestarzałe lub nieprawdziwe informacje.
Brak kontekstu i zrozumienia
. AI nie „rozumie” treści tak jak człowiek — interpretuje wzorce językowe.
Podobne nazwy i kontekstowe pomyłki
. Jeżeli inna marka lub osoba ma podobną nazwę, odpowiedź AI może złączyć różne dane.
Przewidywanie najbardziej prawdopodobnych słów
. Tam, gdzie brakuje jasnych danych, AI „zgaduje” i może wygenerować błędną treść.
Każda z tych sytuacji może doprowadzić do sytuacji, w której użytkownicy zobaczą fałszywe lub mylące informacje, zanim odwiedzą Twoją stronę.
Główne ryzyka nieprawidłowych odpowiedzi AI dla marki
Błędy AI nie są tylko błędami językowymi — mają realne konsekwencje biznesowe:
Utrata reputacji
: Niewłaściwe opisy usług lub historii firmy mogą obniżyć zaufanie potencjalnych klientów.
Negatywny wpływ na SEO
: Błędne odpowiedzi mogą być prezentowane w widocznych blokach wyników (np. Knowledge Panel), co obniża CTR i pozycje w wynikach organicznych.
Mylący komunikat dla odbiorców
: Użytkownicy mogą zrezygnować z wizyty na Twojej stronie.
Szybkie rozprzestrzenianie się błędów
